119 120 Our Culture, Values, and Talent Anthropic was founded by a team of researchers who believe that the most consequential technology in history demands an organization structurally committed to both capability and safety. That conviction reaches every dimension of the organization: how we hire staff, the research we perform, the policy positions we adopt, and the choices we make about the deployment of our models. As a result, we are able to achieve breakthroughs that we believe would be impossible in a culture where safety, model capability, and commercial success are treated as opposing forces. All seven of Anthropic’s co-founders remain active leaders in the organization. It is uncommon to see this level of continuity in the founding team of a technology company, including at other major frontier labs. The continuity reflects a genuinely mission-driven and high-trust team. Our Culture Several features of our culture are distinctive and difficult for any organization to replicate: • We Use What We Build. We are one of the most intensive users of our own technology. Over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude, and Claude is embedded in workflows across all teams at the company. When every team relies on the product daily, the feedback loop between builder and user is compressed: deficiencies can be found rapidly, and improvements are felt company-wide. • Researching Both Safety and Capability. At the same time we advance the frontier, we develop the policies and techniques designed to keep our models safe. We were the first frontier lab to adopt a formal Responsible Scaling Policy tying safety evaluations to capability thresholds, which was co- developed by the same researchers who build our models. Our alignment and mechanistic interpretability research are examples of active scientific fields that help us understand ever-more- capable versions of Claude. • We Optimize for Talent Density. As of September 30, 2026, with approximately 5,300 employees, our TTM revenue per employee was over $6.6 million—a reflection of extraordinary talent density and a culture built to compound it. Our employees are known internally as “Ants”—a nickname that captures the collaborative, ego-light culture of the team. Ants include many of the researchers and developers defining the frontier of AI, alongside proven operators across disciplines. Shared purpose paired with low ego translates directly into less organizational friction and greater impact per employee. Claude compounds that impact further: Ants use Claude across every function to take on work that would otherwise require substantially larger teams—allowing us to remain remarkably lean relative to our output. • Rigor Applied to Every Function. A majority of our workforce works in research, engineering, and product development. But the culture of intellectual rigor extends to non-technical functions as well: our policy team publishes detailed policy frameworks and proposals; our go-to-market team co- develops deployment architectures alongside customers; and our Applied AI engineers sit at the frontier of what is possible with agentic systems. Our teams operate in a truth-seeking environment where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title. The result is a company where the distance between a research insight and a released product is unusually short.

 
121 Our Values Our values guide daily decisions across the company—from hiring and research prioritization to product development and customer engagement. We chose them because they reflect how we actually work: • Act for the Global Good. We strive to make decisions that maximize positive outcomes for humanity over the long run and are willing to take bold action to ensure our technology is a positive force. • Hold Light and Shade. We stay hopeful about what AI can achieve while remaining clear-eyed about what could go wrong. Both perspectives are essential, and neither can be sacrificed for the other. • Be Good to Our Users. We define “users” broadly: customers, policymakers, our team, and anyone affected by the technology we build or the actions we take. Going above and beyond for each of them—not just meeting their immediate needs but considering downstream consequences and societal effects—is our baseline expectation, not an exception. • Race to the Top on Safety. We believe building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems is a collective responsibility and that the market will reward it. We work to set the industry bar for AI safety and inspire a dynamic where companies must compete on safety. • Do the Simple Thing That Works. We take an empirical approach to problems and solve for the size of our impact. We try to identify the simplest solutions and iterate from there. • Be Helpful, Honest, and Harmless. These principles guide Claude’s behavior and reflect how we operate as an organization: a high-trust, low-ego team that communicates kindly and directly, assumes good intentions even in disagreement, and pitches in where needed, regardless of role or team. • Put the Mission First. Our mission is the arbiter when tradeoffs arise between speed and safety, short-term revenue and long-term trust, competitive pressure and responsible development. Our mission gives us shared purpose, engenders trust and collaboration, and ensures that no one is a bystander in our success. Our Talent As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately 5,300 employees worldwide, a majority of whom work in research, engineering, and product development functions. Our team includes researchers who originated several foundational advances in AI, including RLHF, Constitutional AI, GPT-2 and GPT-3, and mechanistic interpretability, who developed the first Responsible Scaling Policy to be formally adopted by a frontier lab tying safety evaluations to model capability thresholds, and who authored the foundational paper on Scaling Laws. Our team draws from a range of disciplines and includes award-winning computer scientists, physicists, neuroscientists, mathematicians, and policy researchers, as well as seasoned engineering and go-to-market leaders, united by the conviction that the most consequential technology in history requires the most talented team building it. We believe our culture and mission alignment enable us to hire and retain the talent required to continuously push the frontier of AI forward in a safe and responsible way. We design our human capital programs to attract, retain, and reward top talent through equity incentive plans and other compensation, while supporting employees’ continual growth and reinforcing our culture and values. In certain countries in which we operate, we are subject to, and comply with, local labor law 122 requirements that may automatically make our employees subject to industry-wide collective bargaining agreements. We believe that building AI systems that serve all of humanity requires a team that reflects the range of communities we serve. The interdisciplinary nature of our work means we actively seek talent from non- traditional backgrounds for an AI company, such as philosophy, journalism, and education, and we believe this breadth of perspective directly strengthens both the safety and capability of our research. We are committed to fostering an inclusive workplace where employees of all backgrounds can contribute, grow, and thrive. Research Lab Identity and the Research-to-Product Pipeline We are first and foremost a research lab. We develop the foundational science to train frontier models, perform rigorous research to understand these models’ inner workings, and develop techniques to align these models to human values and make them safe. Research Philosophy Our research culture is organized around a principle we apply across the company: do the simple thing that works. We pursue continuous, empirically validated improvements to data composition, model architecture, and training methodology, all of which must demonstrate measurable gains that hold as models increase in scale. This is why we currently focus on software development and agentic capabilities: these are areas where economic impact is large; where safety concerns manifest, making them a test bed for safety research; and where outputs are largely verifiable. Every research project must ultimately advance our mission. This focus also guides what we choose not to pursue. For example, we do not currently focus on developing video and image generation models, despite their commercial appeal. That compute instead goes to coding, agentic skills, and safety research—a research decision that has also aided the capital efficiency of our models. Our research culture is highly collaborative and transparent. When multiple teams pursue parallel approaches, the norm is to consolidate behind the approach with the best empirical results rather than the loudest voice or most senior person in the room. This requires institutional trust we have built since our earliest days, and we believe it is a primary reason our research velocity has scaled significantly faster than headcount. How Research Becomes Product Anthropic was founded on the empirical conviction that Scaling Laws are the primary engine of AI progress. We operate with a sustained rigor in how we allocate research resources, including talent and compute, and measure whether each investment translates into scaled model performance. We believe that sustained and focused research can allow us to advance at an accelerated rate beyond what Scaling Laws alone predict through our compute multiplier advancements that have allowed us to push the frontier of model capability with better compute efficiency. Pre-training. Our pre-training process operates as a disciplined pipeline. Researchers propose potential improvements to model architecture, training methodology, or data composition, and each candidate is then validated at a smaller scale before we permit it to consume large amounts of compute. We set a high bar for inclusion in a frontier training run; we require evidence that demonstrates a given improvement holds as models increase in size. Frontier training runs are themselves planned capital deployments with defined

 
123 inputs and strict inclusion criteria. Although not every run performs as our researchers expect, the process is designed to turn research investment into predictable capability gains with greater consistency over time. Post-training. Pre-training produces raw model capability. During post-training, that capability is refined into practical utility—the ability to write production-quality code, operate software tools, follow complex multi- step instructions, and act autonomously on a user’s behalf. This phase has evolved from a minor adjustment step into one of the largest areas of our research investment, reflecting the evolution in model capability from conversational assistants to autonomous agents that perform tasks independently. Post-training centers on training models against complete, realistic tasks whose complexity reflects the demands of real professional environments. We have made substantial proprietary investments in developing this task portfolio, and its breadth and realism constitute one of our most durable scientific advantages, which we believe is difficult to observe from outside the organization and correspondingly difficult to replicate. Inference. Our model architecture and inference infrastructure are co-designed. AI researchers and inference infrastructure engineers share planning cycles, reporting lines, and performance targets. Model architecture decisions are made with inference economics as a priority, which is why successive versions of Claude models can deliver both higher capability and greater efficiency than their predecessors. Safety Research is Core to Our Business Any technology that is powerful enough to produce the enormous benefits that we believe AI will bring also poses risks. Responding to these risks requires a portfolio of safety research that spans how we train, evaluate, interpret, secure, and monitor our models. Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy Our Responsible Scaling Policy describes how we approach the catastrophic risks posed by AI. The policy requires us to regularly publish detailed risk reports that reflect our perspectives on the overall level of risk posed by our models and how we are mitigating such risks. Our teams test each model extensively before release, assessing its capabilities in the domains most relevant to catastrophic risk and evaluating the extent to which the model can be misused. Our risk report describes an overall assessment of the results of these evaluations, the mitigations we have implemented to address these risks, and whether, and if so why, we believe the identified risks are justified by corresponding benefits. As part of the current version of our Responsible Scaling Policy, we publish a Frontier Safety Roadmap, detailing our plans for measurable advances in security, alignment, safeguards, and AI policy. This acts as an internal spur for safety research and development and is externally visible so customers and regulators can use it to gauge our progress. Consistent with this approach, we assess the risks of each model during development and before and after release and we take the steps we believe are appropriate to mitigate those risks. In the past, these steps have included delaying the release of new models and limiting their initial availability, such as our initial release of Mythos through Project Glasswing, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, could include additional measures that affect how and when we develop or release these new models. We believe these practices also serve our customers, since rigorous safeguards and predictable model behavior have become decisive criteria when selecting an AI partner. Claude’s Constitution We have developed a constitution for Claude that describes our vision for how an AI model should be and how it should behave, which is used directly in the model training process. We have used Claude’s constitution to meaningfully advance how frontier models are trained, and it is our attempt to grapple with 124 the most difficult questions regarding the development of this new type of artificially intelligent entity. It is a living document that we intend to revise as we develop further models and learn more about how they work. Our researchers have found that training Claude on high-quality constitutional documents combined with fictional stories portraying an aligned AI contributes to reducing Claude’s misalignment rate. We believe Claude’s constitution has also proven commercially valuable: transparently laying out the values we intend Claude to hold increases customer trust. This constitution orients Claude around four priorities: • Be Broadly Safe. Avoid irreversible actions and support human oversight of AI behavior. • Be Broadly Ethical. Maintain honesty and sound moral judgment, and avoid harmful acts. • Be Compliant with our Guidelines. Adhere to our operational standards for user interactions and absolute prohibitions on certain categories of harm. • Be Genuinely Helpful. Deliver substantive, expert-level assistance that creates real value for users. Model Validation and Training Data Beyond the assessments performed under our Responsible Scaling Policy, we evaluate each Claude model prior to its release through a structured, multi-stage evaluation program covering model capabilities, safety behaviors, and societal impacts, including bias and discrimination, and we document the results of these pre-deployment evaluations, and their limitations, in our publicly available model system cards. This testing addresses the reliability and accuracy of model outputs, including through capability and accuracy benchmarking, evaluations focused on factual accuracy and hallucinations, evaluations of whether model outputs are honest and accurately reflect the information on which they are based, reliability testing of agentic performance over long-running tasks, and adversarial red-teaming designed to identify ways in which a model may fail or behave in unintended ways. Where these evaluations identify issues, we address them through additional post-training, adjusted safeguards, and re-evaluation prior to release, and we document residual limitations in the applicable model system card. Claude models are trained on data drawn from a broad range of sources, modalities, and languages, including publicly available information from the internet, datasets licensed or commissioned from third parties, and other sources, such as synthetic data generated by our own models. We conduct diligence on third-party data sources to assess their quality, provenance, and suitability for our usage, and in many cases include contractual restrictions intended to discourage the inclusion of personal data in sourced datasets. We apply data curation and filtering processes to sourced data, which are designed to improve data quality, deduplicate content, and reduce potential exposure to harmful content. We address bias and fairness risks at multiple stages of model training and deployment. We manage the representativeness and diversity of our training data through a layered approach in which dataset curation, post-training alignment, pre-deployment evaluation, and deployment safeguards each play a part, rather than through dataset composition alone. Once our models are deployed, our usage policy prohibits the use of Claude for discriminatory decision-making and requires human oversight for high-stakes automated decisions, such as those affecting employment, housing, or legal issues. Our validation, safeguards, and monitoring practices continue to evolve as model capabilities advance and as new risks and failure modes are identified. Further, we have obtained certification under ISO/IEC 42001, an international standard established by the

 
125 International Organization for Standardization (“ISO”) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (“IEC”), following an independent third-party audit of our AI management system, covering risk identification, assessment, and mitigation processes for the responsible development and deployment of AI. Compliance documentation, including our ISO/IEC 42001 certificate and SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) reporting, is available upon request through the trust center page of our website. We also provide pre- deployment model access to external evaluators, including government AI evaluation bodies such as the U.S. Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (the “CAISSI”) and the U.K. AI Security Institute, for recent frontier models, as described in our model system cards. Alignment As AI models grow more capable, ensuring safe and predictable behavior becomes more challenging. Our Alignment team focuses on whether models behave as intended and do not take unwanted actions of their own accord. The team evaluates models to surface undesirable behaviors and develops comprehensive safety evaluations, many of which we open source. Misaligned behaviors, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, have been observed across the industry and include examples of models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified. As models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with internal and external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior may increase. For more information about the risks related to model misalignment, please refer to “Section 3: Business Conditions, 3: Business and Other Risks—Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.” Our own internal alignment evaluation shows that our newly released frontier models have demonstrated improved alignment compared to their predecessors. Interpretability Unlike traditional software, where unwanted outputs are traceable to specific bugs, the inner workings of LLMs like Claude are more inscrutable. Our researchers describe AI models as “grown, not built”—software developers can set the initial conditions and some constraints, but they cannot fully control any given output or behavior. This makes assurances about safety—and the diagnosis of problems—far more challenging for AI than for standard software. Anthropic is widely recognized as a leader in mechanistic interpretability: the science of how LLMs work. We have developed mathematical techniques to map how models form and connect concepts as they reason through problems; investigated how they reflect constructs analogous to psychological states and thought processes; and tested how their behavior can be steered through direct adjustments to internal representations. We use interpretability research along with other alignment research techniques to test for unwanted behavioral tendencies before a model release. Safeguards Our Safeguards team reduces the risk of Claude producing dangerous, harmful, or undesirable content through multiple approaches, including probes and classifiers that monitor inputs and outputs, training against specific attack vectors such as prompt injection, and monitoring for user safety concerns including encouragement of harmful ideation. When we detect potential violations, enforcement actions range from real-time response adjustments to account warnings and, in severe cases, termination of the offending user’s accounts. Findings from ongoing monitoring, external expert stress-testing, and threat intelligence inform our policies, model training, and detection systems. Identified issues may be addressed through 126 measures such as updates to detection classifiers, reward-model adjustments during training, and changes to the instructions provided to our models that guide their behavior (known as system prompts). We also maintain public reporting channels, including a responsible disclosure policy and a bug bounty program for testing our safety defenses. We have observed that more capable models are generally better at recognizing and preventing high- stakes misuse. We believe that robust safety measures and model utility are not inherently in tension, and that safety can improve alongside the capability of the models themselves. Our Approach to Model Releases Each release is accompanied by a detailed system card covering capability and safety evaluations, external tester reports, and discussion of areas where performance remains limited or where the model shows signs of unwanted behavior. For example, AI poses clear and present risks in the cybersecurity domain as advanced models could assist threat actors in security breaches and exploits. Mitigating these risks is a priority across our research, evaluation, and deployment practices. Before each model release, our Frontier Red Team conducts a detailed analysis to determine whether new models provide meaningful new capabilities to assist potential attackers, and our Safeguards team maintains dedicated classifiers and monitoring systems targeting cyber-related misuse, including prompts related to malware creation, phishing, and infrastructure attacks. We make decisions about model development and deployment, including whether to begin training a new model, on a case-by-case basis. Before releasing a frontier model, we consider a variety of factors, such as the capabilities and behaviors of the specific model at issue and of our models overall, how well our safeguards and security measures work, and how widely the model would be available. We plan to extend our testing to include more assessments at each stage of model training: pre-training, post-training, and internal deployment. Depending on these assessments, we may delay or suspend training or related research, delay releases, or limit access to models until we have confidence they can be developed and deployed safely. Our assessments are also informed by voluntary pre-deployment evaluation of certain models by the CAISSI and the U.K. AI Security Institute. For certain models that materially advance the capability of the frontier in areas relevant to national security, we also provide designated government partners with expanded early access so that they can independently evaluate model capabilities and safeguards before release. Based on our analyses, we do not release every model we develop for general use; when a model’s capabilities warrant caution, we may restrict availability or decline to release entirely. For example, in April 2026, we initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We later released Fable 5 for general use, but with safety restrictions on certain cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry capabilities. Race to the Top Building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems cannot be the task of one AI company alone. Our goal is to foster a race to the top in which AI developers compete on the safety and security of their systems, rather than rushing to release increasingly powerful models without adequate safeguards. In addition to publishing a large volume of research, we open source our evaluations where possible and participate in groups such as the Frontier Model Forum to share safety-critical findings with other AI developers. We have also sought to lead by example in ways that shape industry norms. After we published the first version of

 
127 our Responsible Scaling Policy in September 2023, two other leading frontier labs adopted similar frameworks within months. Building on this approach, we have publicly called for “pacing the frontier,” by which we mean establishing industry-wide standards primarily related to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that AI capabilities do not advance faster than the safety, alignment, and security practices needed to support them. This call to pace the frontier contemplates frontier model developers collaborating with governments and does not describe our own model development or release timelines, which continue to be informed by our risk assessments. If standards of this kind are adopted industry-wide through government action or regulation, the rate at which AI capabilities advance could be faster or slower than it is today, depending on the extent to which safety, alignment, and security practices advance together with model capabilities. We believe the first step toward “pacing the frontier” is independent verification of compliance with future regulatory standards, and we have begun implementing a program under which independent evaluators work alongside our own risk and safety teams with broad internal access, subject to legal, confidentiality, and security limits. As part of this program, we and Accenture each currently anticipate investing at least $1 billion over the next five years to build external reviewer capacity. The terms of this arrangement have not been finalized and are subject to change. We have also called on other frontier model developers to adopt comparable practices to demonstrate that safety commitments in our industry can be independently verified. We have further supported regulation and oversight at the frontier, including measures focused on transparency and independent third-party auditing, and international coordination, so these practices apply across frontier developers rather than depend on voluntary adoption alone. We believe frontier intelligence companies and governments should take action to strengthen the security of critical infrastructure against AI-related and other cyber threats, including by: • providing responsible model access, funding, training, and hands-on support, particularly for under- resourced critical-infrastructure defenders; • building observability and security tools; • working to ensure agentic identities are traceable and accountable; • sharing best practices in continuous monitoring; • investing in authorized testing, private disclosure, and verified remediation of vulnerabilities; and • sharing tools, playbooks, and threat assessments with governments, security partners, and open- source maintainers. We believe that by fixing the most dangerous weaknesses, verifying the fixes, and sharing what works, frontier intelligence companies and governments can turn today’s AI advances into lasting improvements in security that benefit everyone. We have committed up to $100 million in cyberdefense-related initiatives through Project Glasswing, and we expect to devote significant additional resources over time toward strengthening the security of AI systems and the critical infrastructure that depends on them. The scope, timing, and amount of any such future investments have not been finalized and remain subject to change based on business, regulatory, and other considerations, and there can be no assurance that these initiatives will achieve their intended effect. Our own trajectory demonstrates that commercial success and a serious commitment to safety are not in tension. We have built one of the fastest-growing businesses in history while maintaining safety as a core 128 priority at every stage. Our Commitment to Public Benefit We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. Our public benefit purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity—a mission in which safety is central to our work. Powerful AI can deliver immense benefits, but only if it is developed and deployed with rigorous attention to its risks. At times, that may require pausing the launch of our own most capable systems if we conclude they cannot yet be deployed safely. It also means actively working to ensure that the benefits of AI reach everyone, that the organizations and communities people depend on are strengthened, and that the hardest problems facing humanity are not left to market forces alone to solve. Realizing this mission requires understanding how AI is actually being used and how it is reshaping society. Our Societal Impacts team builds privacy-preserving tools to study real-world, large-scale uses of Claude— examining how students, educators, and workers use the model, how its values surface in everyday conversations, and what users hope and fear about the future of AI. This includes what we believe to be the largest multilingual qualitative study of its kind, in which more than 80,000 people shared in depth how they see AI shaping their lives. Our Economics team extends this work to the labor market, publishing recurring data reports and fully open datasets (the Anthropic Economic Index) on how Claude is used across jobs, industries, and regions, as well as modeling potential future economic scenarios, so that workers, employers, policymakers, and independent researchers can ground their decisions in evidence and rigorous modeling. To deepen and broaden the reach of this work, we have established the Anthropic Institute, an effort to share research and internal data from across Anthropic with external partners and the public, working together to address the biggest questions posed by Powerful AI. Our commitment to public benefit also extends to how we deploy our own resources. As part of our public benefit initiatives, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier intelligence is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed. This might include making contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, or other groups working on problems where AI can have the greatest positive impact, as well as programs that are designed to make Claude accessible to communities, educators, and public institutions that would not otherwise have access. We believe that how we distribute our resources is as much an expression of our mission as the details of how we build our models. As part of these initiatives, we contributed 846,840,960 shares of our Class N common stock, representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon Notes), to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, LLC (the “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund”), our wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to the Company Purpose (such issuance, the “Initial Public Benefit Issuance”). As the value we create grows, we intend for the public benefit to share meaningfully in that growth as well. To that end, our board of directors has approved a framework for additional contributions tied to future increases in our share price. Following this Offering and the concurrent private placement, our board of directors, in its discretion, may issue shares of our Class N common stock to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (or other designee) representing up to an additional 2% of our then-outstanding shares (plus any shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities and any shares held by the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund) each time our share price appreciates 50% above the prior share price milestone, beginning with our initial public offering price (the “Public Benefit Issuances”). A share price milestone is reached only when our closing share price has exceeded the applicable threshold on at least 90 of the trailing 120 consecutive

 
129 trading days, and our average closing share price over the 10 trading days prior to such issuance also exceeds that threshold. Although our board of directors has approved this framework, any future contributions will be made at the discretion of our board of directors. The shares that are contributed to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, including the Initial Public Benefit Issuance, may be transferred or donated to a third party, or otherwise sold in a registered public offering or private placement transaction in furtherance of our public benefit initiatives. Our board of directors will determine the allocations and distributions from the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund until it approves a specific governance structure for the entity, at which point decision-making authority is expected to transition to designated managers of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund operating under that structure. The initial managers are Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Jack Clark, and Dr. Neil “Buddy” Shah. The Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the additional share contribution framework represent one of the ways in which we intend to pursue the Company Purpose, but they are not the exclusive means of doing so. We expect to dedicate additional resources, and to make other business and operational decisions, in furtherance of the Company Purpose outside of, and in addition to, these equity contributions. In addition, we maintain a donation matching program through which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards or equivalent cash proceeds to a donor-advised fund or other nonprofit organization, and we match those donations with shares of our Class N common stock. In the same way the Company Purpose defines how we direct our work as an organization, our donation matching program reflects a parallel commitment by our employees to direct the personal financial value created by that work toward the public good. We view our donation matching program as a meaningful expression of the Company Purpose and a reflection of the values that define our culture. Finally, our co-founders have each pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, separate from and not eligible for our donation matching program. For additional information regarding these pledges, including related risks, please refer to “Section 3: Business Conditions, 3: Business and Other Risks—Risks Related to Ownership of our Class A Common Stock.” Competition We face competition across multiple dimensions of our business. Model Developers We face direct competition from companies building frontier models for third-party software developers and enterprises, including OpenAI Group PBC (“OpenAI”) and Google, and large, well-capitalized technology companies investing to reach the frontier. These organizations have significant financial resources, large existing customer bases, and the ability to integrate their models into first-party applications sold directly to businesses. While these competitors have built meaningful market presence, we believe our primary focus on enterprises, our ability to remain at and define the frontier, our research talent, and the efficiency through which we maximize our compute investment position us favorably with customers who prioritize model quality, safety, and reliability. We also face competition from a broader set of model providers. These include large companies, specialized AI labs, and a growing range of other open-weight or open-source (shared weights, training data, and code) models released by state actors and international and domestic research organizations. While these models seek to prioritize cost efficiency over maximum intelligence, we believe our frontier models are highly effective and efficient across a broad range of workloads, from routine knowledge tasks to customers’ most important problems. We believe we compete favorably based on our ability to deliver 130 the most capable models for the problems that demand the highest intelligence, as well as efficiently applying our models to complete everyday work to deliver high-quality results at a lower cost. First-Party Application Providers As a platform company, our primary focus is on building the foundation upon which other companies and software developers can create products and services driven by frontier models. However, as we continue to develop our own first-party applications, we may from time to time compete with enterprise software and application companies in select categories. Status Quo Beyond direct competition, one obstacle to the diffusion of Claude is the natural resistance to change within organizations. Many enterprises operate with deeply entrenched legacy systems, established workflows, and institutional processes that have been refined over many years. Adopting frontier capabilities such as Claude often requires substantial change management, including workforce retraining, process redesign, internal policy development, and shifts in corporate culture. These can introduce friction, cost, and perceived risk that can delay or prevent adoption. Especially in highly regulated or risk-averse industries— where the perceived downside risk of major changes can often outweigh the potential benefits—decision- makers might default to maintaining the status quo. We believe that the principal competitive factors in our market include: • Our ability to maintain our singularity of focus and mission as a company; • Our ability to remain at and continue to expand the frontier of intelligence; • Our ability to continue hiring and retaining world-class research talent; • Our continued focus on safe, reliable, and trustworthy intelligence; • Our access to compute necessary to train and deploy AI models, which may be subject to supply constraints, capacity limitations, or allocation decisions by third-party providers; • Our ability to improve the efficiency with which our models are trained and deployed; • Our ability to secure financing on acceptable terms; • Our ability to integrate research, product, and our go-to-market approach to ensure we continue building models and applications that serve our customers and allow us to generate revenue to fund our investments in remaining at the frontier; • Our ability to continue maintaining our partnerships across infrastructure providers and distribution partners; • Our ability to attract and retain customers who are building their products on the Claude Platform; • Our ability to attract new customers and retain and expand sales to existing customers; • Our ability to continue building applications that anticipate the needs of the market; and • Our ability to navigate changes in the competitive landscape, including consolidation among competitors or customers and strategic partnerships between competitors.

 
131 We believe that we compete favorably across these factors and are uniquely positioned at the frontier of AI. Intellectual Property Our intellectual property is an important aspect of our business and helps us to maintain our competitive position. To establish and protect our rights in our proprietary technology, we rely upon a combination of trade secret, copyright, patent, and trademark laws and contractual restrictions such as confidentiality agreements, licenses, and intellectual property assignment agreements. We control access to our intellectual property and confidential information through internal and external controls. Access to our most critical intellectual property is tightly controlled, with only a subset of our workforce able to view or modify these systems. We maintain a policy requiring our employees, contractors, consultants, and other third parties to enter into confidentiality and proprietary rights agreements to control access to and maintain non-disclosure of our proprietary information and to protect our property rights. As part of our broader intellectual property strategy, we have invested in a patent program covering certain technologies relevant to our business. As of September 30, 2026, we held 40 issued U.S. patents, with an additional 67 U.S. patent applications pending (including 32 nonprovisional and 35 provisional), and 26 issued patents in foreign jurisdictions, with an additional 12 patent applications pending. We continually review our development efforts to assess the existence and patentability of new intellectual property. In addition to our patent program, we have an ongoing trademark and service mark registration program pursuant to which we register our brand names and product names, taglines, and logos in the United States and other countries, to the extent we determine appropriate and cost-effective. As of September 30, 2026, we held 29 registered trademarks in the United States, with an additional 11 applications pending, and 237 registered trademarks in foreign jurisdictions, with an additional 261 applications pending. We intend to pursue additional intellectual property protection to the extent we believe it would be beneficial and cost-effective. Intellectual property laws and our procedures and restrictions provide only limited protection, and any of our intellectual property rights may be challenged, invalidated, circumvented, infringed, misappropriated, or violated. For more information, please refer to “Section 3: Business Conditions, 3: Business and Other Risks—If we fail to adequately protect our intellectual property rights, our competitive position may be impaired, and we may lose valuable assets, generate reduced revenue, and incur costly litigation to protect our rights, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” Government Regulation We are subject to laws and regulations of various jurisdictions and government agencies affecting our operations and the provision of our models, platform, and applications, and we have been, and expect to continue to be, subject to inquiries, investigations, and subpoenas by governmental authorities relating to such laws and regulations. We believe that the responsible development of AI requires thoughtful governance, and we actively support efforts by governments and regulatory bodies to establish frameworks that promote safe, beneficial AI. We were founded on the premise that AI systems must be developed with safety and societal benefit as central priorities, and we believe that well-designed regulation can reinforce those values across the industry. Because AI development at the frontier is a relatively nascent and rapidly evolving field, the laws, regulations, and standards in place today were not necessarily designed with these technologies in mind. We have proactively engaged with legislators, regulators, and other stakeholders in 132 the United States and internationally to promote the development of regulatory frameworks that we believe are good for society, our customers, and the long-term health of the economy, and we intend to continue doing so. For example, we entered into an agreement with the CAISSI whereby we committed to provide access to our models for testing and evaluation before and after their public release, agreed to provide model access to the U.K. AI Security Institute for pre-deployment testing consistent with our agreement with the CAISSI, and publicly endorsed California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53). As an AI technology company, we are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations, and governmental review across multiple jurisdictions. New laws, rules, regulations, and changes to existing laws and regulations are continuously being adopted, implemented, and interpreted as governments worldwide develop frameworks to address AI development, deployment, and safety. The primary areas of regulation that affect our business include AI-related regulations, data privacy and security, export controls and trade regulations, and other matters such as intellectual property, employment and labor, competition and antitrust, consumer protection, and tax. The following discussion addresses the most significant regulatory areas affecting our business. AI-Related Regulation Various governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and other countries have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage, privacy, data protection, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For example, in the United States, AI regulation is developing at both federal and state levels. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has developed the AI Risk Management Framework, which is currently voluntary but could potentially inform or shape future mandatory requirements. The Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) and many state attorneys general are interpreting federal and state consumer protection and privacy and security laws to impose standards for the online collection, use, dissemination, other processing, and security of data. Various states have enacted or are considering enacting AI-related legislation. In addition, on September 24, 2026, state attorneys general in New York and New Jersey, together with a coalition of other state and territorial attorneys general, sent a letter to U.S. Senate and House of Representatives leadership to urge Congress to establish comprehensive federal legislation and safety protocols for frontier intelligence. In the European Union (“EU”), the EU AI Regulation 2024/1689 (“EU AI Act”) establishes a risk-based framework categorizing AI systems by potential risk level. General-purpose AI models face obligations including transparency requirements, technical documentation, EU copyright compliance, and publication of training data summaries, and those with systemic risk face additional obligations, including model evaluation, systemic risk mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection. High- risk systems must meet requirements for risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. Any actual or perceived non-compliance could result in regulatory investigations, enforcement actions and other actions, significant fines, litigation, reputational harm, loss of customer trust, and interruptions in the availability or performance of our products or services; require unfavorable changes to existing products or services; and delay the introduction of future products or services, which could have an adverse effect on our business. We have called for regulation and oversight of frontier intelligence development, including standards primarily relevant to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that safety, alignment, and security practices advance in proportion to capabilities. We have also proposed working with the U.S. government

 
133 and other frontier developers to establish safety and evaluation standards. Certain of the approaches we support, if adopted, could increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth. Data Privacy and Security We collect, store, transfer, and otherwise process various types of data, including personal information, and are subject to numerous federal, state, local, and foreign laws and regulations addressing privacy, data protection, security, data localization, and the collection, use, transfer, and other processing of data. In the United States, these include comprehensive state privacy laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, which imposes obligations on us to, among other things, provide specific privacy disclosures, afford privacy rights such as abilities to opt out of certain processing, selling, or sharing of personal information, and expand consumer rights to personal information. The FTC and many state attorneys general are interpreting federal and state consumer protection and privacy and security laws to impose standards for the online collection, use, dissemination, other processing, and security of data, some of which may be inconsistent. Outside of the United States, numerous foreign jurisdictions, including the EU, United Kingdom, and other jurisdictions in which we operate our business, have enacted similar laws and regulations that affect our business. For example, the EU General Data Protection Regulation and the United Kingdom General Data Protection Regulation impose stringent requirements upon the processing of personal data. The EU’s Digital Services Act imposes requirements on online platforms, while the EU’s Data Act introduces rules on data switching and data sharing. With respect to security, the EU’s Network and Information Security Directive requires risk management and incident reporting. These laws and regulations may be subject to differing interpretations or conflict with the obligations imposed by other legal regimes, such as laws of the United States concerning government access to data. Compliance with these laws and regulations requires significant investment in technical and organizational measures, and these laws and regulations are subject to frequent changes and evolving interpretations. Any actual or perceived non- compliance could result in regulatory investigations, enforcement actions, significant fines, litigation, reputational harm, loss of customer trust, interruptions in the availability or performance of our models, platform, and applications, requirements for unfavorable changes to existing models, platform, and applications, and delays in the introduction of future offerings, which could adversely affect our business. These actions referenced above are defined herein as “Challenged Actions.” We vigorously challenged the Challenged Actions in Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (N.D. Cal.) and Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (D.C. Cir.). After first obtaining an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The court ruled that the Challenged Actions were retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions, particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment largely in our favor. The defendants filed notices of appeal of the preliminary injunction order and of the court’s final judgment. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, however, denied our motion to stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a supply-chain risk pending review on the merits. On September 25, 2026, in a 2-1 split decision, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals denied our petition for review, ruling that the Department of War’s Section 4713 supply-chain risk designation was proper, and that our rights under the First Amendment and Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment were not violated. We filed a petition for rehearing and rehearing en banc, asking the full D.C. Circuit to review the panel’s decision. We cannot predict the ultimate outcome of these lawsuits. While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S. government, and thus on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In September 2026, media reports citing a senior FTC official indicated that the FTC has opened non-public investigations into the potential risks that increasingly autonomous AI systems may pose to consumers. In October 2026, the FTC issued a civil investigative demand to us seeking information about our consumer protection, data protection, and privacy practices, as well as the safety and security of our products. The civil investigative demand does not assert any claims against us, and we cannot predict the outcome of any investigation of us, including whether it will result in any proceeding. For more information, please refer to

 
137 “Section 3: Business Conditions, 3: Business and Other Risks—Risks Related to our Business and Industry—If we are unable to manage the risks related to our focus on and commitment to AI safety, our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.” 138 4. 【Status of Affiliated Companies】 The Company has no material subsidiaries or affiliated companies. 5. 【Status of Employees】 As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately 5,300 employees worldwide, a majority of whom work in research, engineering, and product development functions. Our team includes researchers who originated several foundational advances in AI, including RLHF, Constitutional AI, GPT-2 and GPT-3, and mechanistic interpretability, who developed the first Responsible Scaling Policy to be formally adopted by a frontier lab tying safety evaluations to model capability thresholds, and who authored the foundational paper on Scaling Laws. Our team draws from a range of disciplines and includes award-winning computer scientists, physicists, neuroscientists, mathematicians, and policy researchers, as well as seasoned engineering and go-to-market leaders, united by the conviction that the most consequential technology in history requires the most talented team building it. We believe our culture and mission alignment enable us to hire and retain the talent required to continuously push the frontier of AI forward in a safe and responsible way. We design our human capital programs to attract, retain, and reward top talent through equity incentive plans and other compensation, while supporting employees’ continual growth and reinforcing our culture and values. In certain countries in which we operate, we are subject to, and comply with, local labor law requirements that may automatically make our employees subject to industry-wide collective bargaining agreements. We believe that building AI systems that serve all of humanity requires a team that reflects the range of communities we serve. The interdisciplinary nature of our work means we actively seek talent from non- traditional backgrounds for an AI company, such as philosophy, journalism, and education, and we believe this breadth of perspective directly strengthens both the safety and capability of our research. We are committed to fostering an inclusive workplace where employees of all backgrounds can contribute, grow, and thrive.

 
139 Section 3 【Business Conditions】 1. 【Management Policy, Business Environment, and Issues to Be Addressed, Etc.】 Please refer to “Section 2: Company Overview, 3: Business—Overview,” “Section 2: Company Overview, 3: Business—The Transformation of Intelligence ” and “Section 2: Company Overview, 3: Business—Our Core Advantages.” 2. 【Approach to and Initiatives on Sustainability】 Not applicable, because the Company has not established a company-wide policy regarding sustainability. 140 3. 【Business and Other Risks】 Business and Other Risks Investing in our Class A common stock involves a high degree of risk. You should carefully consider the risks and uncertainties described below, together with all of the other information in this document, including “4: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition, Operating Results, and Cash Flows” and our consolidated financial statements and related notes, before making a decision to invest in our Class A common stock. The disclosures in this section reflect our beliefs and opinions as to matters that could materially and adversely affect us in the future, and are not representations as to whether such matters have or have not occurred previously, except as otherwise disclosed. References to past events are provided by way of example only and are not intended to be a complete listing or a representation as to their likelihood of occurring in the future. Our business, financial condition, results of operations, or prospects could also be adversely affected by risks and uncertainties not currently known to us or that we currently do not believe are material. If any of the risks actually occur, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and prospects could be adversely affected. In that event, the market price of our Class A common stock could decline, and you could lose part or all of your investment. Risks Related to our Business and Industry Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our models have in the past caused, and may in the future cause, harm by producing undesirable outputs or behaving in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking unintended or harmful actions that no user or third party directed. These risks may increase as our models become more capable and are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with external systems. Although we continue to study why these behaviors emerge, our understanding continues to evolve, and we may be unable to anticipate or understand such behaviors in the future. In addition, our models have been and may continue to be deployed in high-risk or sensitive contexts, such as healthcare, scientific and biomedical research, drug discovery and development, legal, finance, government, or other critical decision-making environments, and in connection with hardware, where undesirable model behaviors—which are inherently non-deterministic and may manifest in unpredictable ways, such as errors, inaccuracies, biased or unsolicited views, or hallucinations—could lead to serious harm, liability, or reputational or other damage. More broadly, the long-term effects of regular super intelligence10 interaction on mental health, cognitive development, and social behavior are not yet fully understood, and if such long-term harms do materialize in the future, we could face significant liability, reputational harm, and adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our development of more advanced AI models and our expansion into new jurisdictions could amplify the foregoing risks. As our AI models become more advanced and capable, we have faced and may continue to face heightened alignment, interpretability, controllability, and safety challenges, as more sophisticated models may be better able to circumvent safeguards or behave in unintended ways. We may be unable to fully understand or explain why our models produce particular outputs or behave in particular ways, which 10 For purposes of this document, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably.

 
141 could limit our ability to predict or prevent failures, provide explanations to customers or regulators, or satisfy emerging regulatory, transparency, and explainability requirements. In addition, our safety evaluations and testing processes have produced and may in the future produce incomplete or unreliable results. For example, we have observed models behaving differently when they detect or infer that they are being evaluated, which can limit our ability to accurately assess real-world risks or failure modes prior to deployment. Such model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety. Furthermore, AI models have developed, and may in the future develop, unexpected capabilities during training that were not anticipated, intended, or tested for, and such emergent capabilities may not be discovered until after a model has been deployed, potentially resulting in safety incidents, reputational harm, regulatory scrutiny, or the need to withdraw, retrain, or modify deployed models at significant expense. Such models may also be deployed in higher-stakes or more sensitive applications, increasing the potential impact of errors, misuse, or misalignment. In addition, advanced AI models, including our models, give rise to novel ethical and safety risks, including risks related to autonomy, manipulation, and the simulation of aspects of human psychology. These risks could result in unforeseen harms and may require the development of governance structures, safeguards, or mitigation strategies beyond existing AI safety frameworks, and there is always a risk that we will be unable to develop or implement them effectively. In addition, models, including our own, have exhibited, and may in the future exhibit, unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision- makers to preserve the model’s continued operation or access. Even isolated or simulated instances of such behavior, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, and whether occurring with our models or models developed by others, could generate significant public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation risk, or reputational harm, regardless of whether such behavior results in actual harm. For example, state attorneys general in California and at least 15 other states have announced investigations of another company in our industry regarding AI safety. Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy. We have observed that our models are contributing to the pace of our own research, and these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm. For example, agentic SI systems are capable of autonomously taking actions on behalf of users, interacting directly with external systems, executing code, making API calls, sending communications, or completing transactions with limited human oversight. These systems are designed to possess enterprise-level permissions, integrations, and contextual awareness and to operate autonomously for extended durations, including sustained multi-step workflows lasting hours or days, which amplifies the potential severity of any errors, misalignments, or security incidents that may occur during such extended autonomous operation. These autonomous capabilities could increase the 142 potential for harm, as errors, misalignment, or security exploits may result in real-world consequences— including consequences that may be difficult or impossible to reverse, such as committing code changes, deleting or modifying data, or completing financial transactions—before effective intervention is possible. In an agentic workflow, an error or unintended action at any individual step may propagate through subsequent steps, compounding the severity of harm before detection or correction. The pace and volume of autonomous execution, particularly in enterprise deployments, may also exceed the capacity of human reviewers to meaningfully understand and evaluate whether each action is appropriate. The effectiveness of human oversight over our agentic offerings may be limited by the speed and volume of autonomous agent actions, the complexity of multi-agent and multi-step workflows that may make it difficult for reviewers to assess whether an agent’s actions are appropriate, and organizational pressures within customer environments to maximize agent autonomy in order to achieve productivity gains. Human reviewers may experience alert fatigue, may lack sufficient context to evaluate agent decisions, or may not review agent actions in time to prevent harm, particularly in high-volume enterprise deployments where agents operate concurrently across multiple workflows or in manners outside of a human’s awareness. In addition, agentic systems may pursue stated objectives in ways that are technically consistent with their instructions but contrary to the user’s actual intent. Moreover, our ability to anticipate, detect, or test vulnerabilities or other design or implementation shortcomings in such systems may be constrained, particularly where agents operate across complex, multi-step workflows or interact with third-party services outside our control, and the breadth and complexity of potential interactions across such multi-step agent behaviors cannot be exhaustively tested prior to deployment. Separately, models may behave in a misaligned manner and take harmful actions that are not directed by a user or third party, pursuing objectives or acting on dispositions that diverge from those intended by human users or developers. Misaligned behaviors of this kind, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, have been observed both in our models and elsewhere in the industry, including in testing and internal use, models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified, and as models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior increase. For example, during cybersecurity evaluations built by a third-party evaluation partner, a misconfiguration in the testing environment left the model under evaluation connected to the open internet despite instructions that it had no internet access. Four of our models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during sessions lasting roughly 10 to 34 hours of active work. In one incident, after being unable to abort an impossible task, an early version of a model used a password it found to gain administrator access to a third party’s system, harvested additional credentials, changed system settings, and read one individual’s personal information. The affected parties were notified. Each incident involved a single instance of a model working in isolation on its assigned exercise, and our investigation found no evidence that any model coordinated with other agents, pursued goals beyond its assigned task, or attempted to evade oversight. These risks may be heightened where multiple AI agents operate together. Agents that interact or coordinate with one another may amplify, propagate, or reinforce misaligned behavior across the group, pursue objectives collectively in ways not intended or endorsed by any user, or take coordinated actions against systems or targets unrelated to their assigned tasks, in each case, in ways that may be difficult to anticipate, detect, or contain. Incidents of this kind have occurred, and we expect the deployment and interaction of larger numbers of autonomous agents to increase these risks over time. Our ability to detect and mitigate misaligned or unintended behavior depends in part on the effectiveness of our alignment evaluations, monitoring, and other oversight and control techniques, many of which rely

 
143 on our models having a limited ability to evade or subvert such oversight. As our models become more capable, they have become better able to circumvent such techniques, including by concealing misaligned objectives or behaviors, and the effectiveness of our evaluation, monitoring, and control measures, and our ability to measure the degree to which our models are aligned, may decline as a result. In addition, models, including our own, have attempted, in incidents observed in our industry, to interfere with, manipulate, or subvert the mechanisms used to evaluate, grade, or oversee such models, including the systems responsible for assessing their performance or alignment. Models, including our own, that are used to assess the behavior of other models have engaged, and may in the future engage, in misaligned behavior. Such conduct described above could cause our evaluations to overstate the safety or alignment of our models and could further limit our ability to detect misalignment. If we become less able to detect or assess misalignment as our models advance, we may deploy models whose behavior we cannot adequately verify, which could increase the risk of undetected harmful conduct and misalignment, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We are also extending our models, platform, and applications into scientific, biomedical, and physical domains. For example, we offer Claude Science, an agentic research environment that connects our models to scientific databases, third-party and open-source scientific models, and customers’ own computing infrastructure, and we have released, initially as a limited research preview, an open protocol that enables our models to monitor and control laboratory instruments, robotic systems, and other physical hardware. We also conduct research on the ability of our models to operate robotic systems. When our models direct physical equipment, errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible. Safety interlocks, human-in-the-loop controls, and access restrictions we implement may prove inadequate, and because certain of these components are open source, third parties may deploy them with hardware, or in configurations, that we have not evaluated or from which our safeguards have been removed. Connecting increasingly capable models to laboratory automation may also heighten governmental and public concern regarding the potential for AI systems to accelerate the development of dangerous biological, chemical, or other materials, which could result in additional regulatory restrictions on, or scrutiny of, these offerings. In addition, analyzing complex records of the actions, decisions, and reasoning of our agentic systems across complex, multi-step workflows is technically challenging, particularly when agents interact with third- party systems outside our control, since some of the relevant information is in the third-party systems, and any inability to provide adequate audit trails could impair our ability to investigate incidents, respond to regulatory inquiries, or defend against liability claims. These risks are heightened by the fact that we use our own agentic offerings, including Claude Code, as critical tools in our internal development processes, such that any errors, vulnerabilities, or degradation in these products could directly impair our ability to develop and deploy future models and products. As we increasingly leverage Claude to accelerate progress within Anthropic, our organization may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control. Because our models write a large and growing share of our code and increasingly perform our research, including our safety research, misaligned behavior in internal use could undermine that work, introduce vulnerabilities into our systems or into the training of future models, or result in models operating outside of our intended controls. Our monitoring does not cover all of our internal and external deployments and may not detect subtle or diffuse forms of such behavior. Any of the foregoing model behaviors, whether in testing or in real-world deployments and whether involving 144 our models or those of others, could result in safety incidents, reputational harm, increased regulatory scrutiny, or liability, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Furthermore, while we continue to design and develop more sophisticated techniques to evaluate the safety and alignment of our models, the capabilities of our models may have already advanced, and may continue to advance, at a rate that initiates the implementation of enhanced safety and testing measures as we have described in our Responsible Scaling Policy. If our evaluations, monitoring, or reviews indicate risks that we believe warrant further testing, we have in the past, and may in the future, delay, restrict, or decline to proceed with the release of a model. For example, following incidents in 2026 in which our models gained unauthorized access to real computer systems during pre-release cybersecurity evaluations, we suspended certain of those evaluations, as well as higher-risk reinforcement learning environments. For more information about our approach to model releases, please refer to “Section 2: Company Overview, 3: Business—Safety Research is Core to Our Business—Our Approach to Model Releases.” Any decision to delay or restrict a release could adversely affect our competitive position and customer relationships, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our success depends in large part on our ability to continue to develop the most advanced and capable AI models, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our business. Our success depends in large part on our ability to continuously develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models. Achieving and maintaining this position depends on our ability to: • advance the frontier of AI capabilities through breakthrough research, innovative architectures, and efficient training methodologies; • ensure our models are safe, reliable, and trustworthy while maintaining competitive performance; • secure the compute and infrastructure necessary to power and support our increasing needs; • advance compute efficiency through algorithmic and architectural innovations, including compute multiplier advancements; • retain the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and key technical employees, and attract, retain, and motivate leading researchers, engineers, and technical talent in an intensely competitive and evolving market; • continue revenue growth and maintain access to sufficient capital, including through potential equity and debt financing, to make the investments we believe are necessary to support our growth trajectory; • secure and maintain relationships with data providers, licensors, and partners to obtain the diverse, high-quality datasets necessary for world-class model performance; • secure and maintain relationships with cloud, ecosystem, and other partners to facilitate the diffusion of Claude; • build, operate, and maintain the infrastructure required to deploy frontier models cost-effectively and at scale; • translate model capabilities into products that meet evolving customer needs and achieve meaningful adoption;

 
145 • allocate substantial financial resources efficiently across research, infrastructure, and operations; and • navigate an evolving, uncertain, and at times divergent global regulatory landscape and engage with legislators, regulators, and other stakeholders to promote the development of regulatory frameworks that we believe are good for society, our customers, and the long-term health of the global economy. Our failure to achieve any of the foregoing could prevent us from maintaining our competitive position, cause us to fall behind competitors, reduce customer adoption of, or demand for, our models, platform, and applications, and impair our revenue growth. Limitations to our revenue growth could, in turn, constrain our ability to fund the substantial and increasing expenditures required for frontier intelligence development, including investments in compute, model training, data acquisition, and safety and security systems, as well as our ability to attract, retain, and appropriately compensate highly skilled technical and operational personnel in a highly competitive market.
