Any such constraints could slow our rate of development and innovation, degrade model performance or reliability relative to competitors, limit our participation in industry standards-setting and regulatory processes, and reduce our attractiveness to enterprises and prosumers. These effects could create a self-reinforcing or compounding cycle in which diminished growth limits our capacity to invest in the resources necessary to remain competitive, which in turn could further weaken our ability to sustain or increase our revenue growth, making it increasingly difficult and costly to regain technological leadership and operate at the frontier of AI. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our ability to maintain our position at the frontier of AI depends in part on our use of AI systems to accelerate our research processes, a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” in which successive versions of our models assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time. Our models have been and are increasingly becoming critical tools in designing, training, testing, and optimizing next-generation AI systems. If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities, enabling the creation of increasingly advanced systems at an accelerating pace. As our reliance on our own AI systems to write production code, conduct research, and build subsequent model versions deepens, any systemic flaw, bias, or error in our current models could propagate into the next versions of models and products built using those systems, compounding across successive versions of Claude models in ways that may be difficult to detect or remediate. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our ability to deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models could be adversely affected. In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. Much of our evidence regarding the pace of such AI-driven acceleration is derived from lagging indicators, and our ability to forecast or measure the rate at which our capabilities are advancing, including any acceleration attributable to our most recent or unreleased models, is limited. As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our use of AI systems has already been accelerating our research and development, and our internal estimates indicate that we may experience a further increase in the rate of progress in AI capabilities. Because the AI research and development capability threshold under our Responsible Scaling Policy applies where we 146 “observe or expect” a specified degree of accelerated progress, we made a determination that we have met this threshold based on what we expect from future models and our overall rate of progress, rather than on what we have observed from current models. We continue to assess the underlying data. We are also evaluating the implications of meeting the AI research and development capability threshold and will release further reports in the future. If our capabilities were to outpace our safety, alignment, and security measures, or if we were unable to anticipate the pace of such advancement, we may be unable to adequately assess or mitigate the resulting risks, which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In light of these uncertainties, including limits on our ability to observe the pace at which our capabilities are advancing, we have adopted, and may continue to adopt, precautionary safety, alignment, and security measures to allow our safety efforts to advance together with model capabilities. In the past these measures have included delaying the release of models and limiting their initial availability, such as with Mythos through Project Glasswing, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, they could include additional measures that affect whether, how, and when we develop or deploy new models or capabilities. We cannot predict with precision when we will determine that such measures are necessary, what measures will be required, or how long they will remain in place, and as the capabilities of our models advance, such measures may become more frequent and more costly. These measures could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints, and could adversely affect our competitive position, revenue growth, and results of operations. The development of frontier models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars. There is no guarantee that any given training run will succeed—a run may fail for a number of reasons, such as failing to achieve the targeted capability or safety thresholds, producing unexpected or undesirable behaviors that cannot be adequately remediated, or yielding a model that is ultimately not competitive with alternatives available in the market. We would also face the additional cost and delay of initiating a new training run to attempt to achieve the intended model improvements. We have in the past experienced, and may in the future experience, such failed or underperforming training runs, resulting in a loss of invested resources with limited or no corresponding benefit to our business. Given the scale of compute and other resources required for frontier model training and the extended timelines involved, a failed or underperforming training run could also delay our product roadmap, affect our competitive position, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. New models, features, or capabilities may not be introduced on schedule, may not perform as intended, may require significant iteration after release, may fail to gain meaningful adoption, or may take longer than expected to gain meaningful adoption, any of which could reduce customer demand or place us at a competitive disadvantage. In addition, considerations relating to model safety, interpretability, alignment, and welfare may lead us to limit or delay the deprecation of older models or to continue supporting legacy versions alongside newer releases, creating tradeoffs in product development and compute distribution that could adversely affect innovation velocity, infrastructure utilization, and revenue. Customers who have integrated older models into their workflows may resist migration to newer versions, and any accelerated or forced deprecation could result in customer attrition, contractual disputes, or reputational harm. We have also changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities, which could adversely affect our reputation and the perceived value of our offerings. Some of these changes have resulted, and could in the future result, in claims that our disclosures regarding model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading.

 
147 Further, the industry benchmarks commonly used to test AI models may not accurately reflect real-world performance or utility, and even models that perform well on such benchmarks may not meet customer expectations when deployed in production environments, which could lead to customer dissatisfaction, reduced usage, or reputational harm. If we are unable to effectively innovate and improve our models, platform, and applications while addressing these challenges, or if competitors are able to deliver AI solutions that are perceived as more capable, safer, or more reliable, or that offer adequate performance at a lower cost, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. In addition, innovation in AI involves addressing complex and evolving challenges related to data quality, data integrity, training methodologies, bias, safety, accuracy, and the behavior of model outputs. AI algorithms may be flawed, and AI systems may contain bugs, errors, or defects or fail to follow instructions or produce inaccurate, misleading, offensive, inappropriate, or otherwise harmful outputs; reflect or amplify unwanted or unknown biases present in training data; or raise concerns relating to intellectual property, privacy, or other legal and ethical considerations. We must continually invest resources to identify, mitigate, remediate, and reduce the occurrence of such issues, including through managing and improving datasets, training techniques, evaluation methods, safeguards, and human oversight. However, we may not be able to obtain the datasets that we need, including through licenses or strategic data partnerships. In addition, we or our data providers may use synthetic or AI-generated data in the training process, which could introduce quality issues, amplify biases or errors, contribute to model degradation, or raise novel legal questions regarding ownership, licensing, or intellectual property rights that may not be timely or clearly resolved by courts or regulators. Such unintended consequences, failures, or misuse of our models could impair customer trust, slow adoption, expose us to legal or regulatory scrutiny, or adversely affect our brand and reputation. If we are unable to secure adequate compute or if we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers. Our ability to develop, train, improve, and deploy frontier models depends on our access to enormous and increasing quantities of specialized compute. The training of Claude models has required, and we expect will continue to require, substantial compute. Industry participants, academic researchers, and our own experience suggest that, in certain contexts, applying greater amounts of compute during model training has been associated with improvements in model capabilities. These observations are consistent with aspects of broader empirical relationships among model performance, model size, training data, and compute scale that are commonly referred to as “Scaling Laws,” although the extent, efficiency, and durability of such improvements are uncertain, and these relationships may plateau, diminish, or fail to materialize at larger scales or under different conditions. Accordingly, our ability to remain at the frontier of AI capabilities is substantially dependent on our ability to secure compute at the scale required to sustain all our workloads, including to train next-generation models, and we cannot provide assurance that increased investment in compute will result in commensurate improvements in model performance. The market for compute is intensely competitive. We compete for access to compute with some of the world’s largest and most well-capitalized technology companies, many of which develop their own competitive AI models and have significantly greater financial resources than us. Many own and operate cloud computing data center infrastructure, maintain captive chip manufacturing or design capabilities, have long-standing strategic relationships with key hardware suppliers, or have significant equity investments from, or other financial arrangements with, such suppliers. These competitors can outbid us for scarce compute, secure priority allocations from chip manufacturers and CSPs, and make long-term capital 148 commitments that we cannot match. We expect demand for advanced compute to continue to grow, and the cost of compute could rise significantly, particularly if AI-driven demand accelerates or if the ability to build highly capable models becomes more broadly available and shifts competition toward access to advanced compute. Additionally, numerous well-funded AI companies are pursuing large-scale AI model development, further increasing demand for limited compute. Certain CSPs from which we obtain substantial compute also develop and offer their own AI models and related services. As a result, our commercial relationships with these providers may not always be fully aligned with our long-term interests, and if the compute we have access to from third parties is curtailed, repriced, or terminated, whether for competitive reasons or otherwise, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. In addition to competition from third parties, our ability to secure compute is subject to allocation decisions by our CSPs. Although our CSPs are generally subject to contractual commitments with us regarding the provision of compute, our ability to obtain such capacity remains dependent on those providers’ operational execution, adherence to the terms of such contractual provisions, and broader business considerations, such as capacity constraints, internal demand for compute to support their own AI and computing operations, relationships with or contractual obligations to third parties (which may include other AI companies), and risk management considerations. As a result, we may not receive the full amount of compute we seek, or such compute may not be delivered on the timelines we require, even where contractual arrangements are in place. Additionally, we have in the past sought quantities of compute from CSPs in excess of what those partners were willing to provide. If our CSPs reduce, limit, or fail to increase our allocations to keep pace with our growing requirements for any reason, we may need to seek alternative compute sources on less favorable terms or timelines, and we may be unable to secure adequate alternative compute, or any at all. In addition, certain of our compute providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing or credit support to acquire chips and develop capacity, and if such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered. Any such shortfall could constrain our ability to train models, serve customers, or maintain our competitive position. Even if we are able to secure compute, we must still direct it efficiently across the full range of workloads that are a part of our business, including research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. While we manage our compute as a single, fungible pool and direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be most productive at any given time, there can be no assurance that this approach to compute will be the most efficient or that it will support the needs of each of our workloads. Because demand for compute has historically exceeded available capacity, any constraint on our ability to procure, maintain, or expand that capacity could adversely affect multiple aspects of our business simultaneously, including our ability to serve customers at the quality and scale they expect, to train and improve our models, and to develop new products and capabilities. While we actively manage and balance such compute capacity across these workloads via our capacity management system, if this system fails to perform as intended, or if our ability to dynamically rebalance capacity across workloads is disrupted, customer-facing service quality or model and product development timelines could be adversely affected. There can be no assurance that we will make optimal resourcing decisions, and any significant inefficiencies, including those related to deployment and rebalancing, could adversely affect both our near-term results of operations and our long-term strategic position. These compute resourcing challenges are heightened by the growth of our agentic offerings, which involve multi-step reasoning chains, iterative tool invocations, extended context windows, and sustained inference sessions that consume significantly more compute per user interaction than single-turn API calls or chat-based interactions. As

 
149 agentic workloads grow as a proportion of our total compute demand, the aggregate compute required to serve our customers could increase disproportionately relative to the associated revenue, placing additional strain on our compute workload management decisions. The majority of our compute is procured under multi-year commitments that are typically entered into well in advance of the periods in which that compute is deployed. Because different accelerators have varying performance characteristics across workload types, the composition of our committed compute portfolio, including the mix of accelerator architectures procured from our partners, reflects our demand forecasts and development roadmap assumptions at the time those commitments are made. If the magnitude or mix of workloads we need to support differs materially from those forecasts, whether due to changes in model architecture, customer demand, internal operations, or research priorities, the composition of our available compute may not optimally match our needs in a given period. This could affect our ability to serve customers, develop models, and support internal operations. If we fail to secure sufficient compute, or if we fail to effectively direct the limited compute we have across our workloads to develop and deploy models with capabilities at least comparable to those of our competitors, we risk falling behind the technological frontier. The pace of AI development is extremely rapid, with successive versions of models emerging in compressed timeframes, often measured in months rather than years. As a result, even a brief period without access to sufficient compute could cause us to fall behind quickly. With AI development, the gap between frontier models and those one or two versions behind can be significant in terms of capability, performance, and commercial applicability. Customers, partners, and software developers may shift to competitors whose models offer superior capabilities, and we may be unable to attract or retain the technical talent necessary for frontier research if our researchers lack access to adequate compute or if we are not perceived as operating at the forefront of model development. Any inability to maintain our position at the frontier could result in loss of customers and revenue, diminished brand and reputation, and a decline in our competitive position, each of which may be difficult to regain. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. If our actual compute requirements differ materially from our projections, we may fail to secure sufficient compute to meet our needs or we may be committed to excess compute that remains underutilized. The competitive and structural dynamics of the compute market require us to make binding financial commitments for compute months or years in advance of our day-to-day delivery and use. Chip manufacturers, CSPs, and data center developers require advance commitments in order to allocate production capacity, plan infrastructure investments, and manage their own supply chains. As a result, we must forecast our compute requirements well in advance of their deployment and commit capital accordingly, often with limited ability to adjust commitments if our needs change. These forecasts for future compute usage are inherently uncertain. Our actual compute requirements depend on numerous factors that are difficult to predict, including the pace of our research progress, the compute intensity of training techniques we develop or adopt, changes in the competitive landscape that may require us to accelerate or modify our development plans, customer demand for inference compute, and the evolution of hardware or other technological efficiencies and changes. If we underestimate our compute requirements, we may be unable to secure sufficient compute to support our forecasted customer demand and model development roadmap. In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment. 150 Further, the timing of compute coming online may not align with the timing of demand growth, which could result in periods of excess or underutilized compute and committed cash outflows that do not produce immediate revenue. Our ability to forecast and secure the compute we need is further challenged by our ongoing transition from a cloud-only, fixed-time arrangement compute model to a hybrid model that includes directly leased chips that are hosted in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification. This transition introduces additional variables into our procurement planning, including the timing of facility completion, the pace at which newly commissioned facilities achieve full operational capacity, our ability to operate, maintain, and integrate on-premise capacity with cloud-based infrastructure, the operational execution of our suppliers, and the performance of hardware in new facility environments. Delays in securing energy, water, and other critical services for these facilities could further slow the pace at which newly commissioned compute becomes available for use. Errors in forecasting any of these transition- related variables could compound our risks related to securing sufficient compute and result in either capacity shortfalls or underutilized capacity during the transition period. We have entered into, and expect to continue to enter into, long-term agreements for compute and related resources that involve minimum purchase commitments, take-or-pay provisions, and other terms that obligate us to pay for resources regardless of actual utilization. These commitments represent substantial fixed obligations. As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure. These commitments include approximately $451.6 billion expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $70.7 billion of these commitments are due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. Please refer to “4: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition, Operating Results, and Cash Flows—Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations” for more information. Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth. We must grow our customer base and expand revenue rapidly in order to generate the cash flows necessary to satisfy these commitments. However, our revenue is primarily consumption-based, and much of it is not subject to long-term contractual commitments, while our compute and infrastructure commitments generally extend over multiple years. As a result, we may enter into these obligations based on revenue expectations that may not be realized. If our revenue growth does not keep pace with our compute-related payment obligations, if we are unable to successfully convert our compute investment into revenue-generating customer workloads, if we fail to raise additional capital on acceptable terms, or if we experience other adverse developments affecting our liquidity, we may be unable to satisfy these obligations. Any such failure could also result in defaults under our agreements, loss of access to critical resources, and reputational harm. In particular, a default under certain commercial agreements could trigger cross-default provisions under the A&R Credit Agreement (as defined below) and certain of our outstanding convertible promissory notes, potentially resulting in the acceleration of substantially all of our outstanding, and any future, indebtedness. Such cross-defaults could set off a cascading series of adverse consequences, including the exercise of remedies by multiple creditors, the termination of key commercial arrangements, enforcement actions against our assets, and severe liquidity constraints. An acceleration of our indebtedness, combined with the loss of access to critical data center infrastructure, among other things, could impair our ability to train and deploy models, serve

 
151 customers, and fund ongoing operations, which could have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. For more information, please refer to “—We have incurred significant indebtedness in order to operate and grow our business, including to fund our substantial compute commitments, and our ability to service this indebtedness may be constrained by our cash flows and liquidity” and “—We may not have the ability to raise the funds necessary to repay the principal and accrued interest of our outstanding convertible promissory notes or the A&R Credit Agreement in cash when required by the terms of the notes or the A&R Credit Agreement, as applicable, or at their maturity” below. Additionally, the rapid pace of technological change across AI infrastructure, hardware, software, system architectures, and model development techniques means that compute secured today may become less efficient or economically attractive relative to future alternatives. We may find ourselves committed to using older-generation hardware and infrastructure while competitors gain access to more advanced systems, or we may be paying premium prices for resources that have declined in market value. These dynamics could adversely affect our cost structure and competitive position. Certain of our financing arrangements require us to enter into exclusive or preferential supply commitments with particular chip suppliers with respect to the compute financed pursuant to such arrangements. These commitments may limit our ability to shift procurement to alternative suppliers or newer chip architectures if our needs or the technology landscape evolve, potentially leaving us committed to platforms that are suboptimal for our actual workload requirements and reducing our ability to adjust our compute portfolio in response to changed circumstances. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. Constraints on the critical inputs supporting compute could limit our ability to secure adequate compute. The compute necessary for training and deploying frontier models depends on a supply chain with multiple potential points of constraint or failure. The availability, pricing, and lead times for compute are affected by the supply of advanced chips and other IT equipment, the availability of sufficient electrical power and the infrastructure required to generate and deliver it, and the capacity of data center infrastructure. Each of these inputs faces significant constraints that may limit our ability to secure the compute we need. In addition, increasing demand for compute has contributed to, and may continue to contribute to, increases in the cost of such resources, which could limit our ability to invest in, develop, or deploy our models, platform, and applications at the pace we anticipate. Supply and Concentration of Chips, Memory, and Data Center Equipment The specialized chips required for AI workloads, particularly high-performance accelerators and memory, are produced by a limited number of manufacturers. The production of advanced chips is extraordinarily complex, requiring manufacturing processes at the leading edge of technological capability. The majority of the world’s most advanced chip manufacturing capacity is concentrated in Taiwan, primarily at TSMC. This geographic concentration creates significant risks, including exposure to natural disasters such as earthquakes and typhoons, potential disruption from geopolitical tensions between Taiwan and China, vulnerability to any interruption in Taiwan’s power grid, water supply, or other critical infrastructure, and susceptibility to developing trade regulations and restrictions. Any military conflict, tariffs and trade restrictions, economic coercion, blockade, natural disaster, or other incident affecting Taiwan could severely disrupt the global supply of advanced chips, with effects that could persist for years given the time required to construct and qualify alternative fabrication facilities. Efforts to establish sufficient advanced 152 chip manufacturing capacity outside of Taiwan, including in the United States, remain in early stages and may not produce adequate compute to materially reduce these concentration risks within the foreseeable future. In addition, due to the demand for advanced chip manufacturing, TSMC has, at times, been unable to fully satisfy market demand for chip manufacturing capacity, and as a result, we have not always been able to obtain sufficient quantities of chips on a timely basis. Accordingly, any restrictions or delays on the supply of advanced chips out of Taiwan or TSMC would adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In addition, both high-bandwidth memory, which is a key component in high-performance accelerators, and other high-performance memory products used in compute infrastructure, are largely manufactured by SK hynix Inc., Samsung Electronics Co., and Micron Technology, Inc. Each of these manufacturers is working to expand its production capacity to meet demand. However, there is no guarantee that these efforts will result in adequate supply fast enough to meet demand, particularly if large customers or competitors secure exclusive supply commitments or otherwise reserve substantially all of a manufacturer’s available production capacity. The concentration and constraints in manufacturing supply expose us to the risk that manufacturers may make allocation decisions or strategic shifts that adversely affect our access to the advanced chips needed for our business. We also face risks that specialized chips may contain defects, or that their production or delivery may be delayed or disrupted, which, given long replacement lead times, could constrain available compute and adversely affect our operations and ability to scale. A meaningful portion of the components we and our partners rely on is sourced from or manufactured outside of the United States, and new or increased tariffs, import restrictions, or trade disputes could delay deliveries, force supply-chain changes, or raise our costs, some of which we bear directly under pass-through arrangements. For more information, please refer to “—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets” below. We also depend on third-party chip design and services companies for the design, manufacture, and support of certain custom accelerator platforms, as well as for related infrastructure financing arrangements. Disruption to these relationships, or any failure by these parties to deliver hardware or services on expected timelines and specifications, could adversely affect the availability, performance, or cost of accelerator platforms on which we rely. Data centers also require electrical, generation, and transmission equipment, cooling systems, backup generators, and networking hardware, some of which are made by only a few manufacturers, must be ordered years in advance, and require substantial pre-delivery payments that we may not recover if our plans change. In addition, certain equipment, such as high-voltage transformers, switchgear, turbines, generators, substations, and transmission components, has been subject to extended delivery timelines, price increases, tariffs and national security requirements, and allocation constraints as demand from data center operators and other large electricity consumers has grown. If such equipment is delayed or unavailable, we may be able to replace it only at higher prices or under less favorable long-term commitments. In order to secure near-term access to compute, we may also elect, or be required, to procure long-lead-time generation and electrical equipment at prices above prevailing market rates on the expectation that it can be deployed on an accelerated timeline to unlock capacity in the near term. Realizing the benefit of paying such prices depends on the timely and successful engineering, procurement, and construction of the associated facilities, which requires specialized expertise that is currently in short supply and involves significant execution risk. Delays, cost overruns, or failure to secure energy on the anticipated

 
153 schedule could mean that we do not obtain the energy and capacity for which we paid such prices. In some cases, these arrangements also depend on a developer or other counterparty agreeing to purchase the equipment at such prices, finance such purchase, and recover those costs and associated financing costs from us over time, and we may bear these costs even if the underlying capacity is delayed or never realized. Our equipment supply framework agreements and similar arrangements may expose us to further risks, including minimum purchase or take-or-pay commitments, price escalation, and obligations that we are unable to align with our actual deployment needs. Additionally, the U.S. government has imposed and may continue to impose export controls restricting the sale of advanced chips and chip manufacturing equipment to certain countries, including China. These restrictions have affected global chip and related equipment supply allocation, and future changes in export control policy could affect the availability or pricing of the compute resources on which we rely. Future export controls could be more restrictive, for example, by placing restrictions on the countries in which advanced chips may be installed or in which model weights may be stored, which could limit where we or our partners are able to build data centers, constrain our international expansion, or increase our costs. Electrical Power and Fuel Constraints The operation of data centers at the scale required for frontier model development and deployment consumes substantial quantities of electrical power. The availability of sufficient electrical power has emerged as a significant constraint on data center development and expansion in many geographies, including the United States. Electric grid infrastructure in the United States and other countries was not designed to accommodate the rapid increase in demand associated with AI development, and the lead times required to build new generation capacity, transmission infrastructure, and grid interconnections can extend for years. Demand on electric grid infrastructure is also increasing as a result of the increased electrification of homes, vehicles, and industry, and this growing demand is occurring at a time when power generation capacity additions, transmission expansion, and grid modernization efforts have not kept pace and certain existing generation resources are being retired, all of which has contributed to higher electricity prices and longer interconnection timelines in certain regions. We have publicly committed to covering the cost of electricity price increases to consumers caused by our data centers, including both the cost of electricity itself and the infrastructure necessary to deliver it. Our access to electrical power also depends on our ability, and the ability of the third parties on which we rely for the construction, management, and operation of our data center facilities, to negotiate and maintain contracts with utility providers and grid operators and to obtain approvals from public utility commissions and other regulators. These parties may be unable or unwilling to approve, or may condition or delay, the connections, capacity expansions, special or negotiated rate arrangements, and infrastructure investments necessary to support data center growth, or may grant them only at costs that limit the economic efficiency and viability of certain facilities, such as by requiring us to bear grid upgrade or interconnection costs beyond those attributable to serving our facilities—representing a larger share of costs than is required under existing or prior regulatory constructs. Interconnection queues for large new electricity loads have also lengthened substantially in many regions, which could delay or limit our access to grid power. Utility providers and regulators may also reallocate previously committed capacity that our data center facilities may require. In many jurisdictions, a single utility provider has substantial control over the terms, timing, and cost of the service and infrastructure necessary to power our data center facilities. The commercial and regulatory priorities of utility providers may differ from ours, including with respect to which infrastructure investments are made, how their costs are allocated, and whether alternative or self-supplied generation arrangements are permitted and on what conditions. Utility providers and other stakeholders may also seek 154 regulatory or legislative measures affecting large electricity loads, self-supply, or alternative power generation arrangements. The outcomes of our negotiations and regulatory proceedings involving utilities are uncertain, and unfavorable results could increase our costs, delay our projects, or limit the alternatives available to us. More broadly, regulatory proceedings relating to cost allocation, rate design, and the treatment of large electricity loads are ongoing in numerous jurisdictions, and adverse outcomes, changes in policy, or the imposition of new tariffs, surcharges, or curtailment obligations applicable to data centers could increase our costs or limit our access to electrical power. In addition, the construction of the generation and transmission infrastructure on which we depend is itself capital-intensive and exposed to labor shortages, supply chain disruptions, permitting delays, changes in interest rates, tariffs, other cost overruns, and financing constraints. The significant and increasing capital required to fund these generation, transmission, and related infrastructure investments, whether incurred by us, our utility and energy supply providers, or our data center development partners, is sensitive to prevailing interest rates and the availability of debt or equity financing on acceptable terms. Any inability of our partners to access capital when needed, and the limitations, cost, and competition for such capital, could increase the cost of the power on which we depend, delay or halt projects, or render certain facilities commercially unviable, and under certain of our arrangements, we bear these financing and capital costs directly or on a pass-through basis. Furthermore, newer sources of generation, such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal power, may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost. Our facilities separately depend on access to reliable water for cooling, which in some regions is scarce, subject to use restrictions, or increasingly costly. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect the availability of the power or water we require, increase our costs, or limit our ability to develop, expand, or operate our data center facilities, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense, and we compete for such access with well-capitalized CSPs, some of which produce and develop competing AI models, cryptocurrency mining operations, and other large-scale electricity consumers. In addition to, or sometimes in lieu of, grid-based electricity, an increasing share of data centers are being developed with dedicated on-site power generation capacity that supplies electricity directly to the facility independent of any utility-operated electric grid. The reliability of such off-grid power generation solutions varies by the underlying technology, the equipment used, and the operator and will reflect site-by-site operational and environmental profiles. Development of this new capacity in turn requires power generation and electrical infrastructure that are themselves subject to supply challenges and operational complexity. For example, certain of our planned data center facilities rely on dedicated on-site natural gas-fired generation, which exposes us to fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of our control and for which we bear the cost on a pass-through basis. These facilities are also subject to constraints on pipeline capacity and firm fuel transportation necessary to deliver natural gas. As data center operators increasingly rely on natural gas-fired generation, and because behind-the-meter and on-site arrangements are feasible only in some jurisdictions given the applicable regulatory frameworks, we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas. This competition could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply and transportation and to secure the pipeline connections and laterals our facilities require. These dynamics present several related risks. We may be unable to secure firm gas supply and transportation during the development of a facility, causing a planned site to be delayed or abandoned; we

 
155 may face fuel supply or delivery disruptions once a facility is operating; and because our arrangements generally provide for fuel and related costs to be borne by us on a pass-through basis without cost caps, we remain exposed to increases in the cost of natural gas and its transportation. More broadly, the cost of electricity is subject to significant variability that is largely outside of our control, as wholesale electricity prices fluctuate with changing supply and demand, weather, fuel prices, tariffs or surcharges, and grid stress, and can rise sharply during periods of peak demand or constrained supply, and such increases in energy costs could adversely affect our results of operations. In some regions, including certain regions where we have contracted compute commitments, data center development has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources. For example, if our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts. More broadly, our access to electrical power is subject to an evolving regulatory framework characterized by complexity, jurisdictional overlap, and rules that were largely designed around service by incumbent utility providers and existing generation arrangements and that may not readily accommodate new entrants or alternative approaches, which can result in significant delay or prevent the development of the generation we require. Grid-tied electrical supply, for instance, is subject to the jurisdiction of federal and state energy regulators, regional grid operators, and public utility commissions, while behind-the-meter and on-site generation is subject to a distinct set of exclusive service franchise protections, permitting, environmental, air quality, interconnection, and siting requirements. In addition, environmental standards applicable to power generation continue to evolve, including as a result of changing governmental priorities and shifting public and political views regarding climate change and the appropriate treatment of various power generation sources. Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers. We have also made, and may in the future make, voluntary commitments to offset the impact of our data center energy consumption on local communities and electricity ratepayers, including commitments to cover grid infrastructure upgrade costs, procure new power generation to match our energy needs, invest in curtailment systems to reduce strain on the grid during peak demand periods, and address environmental impacts. These commitments have increased, and we expect will continue to increase, our operating costs. Moreover, we believe this is part of a broader emerging trend in the AI industry, and such commitments, or similar obligations, may become increasingly standard or required, which could further increase our costs. In addition, the physical effects of climate change may increase our operating costs over time, as higher average temperatures can increase the power consumption and water usage required to cool equipment at the facilities on which we depend. Data Center Infrastructure Even where chips and electrical power are available, the development of data center facilities requires substantial time, capital, and specialized expertise. Data center construction involves lengthy permitting processes, complex supply chains for specialized equipment, and significant lead times for the installation and commissioning of cooling systems, electrical infrastructure, and networking equipment. Labor shortages, including shortages of, and competition for, electricians, facility technicians, and other skilled tradespeople, supply chain disruptions, permitting delays, and other factors can extend construction timelines and increase costs. Further, given data center development projects require significant advance 156 capital commitments with dedicated end users, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements for financing or with partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center capacity that is expected to host such partner’s chips or computing infrastructure. In addition, there are a limited number of qualified third-party vendors with the expertise we require and that support the particular infrastructure we wish to implement. Accordingly, we rely on this limited number of third parties for the construction, management, and operation of certain of our data center facilities, some of which have limited operating history or may have less experience operating data center infrastructure at the scale and complexity our operations require. In certain cases, these third-party operators are trained or supervised by our chip partners to manage facilities on our behalf but are not affiliates of those partners and may not have the same depth of expertise, operational resilience, or resources. Any failure by these third-party operators to perform as expected could disrupt our access to compute. In addition, safety or environmental incidents at facilities built or operated for us, whatever their cause, could expose us to claims, fines, or suspensions of construction or operations, the costs of which we may bear. We also depend on an extended network of suppliers, builders, and facility operators. If any of them engage in practices that are unsafe, unlawful, or contrary to the labor, human rights, environmental, or other standards we or our partners require, we could face legal liability, lose the ability to use affected suppliers or facilities, and suffer harm to our reputation, even where we did not direct or know of the conduct. Our collective data center infrastructure is currently concentrated primarily in the United States, which exposes us to risks associated with regional regulatory changes, power grid constraints or failures, disruptions to network connectivity between facilities, natural disasters, physical attacks—including those motivated by geopolitical events, opposition to AI, and opposition to data center development—and other disruptions that could affect multiple facilities. Certain state, local, and municipal jurisdictions in the United States are also considering or have approved moratoriums on new data center construction, citing public health, safety, and environmental concerns. Such jurisdictions and other regulators, grid operators, or utilities may also adopt other measures that subject users of large electricity loads, including data centers, to curtailment, interruptions, forced reductions, disconnection, or other restrictions during periods of grid stress, whether through changes in law or policy, market or reliability constraints, limits on transmission and distribution infrastructure, or a preference for protecting other utility customers and the broader grid. New large loads on the electric grid may be increasingly subject to mandatory curtailment in regions where there is insufficient grid-connected power generation to reliably supply existing and new electricity loads. For example, states such as New York and Texas have recently moved to regulate large-scale data centers, whether by pausing state permitting for new large facilities, as New York has, or by subjecting large electricity loads to curtailment or disconnection during grid emergencies, as Texas has. Such moratoriums, or similar actions, could delay or prevent the construction or expansion of facilities on which we depend for compute. Opposition to data center development has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions, and our public profile may draw particular attention to projects associated with us. The loss of, or a significant disruption at, any major facility may not be readily absorbed by our remaining or future infrastructure. We are expanding our data center capacity internationally as part of our efforts to diversify our infrastructure footprint and reduce concentration risks associated with operating a significant portion of our compute infrastructure in the United States and to support our international growth strategy, including by entering into letters of intent and negotiating lease and related agreements for data center facilities in multiple non-U.S. jurisdictions, which exposes us to additional risks related to foreign regulatory requirements and approvals, data sovereignty and localization laws, governmental access or assistance requirements, cross-border data transfer restrictions, foreign tax regimes, and increased operational complexity. Our ability to enter into definitive agreements for data center capacity and operations in non- U.S. jurisdictions depends on the timely formation, registration, and receipt of governmental approval of

 
157 local subsidiaries, as well as the establishment of local banking arrangements, and any delay or failure in completing these steps could delay or prevent us from mitigating our infrastructure concentration risks, executing our international growth strategy, securing planned compute capacity, or could result in substantial additional taxes, penalties, or other liabilities. In addition, regulatory, legal, and other constraints in many jurisdictions may limit the locations in which we can practically site or contract for data center capacity, which could constrain our ability to diversify our infrastructure footprint as quickly or as broadly as we currently intend. We and our principal competitors rely on substantially similar inputs to develop and deploy frontier models, including advanced chips sourced from a small number of suppliers and data center capacity and compute obtained from CSPs and other third parties. As we and our competitors increasingly pursue vertical integration, the basis of competition could shift over time to encompass not only which company can develop the most capable models, but also which company can develop the best underlying components. Our future competitiveness may depend in part on our ability to successfully develop vertically integrated compute infrastructure on competitive terms and timelines, and there can be no assurance that we will be able to do so. Our competitors may be better positioned, or may invest greater efforts, to vertically integrate across the compute supply chain, including through proprietary chip design, fabrication, ownership or long- term control of data center infrastructure, access to dedicated power generation assets, exclusive supply arrangements with hardware manufacturers, or by securing the limited sites suitable for large-scale data center development ahead of us. Competitors that succeed in controlling a greater share of these supply chain layers may be able to secure compute at greater scale, lower cost, or with greater reliability than we can, particularly during periods of high demand or supply constraint, when captive supply relationships may confer certain advantages over participants that depend on third-party providers. Such competitors may also develop proprietary hardware-software co-designs that optimize compute efficiency for their specific model architectures, which could compound any capability gap across successive model versions. While we are pursuing initiatives to develop dedicated data center infrastructure, there can be no assurance that these efforts will be completed on the timelines or at the costs we anticipate, or that they will be sufficient to offset any structural advantages that vertically integrated competitors may achieve. Competitors that succeed in these efforts may be better positioned to remain at the frontier of AI regardless of broader market constraints. Natural hazards, extreme weather, or other disruptions affecting the regions where these inputs are produced or where our facilities are located could further constrain the availability of chips, power, water, or data center capacity on which we depend. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. We are highly dependent on the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and key technical employees, and the loss of any of these individuals may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We are highly dependent on the continued service of our Chief Executive Officer, President, co-founders, senior management team, and key technical team. In particular, our Chief Executive Officer and President are critical to setting our strategic direction, advancing our research agenda, shaping our safety and governance frameworks, and generally advancing our mission, and we believe that their leadership would be difficult to replace. If either were to become unavailable for any reason, or if either of their reputations were significantly harmed, regardless of merit, there could be an adverse impact on our operations and competitive position, employee morale, employee retention, pace of innovation, customer and partner confidence in our company, our brand and reputation, and our long-term strategic objectives. Further, the 158 loss of key personnel, including members of our founding team and senior management team, and key engineering, research, product development, marketing, and sales personnel, could also disrupt our operations and have an adverse effect on our business. Many of our key personnel, particularly within our technical and research teams, are strongly motivated by our mission and the opportunity to work on addressing specific problems within the AI landscape. To the extent that their interests evolve, they seek to pursue different technical challenges or areas of focus, or they are drawn to other organizations or initiatives that they perceive as better aligned with their personal beliefs or professional objectives, we may face increased difficulty retaining such personnel. This risk may be heightened as we continue to scale and mature as an organization, which may change the nature of the work environment, priorities, or perceived mission alignment for certain personnel, including personnel who may conclude that the objectives that drew them to us have been substantially achieved. In addition, under certain of our agreements with suppliers, the loss of certain key personnel could accelerate our obligations or otherwise trigger adverse consequences under such agreements. If we are unable to retain key personnel, or if we fail to conduct effective succession planning and find suitable replacements for any losses of such key personnel in a timely manner and on competitive terms, we could experience declines in sales, delays in research and development, and harm to our business and operations. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. We may require additional capital to meet our substantial ongoing obligations and support our business growth, and our ability to generate sufficient revenue and secure additional capital on acceptable terms is critical to our continued operations and competitive position. Our business model requires substantial and increasing capital to support our ability to remain competitive and to stay at the frontier of AI. We intend to continue to make significant financial investments to support our business growth and may require additional funds to acquire sufficient compute and respond to business challenges, including expenditures to create, maintain, upgrade, and enhance our models, platform, and applications, including costs related to investments in infrastructure, human capital, office expansion, and data assets. In addition, we may use a portion of our cash to satisfy tax withholding and remittance obligations related to outstanding RSUs and equity awards that we grant in the future. In addition, to date we have financed our compute primarily under arrangements with CSPs, with costs recognized as compute is made available to us. We may in the future finance a greater portion of our compute on an upfront basis, including through finance leases, prepayments, debt-financed purchases of equipment, or similar arrangements. If we were to do so, we may incur significant cash outflows in advance of compute availability or related revenue, which could increase demands on our cash flows and liquidity and our need to raise additional capital. Such arrangements could also increase our capital intensity and alter our cash-flow profile. Accordingly, it is critical that we maintain strong revenue growth, grow revenue efficiently relative to our committed compute, infrastructure, and personnel costs, and manage our cash flows effectively. To the extent that such efforts are insufficient to meet our capital needs, we may need to obtain additional capital through equity or debt financings. If we raise additional funds through future issuances of equity, equity- linked securities, or convertible debt securities, our existing stockholders could suffer dilution, and any new securities we issue could have rights, preferences, and privileges superior to those of holders of our common stock. Further, the conversion of our outstanding convertible securities will cause additional dilution to our existing stockholders. Any debt financing that we may secure in the future may involve

 
159 restrictive covenants relating to our capital raising activities and other financial and operational matters, potentially making it more difficult for us to obtain additional capital and to pursue business opportunities. In addition, our ability to draw amounts under certain of our note purchase agreements (“NPAs”) is not guaranteed and is subject to the satisfaction of specified conditions. In particular, our ability to access additional amounts under certain of these facilities depends on our achievement of certain revenue performance targets and/or the ability of third parties to deliver additional compute to us. While we have historically surpassed all such revenue performance targets, there can be no assurance that revenue will continue to exceed these thresholds at all times in the future. If these conditions are not satisfied, we may be unable to draw additional amounts under the applicable NPA, which could adversely affect our cash flows and liquidity. For more information about the terms of our convertible promissory notes, please refer to “4: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition, Operating Results, and Cash Flows— Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations—Convertible Notes.” We may not be able to obtain additional financing on terms favorable to us, if at all. We evaluate financing opportunities from time to time, and our ability to obtain financing will depend, among other things, on our development efforts, business plans, and operating performance and the condition of the capital markets at the time we seek financing. The equity and debt markets may experience extreme volatility and disruption from time to time, which could result in higher credit spreads in such markets and higher funding costs for us. If we are unable to generate sufficient revenue growth or obtain adequate financing or financing on terms satisfactory to us when we require it, our ability to continue to support our business growth, scale our infrastructure, develop new models, platform, and applications, enhance our existing models, platform, and applications, and respond to business challenges may be impaired, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected. Our company culture has contributed to our success and, if we cannot maintain this culture as we grow, our business could be adversely affected. We believe that our company culture is a critical component of our success. We are a mission-driven company and our culture reflects a strong emphasis on the Company Purpose. Our ability to continue to cultivate and maintain this culture is essential to our growth and continued success. We face a number of challenges associated with our commitment to our company culture, including: • the need to identify, attract, reward, and retain people in leadership positions in our organization who share and further our culture, values, and mission; • the increasing size and geographic diversity of our workforce, and our ability to promote a uniform and consistent culture across all of our offices and employees; • internal and external perceptions about our mission, values, commitment to safety, and uses of our models, platform, and applications; • engagement with government policymakers on issues that resonate differently across our workforce; • competitive pressures to move in directions that may divert us from our mission and values; • the rigorous, values-driven standards we apply in hiring and decision-making, which may slow the pace at which we can scale our workforce or expand our operations relative to competitors; 160 • the continued challenges of a rapidly evolving industry; • the increased scrutiny and expectations associated with operating as a public company; and • the need to balance our long-term, mission-driven objectives with shorter-term financial performance expectations, which may create internal tension and challenge our ability to consistently reinforce our cultural values and mission across teams and leadership. Our mission-driven culture is one of our core characteristics that helps us to attract and retain key personnel and differentiates us in the market. If we are unable to maintain our culture, as well as balance our commitment to maintaining our culture with the demands of rapid growth, competition, and operating as a public company, our employee morale, engagement, and retention could suffer, requiring us to incur additional costs or adopt alternative recruiting strategies, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. The market for AI models, platforms, and applications is rapidly evolving, intensely competitive, and subject to frequent and significant changes in technology, evolving customer requirements and expectations, shifting industry standards, regulatory developments, new market entrants, and new models, platforms, and applications. We face competition from a wide range of companies across multiple categories. We compete directly with companies developing frontier models for third-party software developers and enterprises. Our primary competitors in this category include Google and OpenAI. These competitors are developing increasingly capable AI systems and compete with us for customers, talent, compute, and strategic partnerships. Many have substantially greater financial, technical, and marketing resources than we do, their own or greater access to sources of compute, longer operating histories, greater brand recognition, and established relationships with current and potential customers and partners, which facilitates their ability to integrate their models into first-party applications sold directly to businesses. We also compete with a broader set of model providers operating at or below the frontier, including large companies, specialized AI labs, and a growing range of other open-weight or open-source (shared weights, training data, and code) models released by international and domestic organizations. Such providers compete for a growing range of enterprise workloads that prioritize cost efficiency over intelligence. In particular, certain large companies compete through proprietary AI models, integrated AI capabilities in existing products, and control of cloud infrastructure and distribution channels. Some of these companies also have substantially greater financial, technical, and marketing resources than we do, their own or greater access to sources of compute, longer operating histories, greater brand recognition, and established relationships with current and potential customers and partners. In addition, some have substantially broader and more diverse product and service offerings and may be able to leverage existing relationships with distribution partners and customers to gain business in ways that discourage customers from purchasing our models, platform, and applications. For example, competitors may bundle AI capabilities with other products, integrate AI functionality into products that customers already use, offer closed technology platforms that lock customers into their ecosystems, sell products at zero or negative margins to gain market share, or use their substantial financial resources to subsidize the cost of AI models, platforms, and applications. Customers may prefer to purchase from existing vendors with which they have established relationships, even if our models, platform, and applications offer superior features or performance. Further, large companies that are currently our customers may choose to develop their own

 
161 AI capabilities internally rather than purchase our models, platform, and applications. Specialized AI labs, on the other hand, are competitive due to their ability to offer specific AI applications and differentiated business models. These companies can move quickly, attract top talent, develop novel approaches, platforms, or business models that disrupt existing competitive dynamics, and introduce technologies or products with greater performance or functionality, lower cost, ease of implementation, or other advantages. Some competitors or customers may have access to proprietary datasets, distribution channels, or domain-specific expertise that we do not possess, or new competitors may emerge that address particular industries or use cases more effectively than our models, platform, and applications, which could enable them to develop more specialized or higher-performing AI systems. In addition, competitors, customers, or other third parties have attempted in the past and will likely continue to attempt to replicate, distill, extract, or otherwise derive the functionality or capabilities of our models through permitted or impermissible means, including through our research previews. These actions could reduce the technological differentiation of our offerings; enable the development of competing products at lower cost, with reduced research and development investment, or that replicate our models without safety controls or safeguards that were incorporated in our versions; implicate national security concerns or strain geopolitical tensions; and intensify competitive pressures. In addition, efforts to prevent or mitigate model replication, distillation, or other forms of extraction may require us to modify our models, platform, and applications, limit features or use cases, or implement technical safeguards that could reduce the usability or attractiveness of our offerings, slow adoption, and adversely affect customer demand and revenue. More broadly, as AI models are increasingly used to develop other AI models, the knowledge and techniques required to build frontier models may become more widely available over time, including through distillation, unauthorized access to or theft of model weights, or the diffusion of AI-assisted research and development capabilities across the industry. If the ability to develop highly capable models becomes more broadly available, our technological differentiation could erode and competition could increasingly depend on access to large-scale compute rather than on model development capability. In such an environment, access to sufficient compute on economical terms could become the primary constraint on our ability to train and serve competitive models, and our business, competitive position, and results of operations could be adversely affected if we are unable to secure compute at the scale or cost or on the timeline we require. Additionally, open-weight or open-source AI models may capture a portion of the market for certain use cases, which could exert pricing pressure on our offerings or lead certain customers to adopt open-source alternatives for those use cases. A significant portion of our customer base consists of startups and technology-oriented enterprises that may be more sensitive to adverse macroeconomic conditions and may reduce or delay spending during a downturn. Because our cost structure limits our ability to rapidly adjust spending, a sustained economic downturn could disproportionately disadvantage us relative to larger, better-capitalized competitors. Such competitors may be better positioned to absorb or withstand adverse economic conditions or reductions in customer technology spending due to their greater financial resources, diversified product offerings and customer bases, and more stable revenue streams. It could also disadvantage us relative to smaller startups with leaner cost structures, lower fixed overhead, and fewer long-term contractual commitments that could help enable them to adjust spending more rapidly than we can. As a result, competitive pressures on our business could intensify, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. If we are unable to differentiate our models, platform, and applications from competing offerings through enhanced functionality, superior performance, better safety features and reliability, lower cost, or other 162 factors, demand for our models, platform, and applications may decline. The rapid pace of technological change in AI means that models, platforms, and applications can quickly become outdated. We must continuously invest in research and development to maintain our competitive position, but there is no guarantee that our investments will result in models, platforms, and applications that customers prefer over competing alternatives. Moreover, we are first and foremost a research lab, and our strategy prioritizes frontier research and model capability. We believe the advancing intelligence and capabilities of our models are the principal drivers of their adoption, and we have historically prioritized research and model development rather than new products and applications or sales and marketing. This approach assumes that model capability will continue to be a meaningful source of competitive differentiation. However, as the AI industry matures, the degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow. This convergence may result from factors such as overlapping or similarly sourced training data, the widespread adoption of comparable model architectures, training techniques, and optimization methods, shared access to computing infrastructure, and the rapid dissemination of research advances across the industry. To the extent competitors are able to achieve comparable model capabilities with lower development or deployment costs, our ability to differentiate our models, platform, and applications on the basis of performance, functionality, or cost may be diminished. If differentiation among advanced models narrows, or if customers increasingly select AI providers on the basis of application features, user experience, distribution, integration into products they already use, or the strength of a sales organization rather than model capability, competitors that have invested more heavily than we have in those areas could be better positioned than we are. Responding to such a shift could require us to increase our investment in product development and sales and marketing substantially beyond our current plans, which could take longer or cost more than we anticipate and could reduce the compute and other resources available for frontier research, and we may not be able to execute such a shift quickly or effectively. See also “—We have a limited history under our current go-to-market strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition, engagement, and retention model may not be successful” below. If we are unable to compete successfully, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. If we fail to attract new customers, retain existing customers, or expand usage of our models, platform, and applications, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. Our future growth depends on our ability to attract new customers, retain existing customers, and expand sales within our existing customer base. We face significant challenges in each of these areas, and failure to execute on our customer acquisition and retention strategies could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We must continue to attract new customers in a cost-effective manner. Potential customers may not understand the benefits of our models, platform, and applications or may be unable to justify the investment in our models, platform, and applications, particularly as existing competitors continue to enhance their offerings, improve performance, expand functionality, or reduce costs. Our ability to demonstrate differentiated value to potential customers may become more difficult as this competition intensifies, or as large technology companies bundle AI capabilities into existing products. If we continue to focus on enterprise customers, we may face longer sales cycles that demand significant upfront investment in enterprise sales teams and customer service. These sales efforts are costly and may not result in customer conversion.

 
163 Even if we successfully attract new customers, we face significant challenges in retaining them. Many of our customer contracts allow customers to reduce usage or terminate with limited or no notice. Customers are not obligated to renew their subscriptions or contracts with us. Customer retention and usage levels may decline due to a number of factors, including: • dissatisfaction with the performance, reliability, safety, or accuracy of our AI models; • availability of competitive alternatives; • customers developing their own AI capabilities internally; • our models, platform, and applications reducing demand for our customers’ offerings or causing disruptions to their businesses, which could lead to reduced usage or customer attrition; • changes in customer budgets or strategic priorities regarding AI investment; • concerns about data privacy, security, or our data handling practices; • negative publicity regarding AI generally or our business specifically; • changes in the regulatory and legal landscape surrounding AI and our models, platform, and applications in particular; • pricing changes or perception that our pricing is not competitive; and • general economic conditions or industry-specific downturns affecting our customers. Our ability to retain customers and drive expansion also depends on our continued investment in product development. The process of developing products and incorporating new technologies is complex and uncertain, and if we fail to accurately predict customers’ changing needs and emerging technological trends and opportunities, we may not be able to compete effectively and our business and ability to generate revenue could be adversely affected. As AI technology evolves rapidly, customers may perceive our models, platform, and applications as becoming outdated or may expect continuous improvements to model performance and capabilities. Even minor degradations in model performance or increases in response latency could cause customers to reduce usage or switch to competitors. If we are unable to retain existing customers or if our customers do not maintain their usage levels, our revenue and growth could be adversely affected. For additional discussion on product development, please refer to “—Our success depends in large part on our ability to continue to develop the most advanced and capable AI models, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our business” above. Some of our enterprise customers may have the financial resources, technical capabilities, and access to the talent and compute necessary to develop and deploy proprietary AI models, and may reduce or cease usage of our models, platform, and applications as their internal AI capabilities mature, even where they initially adopted our offerings as a foundation for their AI strategy.
