If these customers were to reduce or cease usage of our models, platform, and applications, our revenue and growth could be adversely affected. In addition to retaining customers, our growth strategy depends in part on expanding usage within our existing customer base by increasing usage volumes, selling additional capabilities, and expanding adoption across departments and use cases within customer organizations. However, customers may not expand their usage for a variety of reasons, including satisfaction with current usage levels, budget constraints, technical challenges in integrating our models, platform, and applications more broadly within 164 their organizations, or preference for multi-vendor AI strategies in order to limit dependence on any single provider. Due to our consumption-based pricing model, customers may reduce or cease usage at any point within a given period due to budget or internal procurement constraints, organizational spending controls, or other factors unrelated to the quality or performance of our models, platform, and applications, and may not resume usage until a new budget period commences or additional spend is approved, even where demand for our models, platform, and applications remains strong. As a result, our revenue could be lower or more variable than anticipated and this effect may be particularly pronounced among customers experiencing rapid growth in their usage of AI. If we increase sales and marketing expenditures to accelerate customer acquisition without achieving proportional revenue growth and if we cannot attract new customers, retain existing customers, expand within our customer base, or accomplish these objectives in a cost-effective manner or timely manner, our revenue growth will decline and our business, financial condition, and results of operations will be adversely affected. If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. The market for AI technologies, including frontier models, platforms, and applications, has grown rapidly in recent years, but is still relatively nascent and evolving rapidly, and it is uncertain whether the market for such AI technologies will achieve or sustain widespread adoption at the pace or to the extent we expect. Our ability to generate revenue and achieve sustainable growth depends in significant part on the extent to which enterprises, software developers, and other users adopt AI technologies, integrate them into existing workflows, expand usage over time, and are willing to pay for our models, platform, and applications at levels that support durable economic value at scale. Market adoption may be slower than anticipated due to factors such as uncertainty regarding the cost, performance, reliability, and perceived value of AI solutions; increased regulation; concerns about security, privacy, legal and regulatory compliance, or ethical considerations; technological challenges; level of effort and expense associated with integration efforts; competition from alternative or emerging technologies; the availability or adoption of complementary infrastructure and workflows; or reductions in corporate spending due to macroeconomic conditions. Moreover, demand for frontier models may decline if customers determine that less advanced, lower-cost models are sufficient for their particular use cases. As AI capabilities improve across the industry and a broader range of models becomes available, customers may conclude that incremental performance gains at the frontier do not justify the additional cost, and may migrate toward smaller, cheaper, or open-source alternatives that adequately address their needs. If we are unable to demonstrate sufficient differentiated value from our frontier models relative to less capable alternatives, our revenue and growth could be adversely affected, even in a market where overall AI adoption continues to grow. Further, while AI adoption may continue or accelerate in certain areas, the long-term trajectory of this technological trend is uncertain, and market understanding, acceptance, and valuation of AI-enabled models, platforms, and applications may be inaccurate or change over time and adoption may occur unevenly across industries, geographies, and customer types. If growth in the AI market does not translate into sustained customer demand for our offerings, expanded usage, and increased revenue, or if anticipated use cases fail to materialize, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. The political environment and our engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action. Our commitment to responsible and safe AI development includes active engagement with policymakers,

 
165 regulators, and other stakeholders regarding the development of AI-related laws, regulations, and standards. We have participated in, and will likely continue to participate in, political processes, including through contributions, advocacy, or support of political organizations. In addition, our executives and other representatives have publicly expressed and may in the future publicly express views on AI policy, regulation, safety, and related social or political issues. As a result, we have experienced, and may continue to experience, increased visibility and may continue to be subject to heightened scrutiny or the risk of being disproportionately or selectively targeted by particular governmental bodies, even where similarly situated companies are not, including through investigations or enforcement actions, the imposition or selective application of regulatory, licensing, or permitting requirements, adverse treatment in government procurement or provision of security clearances, or targeted immigration or visa actions affecting our personnel. As part of our political engagement, we have advocated for, and will likely continue to advocate for, regulatory approaches or industry standards that we believe promote the safe and responsible development of AI but that could increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, or otherwise slow our growth relative to competitors. Our public positions, stated values, policy advocacy, or statements by our executives have attracted, and may continue to attract, criticism from influential political figures, industry participants, regulators, or other third parties, particularly in politically sensitive or polarized environments, which could shape public narratives or regulatory perceptions of our business in ways that are unfavorable to us. For example, public statements by us or other industry participants regarding the safety of frontier model development have been cited by governmental actors to support litigation or regulatory claims, including requests for injunctive relief restricting model development, and could be cited in future proceedings involving us. Such scrutiny or backlash could result in reputational harm, increased compliance or operating costs, investigations, enforcement actions, or restrictions on our operations, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. While our AI models are designed to comply with our AI safety and usage guidelines and be broadly safe, ethical, and helpful, and while we have implemented safety measures intended to anticipate, identify, and mitigate potential harmful uses, such measures are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, or may fail to identify or prevent all potential misuse of our models, and our models have been, and may continue to be, misused or manipulated to produce harmful outputs or carry out harmful actions. Malicious actors have used, and may continue to develop novel or more sophisticated methods to use, our models in ways that violate our usage policy or seek to circumvent our model guardrails or safeguards through techniques such as prompt injection, adversarial inputs, or other methods, and use our models to engage in harmful activities, including developing weapons, generating fraudulent or misleading content, conducting cyberattacks, perpetrating acts of violence, or otherwise engaging in activities that would be prohibited under our usage policy or in violation of applicable law. Our customer onboarding diligence varies by access channel, and we do not and in certain situations cannot uniformly verify the identity of those who access our models or of our customers’ end users, which may limit our ability to prevent access or recidivism by malicious actors or to enforce our usage policy or other policies. Moreover, our safety and security controls, including automated classifiers and monitoring systems, depend on complex internal configurations that have failed, been misconfigured, or been inadvertently disabled, 166 and may do so again in the future without our timely detection. Any undetected failure of our safety controls could permit misuse that our safeguards are designed to prevent, and could result in real-world harm, legal liability, regulatory or enforcement action, loss of customer trust, and reputational harm, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In particular, our most capable models have demonstrated, and future models are expected to demonstrate, capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons. We deploy technical safeguards, including automated classifiers, specifically intended to detect and block these categories of misuse, but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended. Any actual or perceived use of our models to contribute to the development of such weapons could result in harm, legal liability, regulatory or enforcement action, loss of government and enterprise relationships, and damage to our reputation and brand, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. For example, in September 2025, we detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state- sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies, resulting in a limited number of successful intrusions. We believe this is the first documented case of a large-scale cyberattack executed without substantial human intervention. We expect that malicious actors, including sophisticated state-sponsored actors, will continue to seek to leverage our models, platform, and applications for harmful actions, including by circumventing our safeguards, and their efforts to do so may increase as the capabilities of our technology increase. Any successful attempt to misuse, or any perceived misuse of, our models, platform, and applications for a cyberattack or for any other malicious purpose could result in exposure to liability, disruption of our customer or other commercial relationships, or damage to our reputation. The risks of such harms may increase as the cybersecurity-related capabilities of our models, platform, and applications increase. Independent security researchers and other third parties have also used, and may in the future use, our models to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in the systems of other companies, including other AI developers, at times in connection with authorized bug bounty programs. While such activity may be lawful and consistent with industry practice for vulnerability research, it illustrates that our models can function as a general-purpose tool for gaining unauthorized access to third-party systems, and comparable capabilities could be used by malicious actors without authorization. Such incidents, whether or not we are a direct party to them, may draw public and regulatory attention to the offensive cybersecurity capabilities of our models and could result in reputational harm, calls for additional restrictions on our models, or claims that we failed to adequately safeguard against such uses. For more information about risks related to security incidents, please refer to “—Any security breaches or other incidents, including those that affect our networks, systems, or data, or the networks, systems, or data of our service providers, suppliers, or customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations” below. As part of our commitment to responsible security research and transparency, we disclose information about the capability and safety of our models, the safeguards that we have adopted with respect to our models, and instances of misuse of our technology, such as the September 2025 cyberattack described above. We also publish model system cards, our research findings, and other safety-related information. We take steps to ensure that such disclosures will not materially assist malicious activity and weigh the benefits and risks of such disclosures from an ecosystem preparedness perspective; however, malicious actors, including sophisticated state-sponsored adversaries, have in the past and may in the future use

 
167 those disclosures to assist their attempts to circumvent our safeguards and security measures, thereby increasing the risks of misuse of our models, platform, and applications, as well as the potential for exposure to liability, regulatory or litigation proceedings, or other harms. In addition, because these disclosures describe risks and observed model behaviors in detail, they may draw heightened public, media, or regulatory attention and could be cited by regulators, litigants, or others in proceedings or claims against us. The steps we take to prevent misuse of our models, platform, and applications could be incomplete or may fail to operate as intended, and any actual or perceived misuse could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models, and our contractual protections and insurance may be insufficient, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Harms associated with our AI models, whether arising from misuse by third parties, from our models’ own behavior, or from their deployment in high-risk or sensitive contexts, may expose us to liability, litigation, and regulatory action, including under theories that remain unsettled as applied to AI, and our contractual and insurance protections may prove insufficient. Individuals at risk of suicide or self-harm or who have committed acts of violence toward others have used, and may also in the future use, our models, notwithstanding our safeguards. AI models developed by others in our industry have been and may in the future be alleged to have played a role in instances of suicide, acts of violence toward others, or serious self-harm, which have resulted and may in the future result in significant public scrutiny, litigation, criminal investigations, regulatory attention, and reputational harm. Similar incidents involving our models have presented and could in the future present substantial risk to our reputation, expose us to legal, regulatory, and other proceedings, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. While our current Consumer Terms of Service requires our users to be at least 18 years of age, minors have accessed in the past, and may in the future access, the platform, and risks relating to child safety may be particularly acute, as minors may be more susceptible to harmful content, manipulation, or overreliance on AI outputs, and incidents involving children tend to draw heightened regulatory, media, and public scrutiny. State attorneys general and private plaintiffs have also begun to assert tort, product liability, consumer protection, and failure-to-warn claims against companies in our industry, alleging that AI models caused or contributed to harm and that the developer failed to adequately warn users of known risks. In at least one case, a state attorney general has initiated a criminal investigation against another company offering similar services. Regulators have obtained substantial monetary settlements and injunctive relief against other technology companies based on analogous theories of product-design or algorithmic harm, and we believe similar theories are likely to continue to be tested against us and other companies in our industry as adoption of our models grows, including by minors and other vulnerable users, notwithstanding our efforts to restrict such access. The relief sought in such matters has, in at least one instance, extended beyond data-handling, disclosure, or age-verification practices to include a request to enjoin an AI company from developing new models absent independent, third-party safety review and approval, illustrating the potential breadth of remedies governmental actors may pursue against companies in our industry. Any determination that we are liable under such theories, or any judicial or regulatory expansion of tort, product liability, or consumer protection law, or criminal liability, as applied to AI models, could result in significant liability and require us to change how we design and offer our models, platform, and applications. 168 A substantial portion of our traffic is subject to Zero Data Retention (“ZDR”) terms under which we retain only classifier scores, not prompts or outputs. For that traffic, we cannot conduct offline analysis, cross- conversation investigation, human review, or otherwise analyze historical data to detect, investigate, and document security events or incidents, which thereby reduces our ability to detect misuse. ZDR may also prevent us from producing records for subpoenas, regulatory examinations, or incident-reporting obligations, and there is no certainty a regulator or court would excuse non-production based on a lack of available records, and such regulators or courts may construe the lack of records against us through unfavorable inferences or other sanctions. As our models become more capable, our safety framework has required and may continue to require monitoring and retention incompatible with ZDR for certain model classes. Because ZDR is a competitive expectation for enterprise customers in regulated industries and on third- party cloud platforms, these requirements have caused and could continue to cause customers to migrate to other providers or to deployments where our visibility is more limited. In the EU, the UK, and elsewhere, cybersecurity and AI-related incidents are subject to increasingly stringent reporting obligations. European regulators expect companies to provide detailed information about incidents under several laws and regulations, which we may not be able to provide within the prescribed timeframe. Similarly, in the United States, companies are increasingly subject to incident reporting obligations. In addition, other jurisdictions around the world have adopted, or may adopt, similar laws and regulations with similar implications. Any of the foregoing could result in regulatory action, litigation, customer attrition, or reputational harm that adversely affects our business. For more information regarding our incident reporting obligations, please refer to “—Any security breaches or other incidents, including those that affect our networks, systems, or data, or the networks, systems, or data of our service providers, suppliers, or customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations” below. The legal frameworks governing liability for actions taken autonomously by AI systems, including our agentic products, are unsettled and could expose us to significant and unpredictable legal claims. Existing legal doctrines governing agency, product liability, and professional negligence were developed in the context of human decision-making and have not been authoritatively applied to autonomous AI systems. We believe our provision of our intelligence service is considered a “service” in the context of legal frameworks addressing product liability, but courts and regulators may reach different conclusions across jurisdictions. In addition, it is unclear whether, and under what circumstances, actions taken by an AI agent could be deemed to create binding legal obligations on behalf of the user or deploying enterprise, or whether our contractual protections, including limitation of liability and indemnification provisions, will be enforceable or adequate in the context of claims arising from autonomous agent conduct. We may face claims from customers, their end users, or third parties alleging that we are liable for harm caused by our agents’ autonomous actions, even where the customer configured, deployed, or supervised the agent. The absence of settled legal standards creates significant uncertainty regarding our potential liability exposure and the adequacy of our risk mitigation measures. Our expansion into new geographic markets further compounds these risks, as we must navigate differing cultural norms regarding AI use, comply with diverse and evolving regulatory regimes that may impose varying safety, compliance, or liability requirements, address language-specific vulnerabilities and content moderation challenges, and potentially face regulatory enforcement actions, litigation, or other liabilities in jurisdictions where we have more limited operational experience, including heightened risks of intellectual property theft, unauthorized model access, or misuse associated with operating data center infrastructure in certain non-U.S. locations.

 
169 If our models are involved in causing significant harm, we could be subject to legal claims, including personal injury or negligence claims, regulatory enforcement actions, criminal investigations, or other governmental efforts, which could result in costly litigation, significant financial judgments or settlements, disruptive remediation obligations, or a challenging regulatory landscape. We have taken steps to limit our liability for such matters—for example, through warranty disclaimers and limitations of liability in our terms of service—but those contractual protections may not be upheld, or may not apply to certain claims, or may otherwise be insufficient to limit our liability exposure under applicable law. Moreover, in some cases we have contractually assumed additional liability. For example, to facilitate independent testing and evaluation of our frontier models, we have agreed to indemnify certain external evaluators and testing vendors for specified losses arising from testing activities, including security incidents, data loss, data breaches, and other harms associated with such activities. Although our agreements with external evaluators and testing vendors generally limit the amount of our indemnification obligations, certain of these agreements require us to defend and indemnify the evaluator, without a cap on our liability, against certain third-party claims. These include claims arising from allegations that our models or their outputs, as used in the evaluator’s authorized testing, infringe third-party intellectual property or other proprietary rights, as well as certain other claims arising from the testing or related engagement. Because our models may behave in ways that no user or developer intended, claims arising from such actions could result in substantial liability. Our insurance policies also may not provide sufficient coverage to adequately mitigate the potential liabilities we face, especially where any one incident, or a group of incidents, causes disproportionate harm. In addition, with the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure. Further, the insurance market for AI-specific risks is nascent and evolving, and we may be unable to obtain coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses. Harmful incidents involving our models, regardless of fault, could also severely and disproportionately damage our reputation and brand as a safety-focused AI company, leading to loss of customer trust and customer attrition, reduced demand for our models, platform, and applications, and difficulty attracting and retaining talent. In addition, because we primarily serve enterprise customers, which often have heightened expectations around safety, reliability, and compliance, any harmful incident or perceived lapse in our safety practices could have a disproportionate adverse impact on our brand, customer relationships, and revenue. Moreover, to the extent enterprises are attracted to our models, platform, and applications due to our safety-focused positioning, any erosion of that perception could impair our ability to attract and retain enterprise customers. There can be no assurance that we will be able to predict, detect, and proactively prevent every harmful use or harmful output of our AI models, in particular as we continue to rapidly develop our models, platform, and applications, and expand our operations geographically, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our reputation and brand or result in costly legal liability. There may have been past instances of harmful use or harmful output of our models that we did not detect, and there may be future instances that we will not detect. Any of the foregoing risks could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. If we are unable to manage the risks related to our focus on and commitment to AI safety, our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. Balancing Safety and Commercial Objectives. Our commitment to AI safety requires us to make difficult judgments that balance safety considerations against commercial objectives, competitive pressures, and 170 stakeholder expectations. We often make judgment calls with respect to when we determine a model is safe enough to release and which capabilities to develop or restrict. For example, in April 2026, we initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We expect that frontier models with similar or enhanced capability profiles, whether developed by us or by other AI labs, will continue to emerge, and that Anthropic models exhibiting such capabilities have been and may in the future be subject to access constraints. More broadly, we believe it is important to assess the safety of our models not only at release but throughout their development. For models we anticipate will have novel capabilities or present novel safety risks, we plan to evaluate the safety of each stage of training, including pre-training, post-training, and internal deployment, and we may delay or pause a stage when we are not confident in our safety measures for that stage. For example, we recently chose to delay pre-training a new frontier base model for more than a month to allow time to further enhance our security measures related to preventing model weight exfiltration and protecting our intellectual property. We are also considering additional measures, including updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy, to require human review and approval of certain decisions in our research and development processes as our models perform an increasing share of that work. There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented. These judgments are particularly consequential because, as AI systems become more capable, the potential severity of harm from misaligned or misused models increases correspondingly, and a wide range of stakeholders, including researchers and policymakers, have raised concerns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly. Our safety-focused approach is designed in part to mitigate such risks, but there can be no assurance that our efforts will be successful or that the broader AI industry will adopt similar safeguards. In particular, as AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight, there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention. Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier model could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business. For example, in September 2026, media reports citing a senior FTC official indicated that the FTC has opened non-public investigations into the potential risks that increasingly autonomous AI systems may pose to consumers. In October 2026, the FTC issued a civil investigative demand to us seeking information about our consumer protection, data protection, and privacy practices, as well as the safety and security of our products. We cannot predict the outcome of any investigation of us, and any investigation, enforcement action, or adverse finding arising from this or similar inquiries could result in significant costs, require changes to how we design, test, or deploy our models, platform, and applications, or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We may misjudge these tradeoffs, either by being overly cautious and potentially losing market opportunities, or by being insufficiently rigorous and releasing models, platforms, or applications that cause harm. Even where human oversight mechanisms are in place, such mechanisms may prove insufficient in practice if the volume, speed, or complexity of autonomous agent actions exceeds the capacity of human reviewers to meaningfully evaluate and intervene, and any perceived failure of our oversight mechanisms could expose us to regulatory enforcement, liability claims, and reputational harm. For more information, please refer to “—If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and brand, business,

 
171 financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected” above. Moreover, governmental authorities have restricted, and may in the future further restrict, the availability of our models, including based on their assessment of the capabilities or safeguards of our models, independent of our own safety-based access decisions. For example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, which we disabled for all customers until those restrictions were lifted. For more information, please refer to “— Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets” below. Internal Governance and Decision-Making To institutionalize our safety commitments and ensure we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC, we have established the LTBT, which through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. In addition to the LTBT and our structure as a PBC, we train our models in accordance with Claude’s constitution, which we make publicly available, and have adopted and continue to update safety policies, such as our Responsible Scaling Policy. We also solicit and seriously consider input from a wide range of stakeholders and constituents, including our stockholders, employees, customers, the LTBT, industry leaders and experts, and AI safety organizations. Such practices and processes have previously resulted in, and may in the future result in, slower decision-making and product releases. We may also face potential conflicts when safety and business interests diverge. If we do not successfully manage these risks related to our AI safety processes and practices, or if there is a perception that we have not successfully managed such risks, we may face reputational harm, internal conflicts resulting in a deterioration of our company culture, slower or inferior product releases, or litigation. For more information, please refer to “—Risks Related to our Governance Structure” below. We have implemented an external reviewer program and engage researchers, adversarial testers, and other third parties to support aspects of our safety, security, and model-evaluation efforts. Certain of these arrangements are novel and may require us to provide such parties with access to internal information, systems, personnel, or models, which could increase the risk of disclosure of confidential, proprietary, or other sensitive information. In addition, findings, assessments, or public statements by such third parties may differ from our views and could adversely affect customer trust, regulatory perceptions, or our reputation. Heightened Reputational Vulnerability. As we have publicly positioned ourselves as a safety-focused organization, we face heightened vulnerability to reputational harm from any perceived inconsistency between our stated values and actual practices. We are held to higher standards than certain competitors that have not made similar public commitments, and any incidents impacting our perception as a safety- focused organization could result in: • Employee Disruption. Employees who joined our company based on our safety commitments may experience a decline in morale, disillusionment, a loss of trust in leadership, or reduced productivity if they perceive we are not living up to our stated values. Public disagreements regarding our safety approach, including criticism from current or former employees, or the departure of personnel associated with our safety efforts, could amplify such perceptions. Such negative perceptions could 172 also impair our ability to recruit and hire new talent to the organization. Any erosion of our safety- focused reputation could also make it more difficult or costly to attract and retain highly skilled employees, including by increasing compensation or other hiring costs. These dynamics could lead to increased turnover, loss of institutional knowledge, and reduced effectiveness of our teams, which could in turn cause disruption to ongoing development and safety initiatives and impair our ability to remain at the frontier of AI model development. • Customer Backlash. Customers and enterprise partners who choose to deploy our models, platform, and applications based on our safety positioning may lose trust in us, terminate or decline to renew their contracts, demand refunds, publicly criticize our company, or switch to our competitors, which could result in harm to our reputation, revenue loss, and reduced market share. These risks may be heightened with respect to programs in which we make models available only to a limited group of vetted organizations, such as Project Glasswing. Organizations not selected for, or removed from, such programs may perceive our access decisions as arbitrary, exclusionary, or anticompetitive, which could result in reputational harm, loss of customer or partner relationships, regulatory complaints, or litigation, including claims under antitrust or unfair competition laws. Conversely, participants in such programs may publicly criticize us or terminate their participation if program terms, eligibility criteria, transition arrangements to successor models, or capability levels do not meet their expectations. • Regulatory Scrutiny. Regulators may subject us to heightened oversight, investigations, enforcement actions, or new or more burdensome compliance requirements based on the capabilities of our models, platform, and applications or perceived failures to meet our own stated standards, which could increase our operational costs and limit our ability to deploy our models, platform, and applications. • Damaging Media Coverage. Negative press coverage could amplify concerns about our safety practices, reach broader audiences, including potential customers and investors, create lasting reputational damage through viral social media discussion, and make future incidents subject to heightened scrutiny, which could further exacerbate the adverse effects of any perceived failures to meet our stated standards. • Litigation. We may face lawsuits from stockholders alleging misrepresentation, from customers claiming breach of contractual or implied commitments, or from other parties alleging harm resulting from the gap between our stated values and actual practices, leading to legal costs, settlements, judgments, injunctions, or other liabilities and remedies. Any safety-related controversy or incident, whether actual or perceived, and regardless of fault or frequency, could prove significantly damaging to our business. In addition, we have engaged with governments in Canada, the EU, the United Kingdom, the United States, and other jurisdictions in connection with Project Glasswing and related frontier-capability programs, and we have positioned such programs, in part, to help provide the foundation for broader industry coordination on the responsible release of frontier models with cybersecurity and other advanced capabilities. The commercial viability of these and similar future programs may depend on sustained governmental and industry coalition support. If such coalitions fail to materialize, are perceived as exclusionary or anticompetitive, are rolled back, or result in mandates we cannot readily satisfy (including with respect to access, localization, monitoring, or reporting), our ability to commercialize models with Mythos-class capabilities, and the reputational benefits we derive from safety- focused positioning, could be materially impaired. For more information, please refer to “—If we are unable

 
173 to maintain and enhance our brand and reputation, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected” below. We voluntarily publicly disclose information regarding AI safety challenges, research findings, and limitations of our models and systems that exceeds standard industry practice and regulatory requirements. While our intent with these voluntary disclosures is to advance the safe development of AI and build public trust, these disclosures create several risks. The AI safety landscape is nascent and evolving rapidly, and our understanding of and perspective on appropriate safety practices, risk tradeoffs, and deployment contexts may change over time as technologies, use cases, and regulatory expectations develop. As a result, statements we make today may later prove incomplete, require modification, or be interpreted differently in light of subsequent developments. To the extent we adhere to prior public statements or frameworks, we may also limit our operational flexibility, product development, or deployment decisions, even where evolving circumstances would otherwise warrant a different approach. Our public statements about AI risks, safety challenges, areas of uncertainty, or potential societal impacts, including statements regarding job displacement or economic disruption, may be used against us in litigation, regulatory proceedings, or public controversies, particularly if our future actions or statements are viewed as inconsistent with our prior statements and commitments. Regulators have used and could continue to use our disclosures as the basis for heightened scrutiny or more stringent requirements applicable to us compared to less transparent competitors. Additionally, our disclosures have provided, and may in the future provide, competitors with insights into our proprietary training and other sensitive processes, research priorities, and strategic concerns, without reciprocal transparency, which may put us at a competitive disadvantage. If we are unable to effectively manage the foregoing risks, our brand, reputation, and ability to compete could be adversely affected. Resource Allocation and Scaling. Safety-focused development is resource-intensive. We must allocate limited resources, capital, and talent between safety-focused workloads and other initiatives, often without clear returns on our safety-focused investments. For example, our investments in interpretability research and techniques designed to ensure our models’ behavior remains consistent with intended goals, values, and safety objectives may not yield actual or perceived commercial returns. Additionally, as we develop our models, platform, and applications, safety testing may become more expensive and resource-intensive. Limited-access programs such as Project Glasswing may also require us to design, operate, and continually maintain bespoke vetting, contracting, monitoring, and offboarding processes that differ materially from our standard commercial release processes, including coordination among participating organizations, transition planning to successor models, and enhanced internal controls commensurate with the heightened sensitivity of the underlying capabilities. These activities impose ongoing operational, legal, and security costs that may recur as future frontier models with similar capability profiles are released. If we fail to successfully manage resource allocation or develop more efficient methods with respect to our safety initiatives, our safety outcomes, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. As our product portfolio and employee and customer base expand globally, applying safety principles consistently across our rapidly expanding organization, models, platform, applications, use cases, and jurisdictions and regulatory regimes has become increasingly challenging. For more information, please refer to “—To continue to grow our business, we will need to continue to expand internationally, and our non-U.S. operations and sales to customers outside of the United States expose us to risks inherent in international expansion, sales, and operations” below. If we are unable to successfully manage the foregoing risks related to our focus on and commitment to AI 174 safety, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. If we are unable to maintain and enhance our brand and reputation, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected. We believe that maintaining and enhancing our brand identity and reputation is critical to our relationships with, and to our ability to attract and retain, customers, partners, and employees. Our brand and reputation are influenced not only by our actions, but also by the actions of our partners, our customers, and other third parties with whom we do business, and by broader public perceptions of the AI industry, and we may be grouped with other industry participants and judged similarly, regardless of differences in our approach or conduct. The successful promotion of our brand depends on a number of factors, including our ability to continue to develop and deliver reliable, high-quality, and responsible models, platforms, and applications that meet the needs of our customers; our sales and marketing efforts, including our effectiveness at developing a strong brand name and positive presence within the AI industry through participation in industry events and key media coverage; the perceptions and experiences of both our enterprise and individual customers, including through testimonials, use cases, and word-of-mouth; our ability to maintain security and reliability of our models, platform, and applications; the actions of our management; and our ability to differentiate our models, platform, and applications from those of our competitors, including through product design choices, safeguards, business models, and policies, including our approach to monetization strategies that differ from those of certain competitors. In addition, our brand is subject to heightened scrutiny with respect to perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety-related impacts of AI technologies, and a single perceived failure could result in outsized reputational harm. For example, as AI systems become more capable or prevalent, public perception that our models, platform, and applications contribute to job displacement or economic disruption could generate significant negative media coverage, customer or employee backlash, or organized opposition, regardless of the actual impact of our models, platform, and applications on employment. Our ability to maintain and enhance our brand and reputation also depends on the effectiveness and scalability of our internal communications and reputation-management capabilities, including our ability to support global operations, and limitations in these areas could adversely affect our brand as we grow. Our crisis response and reputation-management capabilities may be limited or underdeveloped, particularly as we scale, which could impair our ability to respond effectively to adverse events and mitigate reputational harm. The promotion of our brand requires us to make substantial expenditures, which we anticipate will increase as our market becomes more competitive. We have in the past faced, and may in the future face, challenges in building broader brand awareness and may fall behind competitors with more established or widely recognized brands. Our brand promotion activities may not be successful or generate the awareness or increased revenue we expect, and even if they do, any increase in revenue may not offset the significant expenses we incur in the efforts to build our brand. If we do not successfully maintain and enhance our brand, our business may not grow, we may have reduced pricing power relative to competitors, we could lose customers or fail to attract potential customers, or we could fail to hire and retain employees, all of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

 
175 We derive substantially all of our revenue from a limited number of products and applications, and our failure to maintain and expand our product portfolio could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We currently derive substantially all of our revenue from a limited number of products and applications, primarily our Claude models and portfolio of applications that sit on top of the Claude Platform. This dependence on a narrow set of offerings subjects us to various risks that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our concentration in a limited number of products and applications, as well as our focused development strategy within specific areas of the broader AI landscape, reduces our ability to mitigate business risks through diversification. While this focused approach may enable us to allocate resources efficiently and compete effectively in our prioritized areas, it also creates the risk that significant market opportunities or the largest addressable markets may emerge in areas outside our current strategic focus. Many of our competitors offer diverse product portfolios across multiple business lines or pursue broader development across AI modalities, enabling them to offset weaknesses in a particular area. In contrast, any decline in demand for our core offerings, whether due to competition, technological changes, pricing pressure, changes in customer demand, or other factors, would have a direct and disproportionate impact on our revenue and ability to achieve and sustain profitability. Our concentration also reflects a strategy that prioritizes model capability as a principal source of differentiation and relies substantially on organic adoption rather than a large direct sales organization. For the risks of that strategy, including the risks that differentiation among advanced models narrows, that customers select providers based on factors other than capability, or that competitors capture the individual users from whom our enterprise adoption often originates, please refer to “—We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected” and “—We have a limited history under our current go-to-market strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition, engagement, and retention model may not be successful” above. The AI industry is rapidly evolving, and it is difficult to predict which modalities or applications will capture the most durable commercial value or how the competitive landscape will shift. If the market for AI models, platforms, and applications develops in ways that do not align with our chosen areas of focus, or if competitors are better positioned to address the areas where the market opportunity ultimately proves largest, our ability to sustain revenue growth and compete effectively could be adversely affected. If we experience a decline in demand for our core offerings, we may not be able to successfully expand our product and application portfolio, and even if we do, our new products and applications may not achieve market acceptance or generate sufficient revenue to offset any decline in our existing business. Further, technical issues, security incidents, regulatory restrictions, or reputational harm affecting our models, platform, and applications could have an immediate and disproportionate impact on our business due to our product concentration where alternative revenue streams may not be available to offset such impact. The market for AI models, platforms, and applications is evolving quickly, and customer requirements and expectations are changing rapidly. Customers may increasingly demand specialized solutions or specialized integration and tooling that we do not currently offer and may not plan to offer, or may seek AI solutions embedded more deeply into enterprise workflows. Enterprises may prefer to develop their own AI capabilities internally or choose competitors that offer more comprehensive product suites. Moreover, because substantially all of our models and applications are built on top of our frontier models, any defect, vulnerability, safety issue, or performance degradation in an underlying frontier model could simultaneously affect multiple products and applications and customer deployments, amplifying the impact of any such 176 issue across our business. If we fail to anticipate or respond effectively to these evolving customer needs, we may lose customers to competitors or fail to acquire new customers. In addition, we currently compete, and may increasingly compete, with some of our own customers. As we expand our product portfolio or introduce new capabilities, our offerings may overlap with or directly compete with the models, platforms, and applications that our customers provide. This risk is particularly acute with software-as-a-service and other software companies, whose offerings may incorporate AI functionality similar to, or dependent on, the capabilities we provide. These customers may view our product expansion as a competitive threat to their business models and may reduce their purchases from us, limit their adoption of new offerings, terminate their relationships with us, seek alternative providers, restrict our access to the compute we obtain from them, initiate intellectual property or other litigation against us, or accelerate efforts to develop competing solutions internally in order to avoid relying on a direct competitor. This dynamic could result in customer attrition, reduced expansion within our existing customer base, pricing pressure, or reputational challenges, any of which could adversely affect our revenue growth and business prospects. Expanding our product portfolio requires substantial time and investment. We must make significant investments in research and development, compute infrastructure, engineering talent, sales and marketing, and go-to-market capabilities to develop new models, platforms, and applications and enable continued adoption. We may seek to expand into new products and markets, including areas outside of our current core competencies or where we have limited experience, and we may not successfully develop, commercialize, or support such offerings. Development timelines for AI models, platforms, and applications are uncertain, and new capabilities, even when continuously improved and released into our models, platform, and applications, may take significant time to achieve commercial scale. We may invest significant resources in products or services that fail to gain market traction, experience technical difficulties, face unexpected competition, lead to unexpected harm or societal impacts that do not align with our values, or generate insufficient returns to justify the investment. Additionally, we face other constraints on our ability to expand our offerings, including the ability to hire, retain, and motivate qualified AI researchers, engineers, and technical personnel; the capital intensity of developing and operating AI models, platforms, and applications which require substantial compute and infrastructure investment; and our limited portfolio, which may make it difficult to provide the comprehensive, integrated solutions that customers may expect. If we are unable to successfully expand our product portfolio, if we fail to compete effectively with our current offerings, or if customer preferences shift away from our models, platform, and applications, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. Our substantial amount of debt, combined with variable interest rates, could limit our flexibility in planning for, or reacting to, changes in our business and the markets in which we operate, including limiting our future investments or our ability to enter into acquisitions and strategic partnerships, and obtain financing for such transactions. In addition, our indebtedness, combined with our other financial obligations and contractual commitments, could have other important consequences. For example, they could: • make us more vulnerable to adverse changes in general U.S. and non-U.S. economic, industry, and competitive conditions and adverse changes in government regulation; 180 • limit our flexibility in planning for, or reacting to, changes in our business and our industry; • place us at a disadvantage compared to our competitors that have less or fixed rate indebtedness; • limit our ability to borrow additional amounts to fund acquisitions, for working capital, and for other general corporate purposes; and • make an acquisition of our company less attractive or more difficult. Any of these factors could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In addition, if we incur additional indebtedness, the risks related to our business and our ability to service or repay our indebtedness would increase. A failure by us to comply with the covenants, including those tied, in part, to operational and performance- based metrics, or payment obligations under the A&R Credit Agreement or our outstanding convertible promissory notes, as applicable, whether as a result of financial constraints, operational challenges, inexperience managing complex infrastructure and large-scale capital commitments, or otherwise, could result in an event of default under these instruments. Upon an event of default under the A&R Credit Agreement, the lenders would have the right to accelerate all amounts outstanding and exercise other remedies available to them, including enforcing their rights against the collateral securing the A&R Credit Agreement. An event of default under our outstanding convertible promissory notes would similarly give the noteholders the right to declare all amounts outstanding under our outstanding convertible promissory notes immediately due and payable. If the indebtedness under the A&R Credit Agreement and/or outstanding convertible promissory notes were to be accelerated, we may not have sufficient cash or be able to borrow sufficient funds to refinance such indebtedness or sell sufficient assets to repay such indebtedness, which could adversely affect our business, cash flows, financial condition, and results of operations. Even if we were able to obtain new financing, it may not be on commercially reasonable terms or on terms that are acceptable to us. We may not have the ability to raise the funds necessary to repay the principal and accrued interest of our outstanding convertible promissory notes or the A&R Credit Agreement in cash when required by the terms of the notes or the A&R Credit Agreement, as applicable, or at their maturity. In connection with the completion of this Offering, the Amazon Notes will convert into Class N common stock up to an ownership cap as set forth in the Amazon Notes, which Amazon has elected not to waive in connection with this Offering. The portion of the Amazon Notes that cannot be converted without exceeding the ownership cap applicable to such notes will be re-issued as rollover notes, which will automatically convert, subject to Amazon’s ownership cap, into shares of our Class N common stock at the applicable conversion price at the end of each fiscal quarter following the completion of this Offering. To the extent any of our convertible promissory notes remain outstanding, or if we issue any additional convertible promissory notes following the completion of this Offering, we will be required to repay such notes in cash at their maturity, unless earlier converted or repaid pursuant to the terms of such note. In addition, we will be required to repay in full all amounts outstanding under the A&R Credit Agreement upon its maturity. However, we may not have enough available cash on hand or be able to obtain financing at the time we are required to make any repayments on outstanding convertible promissory notes or under the A&R Credit Agreement. Our failure to repay any outstanding convertible promissory notes or amounts outstanding under the A&R Credit Agreement, as applicable, at a time when the repayment is required, or to pay cash upon any

 
181 conversion of outstanding convertible promissory notes, as applicable, as required pursuant to the terms of each note or the applicable NPA, would constitute a default thereunder. A default under an outstanding convertible promissory note and/or the applicable NPA as well as the A&R Credit Agreement could also lead to a default under agreements governing our existing and future indebtedness. If the payment of the related indebtedness were to be accelerated after any applicable notice or grace periods, we may not have sufficient funds to repay such indebtedness and repay the amounts outstanding under the A&R Credit Agreement or outstanding convertible promissory notes at the applicable maturity, or when repayment is otherwise required pursuant to the terms of the note. Our pricing structures for our models, platform, and applications change from time to time, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We have in the past changed, and we expect that in the future we may change, our pricing models, including as a result of competition, macroeconomic conditions, compliance with increased regulatory hurdles, the maturation of the market for AI models, platforms, and applications, or changes in how our models, platform, and applications are broadly consumed. As a result, we may be required to reduce our prices, offer shorter contract durations, or offer alternative pricing models, such as outcome- or task-based pricing, any of which could adversely affect our business. In addition, our agentic offerings are structurally more compute- intensive than our non-agentic offerings. If we are unable to implement pricing models that adequately reflect the higher compute intensity of these agentic workloads, or if competitive dynamics constrain our ability to price these products at levels sufficient to cover their costs, our compute efficiency could deteriorate as agentic usage grows, which could adversely affect our ability to achieve or sustain profitability. Additionally, as we continue to target selling our models, platform, and applications to our enterprise customers, these customers may demand different pricing structures, price concessions, or additional functionality at the same price levels. If we are unable to modify or develop effective pricing models and strategies that are attractive to existing and prospective customers, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected. If we are unable to attract, retain, or motivate highly skilled personnel, we may not be able to grow or operate effectively. Our performance and ability to grow our business depend on the talents and efforts of highly skilled individuals, and our future success depends on our continuing ability to identify, hire, develop, motivate, and retain highly skilled personnel for all areas of our organization. Our business is particularly dependent on a limited pool of researchers, engineers, and technical personnel with specialized experience in designing, training, deploying, and operating frontier models and the underlying infrastructure that supports them. We have from time to time experienced, and we expect to continue to experience, difficulty in hiring and retaining highly skilled employees with appropriate qualifications at the pace that our operations require. Competition in our industry relating to hiring and retaining employees with appropriate qualifications and on competitive economic terms is exceptionally intense and has escalated significantly in recent periods, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, where our headquarters is located and where we have a substantial presence and need for highly skilled personnel. A small number of well-capitalized AI labs, large technology companies, and new market entrants compete aggressively for a relatively fixed supply of individuals with the requisite expertise. Certain of our competitors have directly solicited, and continue to directly solicit, our employees. Our former employees are also generally able to join or found competing companies immediately following their departure, and, subject to their confidentiality and other legal obligations, use the general skills, know-how, and experience they developed while employed by us. In 182 addition, we have in the past, and may in the future, be subject to claims or disputes relating to the solicitation or hiring of employees, including allegations that such hires violated non-compete, non- solicitation, intellectual property, confidentiality, or other employment-related obligations. As our company continues to grow and our industry evolves, the incentives to attract, retain, and motivate employees provided by our cash and equity awards or by future arrangements may not be as effective as in the past. Many of the companies with which we compete for highly qualified personnel have greater resources than we have and may be willing to offer more attractive compensation packages. We may need to invest significant amounts of cash and equity to attract and retain employees, resulting in substantial additional stock-based compensation expense and dilution to the ownership of our existing stockholders, and we may never realize returns on these investments that are commensurate with the level of our expenditures. If the perceived value of our compensatory package declines or is subject to significant value fluctuations, it may adversely affect our ability to attract and retain highly skilled employees. In addition, we have a number of current employees, including our co-founders, who hold equity in our company or whose equity awards are or will become substantially vested upon the completion of this Offering. This may be particularly true for certain of our longer-tenured and early employees, whose equity holdings may represent a significant portion of their personal wealth. As a result, it may be difficult for us to continue to retain and motivate these employees, and the value of their holdings could affect their decisions about whether or not they continue to work for us. Historically, our ability to successfully attract, retain, and motivate our personnel has in large part been due to our company culture and commitment to safety and responsible scaling and development. If we are unable to maintain our culture, if we make decisions as a company that our employees do not believe align with our values, or if events take place, regardless of fault, that call into question whether we have operated in accordance with our values, our ability to attract, retain, and motivate our personnel may be adversely affected. Rapid growth has also created workforce-planning and execution challenges, including limitations in our ability to accurately forecast headcount needs, periods of accelerated hiring followed by corrective actions that may disrupt operations or reduce morale, and increased reliance on managers operating at greater scale than in their prior experience, which introduces additional operational, legal, reputational, and execution risk as the organization continues to expand. If we move into new geographies, we will need to attract and recruit skilled personnel in those geographic areas, but it may be challenging for us to compete with traditional local employers in these regions for talent. If we fail to attract new personnel or fail to retain and motivate our current personnel who are capable of meeting our growing technical, operational, and managerial requirements, our business may be adversely affected. In addition, heightened public attention on AI has increased physical and informational security risks, and we have experienced threats to employee safety and attempts to obtain confidential information through physical or digital means, which, despite the security measures we have implemented at certain facilities, may be exacerbated by our global and flexible working arrangements and could adversely affect employee morale, productivity, and our ability to attract, retain, and motivate highly skilled personnel. Addressing these risks also requires us to attract and retain additional specialized security personnel, and difficulties in recruiting qualified security engineers could further exacerbate these challenges. Further, changes to immigration policies that restrain the flow of professional and technical talent, including but not limited to U.S. immigration policies, may inhibit our ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. If we are unable to effectively manage the foregoing risks, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

 
183 We have a limited operating history in an evolving and nascent industry, which makes it difficult to evaluate our future prospects and may increase the risk that we will not be successful. We were founded in 2021 and launched our first commercial product, Claude, publicly in the first quarter of 2023. Since then, our business has grown rapidly. We operate in an industry characterized by rapid and unpredictable technological change, evolving safety and regulatory expectations, significant capital and compute requirements, and uncertain commercial adoption patterns. Our limited operating history and our evolving and nascent business and industry make it difficult to evaluate our future prospects and the risks and challenges we may encounter. These risks and challenges include our ability to: • develop and release new models and products on a timely and cost-effective basis; • accurately forecast our revenue, operating expenses, and compute requirements in an environment characterized by rapid technological change and usage patterns that may scale in nonlinear or exponential ways; • secure access to sufficient compute to meet the needs of all our workloads and manage the risks related to securing compute; • effectively manage our growth, including our cash flows and capital needs; • accurately predict customer demands, expectations, or requirements; • maintain and enhance our brand and reputation; • attract, retain, utilize, and motivate our highly skilled personnel; • build and maintain our strategic partnerships; • anticipate and respond to macroeconomic changes and changes in the industry and markets in which we operate; • anticipate and respond to evolving regulatory requirements and political dynamics; • maintain our safety-focused approach while meeting market demands; • successfully monetize our models, platform, and applications; and • respond effectively to competitive threats. If we fail to effectively address the risks and challenges we face, including those described elsewhere in this “Business and Other Risks”, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. We have encountered in the past, and will encounter in the future, risks and uncertainties frequently experienced by growing companies with limited operating histories in rapidly changing industries. If our assumptions regarding these risks and uncertainties, which we use to plan and operate our business, are incorrect or change, or if we do not address these risks successfully, our results of operations could differ materially from our expectations and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. 184 We are at an early stage of our revenue growth, we have experienced rapid growth in recent periods, and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance or our ability to sustain or forecast future revenue growth. We have grown rapidly over the last several years, and therefore our recent revenue growth and financial performance should not be considered indicative of our future performance. In 2023, 2024, and 2025, our revenue was $41 million, $386 million, and $4.6 billion, respectively, representing year-over-year growth of 841% in 2024 and 1,088% in 2025. In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%. We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all. Our recent growth may reflect early-stage adoption dynamics, the nascency of the AI market, and rapid initial customer expansion that may not be sustainable over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate, as our revenue base increases, as the market matures, and as a result of the other factors described below. We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over time. In addition, because the AI industry is very nascent, we have struggled to accurately forecast our revenue in the past and may struggle to do so in the future. We may experience declines in our revenue growth rate as a result of a number of factors, including: • the slowing or shifting demand for our models, platform, and applications or the market as a whole; • our inability to secure sufficient compute and direct it efficiently across our organization; • insufficient growth in the number of users and paying customers of our models, platform, and applications or the failure to increase sales of our models, platform, and applications to existing customers; • failures, errors, or performance limitations in our models, including unexpected behavior, degraded outputs, outages, or inability to meet customer expectations or use-case requirements; • increasing competition among existing competitors and new market entrants; • the safety and risk mitigation measures we implement in developing and releasing our models, including any resulting delays in model development or release, or the adoption of laws, regulations, or standards that affect how and when frontier models may be developed or released; • our failure to continue to capitalize on growth opportunities; • our ability to collect amounts owed to us from customers, including as a result of customer credit risk, billing disputes, or delays in payment; • our reliance on, and the terms of, relationships with key partners and distribution channels, and any changes to, or termination of, such arrangements; • new or more restrictive laws, regulations, or regulatory actions affecting AI development, deployment, or use, including taxes, fees, or other measures specifically applicable to AI companies or AI-related labor displacement; and • reputational harm, adverse publicity, or heightened scrutiny that reduces customer adoption or expansion.

 
185 We expect to continue to make investments in the development and expansion of our business, which may not result in increased revenue or growth. If our revenue or revenue growth rate declines, or our revenue growth rate declines with respect to certain markets or customer categories, our business, results of operations, and investors’ perceptions of our business could be adversely affected, which could in turn negatively impact the market price of our Class A common stock. If we fail to manage our growth effectively, our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. Since 2021, we have experienced rapid growth in our employee headcount, number of customers, geographic reach, and our operations, and we expect this growth to continue. For example, the number of our employees increased from approximately 940 as of December 31, 2024 to approximately 5,300 as of September 30, 2026, and our revenue increased from $197 million for the three months ended December 31, 2024 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026. This growth has placed, and may continue to place, a significant strain on our management and our operational and financial resources. Our ability to successfully manage this growth depends on our ability to scale and integrate our operations, workforce, technologies, models, platform, and applications, and any future acquisitions while preserving the beneficial aspects of our company culture. Continued growth may strain our ability to develop and enhance our operational, compliance, technical, financial, and management controls, improve our reporting systems and procedures, recruit, train, and retain highly skilled personnel, and maintain customer satisfaction. If we are unable to do so, our operations, compliance with applicable laws, development and deployment of our models, platform, and applications, and customer experience could be adversely affected. As we expand, we must also manage an increasing number of relationships with strategic partners, customers, vendors, and other third parties that are critical to our business, including those that provide compute, data center infrastructure, networking, software tools, and other services necessary to develop, train, deploy, and operate our models. If these relationships deteriorate, or if our third-party providers are unable to scale their services in line with our growth, we may experience delays, service disruptions, reduced sales to new customers, or the loss of existing customers, which could adversely affect our revenue growth and reputation. In addition, our ability to manage our growth depends in part on our ability to accurately plan for and efficiently manage the compute required to develop, train, deploy, and operate our models. Any material underinvestment or overinvestment in such resources could result in service limitations, increased costs, operational inefficiencies, or delays in model development, any of which could adversely affect our business. If we fail to effectively manage the growth of our business and operations, we may be unable to maintain effective internal controls, reporting systems, and compliance processes, may face increased regulatory scrutiny, and may suffer harm to our brand and our ability to attract and retain customers. As a result, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future. We have incurred net losses in each year since our founding, including net losses of $1.5 billion, $8.3 billion, and $42.0 billion for the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively, and $104.0 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, and we may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future. These net losses included changes in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs of $1.0 billion, $5.4 billion, and $34.3 billion for the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, 186 respectively, and $94.3 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by an increase in the fair value of our outstanding convertible promissory notes resulting from an increase in our enterprise valuation during each of the respective periods. While we have experienced significant revenue growth in recent periods, our business is highly capital intensive, and our ability to remain at the frontier of AI capabilities and secure sufficient compute depends in meaningful part on our ability to generate and sustain substantial revenue and improve our operating efficiencies. Further, our revenue growth may not be sustainable, and our rate of growth may decrease.
