We expect our costs will increase over time and our losses will continue as we expect to invest significant resources towards growing our business and operating as a public company. We have expended and expect to continue to expend substantial financial and other resources related to the growth of our business, including: • investments to enhance our access and ability to secure compute; • continued investments in research and development to remain at the frontier of AI model development and introduce new features and enhancements to our models, platform, and applications; • expansion of our sales and marketing activities; • hiring additional employees; • expansion of our operations across our multiple geographies; • investments in our expanding general and administrative organization; • costs associated with complying with existing and evolving laws, regulations, and industry standards applicable to AI, data protection, privacy, and security, among other things; • investments in AI safety, risk management, monitoring, evaluation, and mitigation efforts; • additional expenses associated with operating as a public company; and • costs related to legal proceedings. For example, as of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion, which may substantially increase our operating expenses and cash requirements. These expenditures and investments may be more costly than we expect and may not result in increased revenue or growth in our business. If we are unable to successfully address these risks and challenges as we encounter them, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. In addition, before September 30, 2026, we granted RSUs to our employees and other service providers, which vest upon the satisfaction of both a service-based condition and a performance-based condition. The service-based condition for a majority of such RSUs is satisfied over a period of four years. The performance-based condition for such RSUs will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement in the United States relating to this Offering. We account for award forfeitures as they occur. As of September 30, 2026, no stock-based compensation expense had been recognized for such RSUs because the achievement of the performance-based condition described above was not probable. In the

 
187 quarter in which this Offering is completed, we will begin recording stock-based compensation expense based on the grant-date fair value of the RSUs (or, for RSUs modified as part of the RSU Modification, their modification-date fair value) using the accelerated attribution method. If this Offering had been completed on September 30, 2026, we would have recorded $8.2 billion of cumulative stock-based compensation expense related to the RSUs on that date, and an additional $24.1 billion of unrecognized stock-based compensation expense related to the RSUs, would be recognized over a weighted-average period of approximately 2.0 years. In addition to stock-based compensation expense associated with the RSUs, as of September 30, 2026, we had unrecognized stock-based compensation expense of approximately $2.1 billion related to other outstanding equity awards, which we expect to recognize over a weighted-average period of approximately 1.4 years. Subsequent to September 30, 2026, our board of directors approved the grant of 47,041,287 RSUs to our employees and other service providers. These RSUs will vest upon the satisfaction of a service-based condition only, generally over four years. Assuming a grant-date fair value of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the Initial Preliminary Price Range (or, if subsequently revised, the Revised Preliminary Price Range), we would expect to record stock-based compensation expense of approximately $3.5 billion related to such RSUs, over a weighted-average period of approximately 3.8 years, commencing in the quarter in which this Offering is completed. Following the completion of this Offering, the stock-based compensation expense related to RSUs and other outstanding equity awards will result in increases in our expenses in future periods, in particular, in the quarter in which this Offering is completed. If we fail to generate adequate revenue to offset increases in our operating expenses, improve our operating efficiencies, or otherwise manage our costs as we invest in our business, we may continue to incur significant losses in the future and may not be able to achieve or sustain profitability. Our results of operations may fluctuate significantly on a period-to-period basis, including as a result of strategic investment decisions and substantial compute-related expenditures, which could cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline. Our results of operations have historically varied from period to period, and we expect that our results of operations will continue to vary significantly from quarter to quarter and from year to year in the future, such that the results of any one period should not be relied upon as an indication of future performance. In particular, our financial performance may be significantly influenced by strategic decisions we make regarding the allocation of resources and the amount and timing of operating expenses and capital expenditures that we may incur to maintain and expand our business and operations and to remain competitive. We may make significant and, at times, discrete investments in areas such as research and development, compute and related infrastructure, product development, safety and security initiatives, and go-to-market expansion, which may be uneven in size and timing. These investments may materially increase our expenses in a given period and cause our results of operations to fluctuate significantly or vary meaningfully from period to period, and may result in periods of reduced margins or increased losses even if our underlying business trends remain unchanged or continue to improve. As a result, our financial performance may not follow any consistent pattern, and prior or interim periods of improved results of operations should not be viewed as indicative of our future performance. Our revenue in any period has also included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms, and whose revenue would not be expected to recur following restriction or termination of their access. We believe this dynamic is common in our industry. Detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, and we cannot assure you that we will identify such usage, or restrict or terminate a customer’s access, on a timely basis or at all. Customers may evade our controls, 188 and customers whose access is restricted or terminated may re-register under new accounts. As a result, revenue from such customers may continue or recur notwithstanding our enforcement efforts. Our continued detection and enforcement efforts, and in particular, the enhancement of such efforts in August and September 2026, and the timing of any resulting restrictions or terminations, are expected to reduce the percentage of revenue from customers using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms, and may reduce our overall revenue and growth rates in future periods and contribute to variability in our results from period to period. Our results of operations are also affected by seasonal variations in the usage of our models, platform, and applications. Because our revenue is primarily consumption-based, we have experienced, and expect to continue to experience, lower usage around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, when certain customer workflows slow down and overall customer activity declines. Our results of operations may also vary with the timing and cadence of our model and product releases, which are uneven from period to period and may cause usage, and therefore revenue, to increase or decline between periods. Our historical growth rates may have masked the impact of seasonal trends on our results. As our growth rate declines over time, we expect seasonal effects to become more apparent in, and to have a greater effect on, our period-to-period results. In addition, other seasonal trends may develop, and the seasonal trends that we currently experience may become more pronounced, as we continue to scale. Our results of operations may also fluctuate due to a variety of additional factors, many of which are outside of our control and difficult to predict, including, but not limited to: • the level of demand for our models, platform, and applications, and our ability to forecast such demand; • our ability to forecast required compute and to obtain additional compute as needed, and any increase in costs thereof; • our ability to expand usage within organizations; • our ability to attract and retain customers and increase sales of our models, platform, and applications to existing customers; • our ability to effectively manage our relationships with our third-party service providers and our reliance on such providers for critical infrastructure and services; • the timing and success of new features, integrations, capabilities, and enhancements by us to our models, platform, and applications, or by our competitors to their products; • the safety and risk mitigation measures we implement in developing and releasing our models, including any resulting delays in model development or release, or the adoption of laws, regulations, or standards that affect how and when frontier models may be developed or released; • our ability to achieve widespread acceptance and use of our models, platform, and applications; • changes in the competitive landscape and introduction of competitive companies, models, platforms, and applications; • security breaches, technical difficulties, or interruptions to our models, platform, or applications;

 
189 • real or perceived improper or unauthorized use of, disclosure of, or access to confidential, proprietary, personal, or sensitive data; • pricing pressure as a result of competition or otherwise; • adverse litigation judgments, other dispute-related settlement payments, or other litigation-related costs; • the number of employees hired; • the timing of the grant or vesting of equity awards to employees, directors, or consultants; • the vesting and settlement of equity awards, including any cash used to remit taxes on behalf of employees in connection with the settlement of RSUs and the recognition of stock-based compensation expense; • our ability to maintain, protect, and enhance our brand; • declines in the values of foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar; • changes in, and continuing uncertainty in relation to, the legislative or regulatory environment with respect to our industry; • enforcement by government regulators, including investigations, proceedings, fines, orders, designations, or consent decrees; • increased legal and regulatory compliance costs in new and existing markets; • costs and timing of expenses related to the potential acquisition of businesses, talent, technologies, or intellectual property, including potentially significant amortization costs and possible write-downs; • catastrophic events, and resulting interruptions in the availability of our models, platform, and applications; and • general economic conditions in either U.S. or non-U.S. markets, including geopolitical uncertainty and instability and their effects on software spending. Any one or more of the factors above, or other factors in this “Business and Other Risks”, may result in significant fluctuations in our results of operations or other key metrics, which may cause such results to fall below our financial guidance or other projections or the expectations of analysts or investors, and cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline. Certain of our operating metrics are subject to assumptions and limitations. As a result, these metrics may not provide an accurate indication of our actual performance or future results. Certain of our operating metrics, such as Run-Rate Revenue, Net Revenue Retention, customer counts, and Claude’s success rate, are based on numerous assumptions and limitations, are calculated using data from internal systems and tools, have not been independently verified by third parties, are subject to inherent limitations in measurement, and may not accurately reflect actual results or provide an accurate indication of future or expected results. Run-Rate Revenue is not a substitute for revenue prepared in accordance with GAAP or a forecast of 190 revenue. Because Run-Rate Revenue annualizes our consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and our subscription-based fees for a single month, it assumes that activity during those measurement periods has continued at the same rate for a full year. Because it annualizes a short measurement period, Run-Rate Revenue measured during a period of seasonally higher or lower usage, such as the reduced usage we have typically experienced around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, may differ significantly from Run-Rate Revenue measured at other times, and in each case may not correspond to the revenue we ultimately recognize over any quarter or fiscal year. Our actual historical revenue and future revenue may differ materially from this measure. Both our consumption-based and subscription- based revenue may fluctuate from period to period, and in particular, our consumption-based revenue may fluctuate significantly or decline if customers reduce, limit, or do not expand their usage or spend, or shift usage to lower-priced models, including in response to competitive offerings, pricing changes, changes in customer budgets or strategic priorities regarding AI investment, seasonality, or general economic conditions. In addition, sustaining and growing this revenue depends on our ability to continue to offer models at the frontier of AI capability, which we may not be able to do. Our ability or decision to remain at the frontier may also be affected by the safety and risk mitigation measures we implement in developing and releasing our models. Our recent Run-Rate Revenue growth has also been driven in part by rapid initial customer adoption and expansion often characteristic of an early-adoption period and the nascency of the AI market that may not be sustainable, and we expect our Run-Rate Revenue growth rate to decline over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate, as our revenue base increases, as the market matures, and as a result of other factors. In addition, our Run-Rate Revenue has included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms. When we identify such usage, we seek to restrict or terminate the customer’s access; however, because our detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, our Run-Rate Revenue as of any measurement date includes amounts from customers that have not yet been restricted or terminated and whose revenue would not be expected to recur following restriction or termination of their access. Our continued enforcement efforts may reduce our revenue, Run-Rate Revenue, and growth rates in future periods. Please refer to “—Our results of operations may fluctuate significantly on a period-to-period basis, including as a result of strategic investment decisions and substantial compute-related expenditures, which could cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline” below. Accordingly, our Run-Rate Revenue as of any measurement date is not indicative of historical revenue and may not be indicative of our revenue for any future period. The determination of the number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis is based on our internal records and involves judgment, including in determining which accounts should be aggregated and treated as belonging to the same organization. We apply our most current customer records in calculating this metric, and our determination of which accounts belong to a single organization may change over time, including as a result of acquisitions and account consolidations. We do not separately define or internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.” Because spending $100,000 or more on our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this document, including in references to “enterprise customers” and “enterprise adoption.” As a result, this measure may not precisely correspond to the population of organizations that would otherwise be characterized as enterprises, and may over- or understate that population. Certain success rates and similar AI performance metrics with respect to Claude referenced in this

 
191 document are measured using internal benchmarks developed and maintained by us. These benchmarks reflect our proprietary testing methodology and are based on tasks, datasets, and evaluation criteria selected by us. Performance results derived from these internal benchmarks may not be replicable by customers, researchers, or other third parties who evaluate our models using different tasks, datasets, evaluation criteria, or computing environments. Accordingly, such metrics may differ materially from performance outcomes experienced by any particular customer or user in their specific deployment environment or use case, and should not be relied upon as indicative of the results any customer or user will achieve. Because AI performance benchmarking methodologies vary significantly across developers, such performance metrics as we measure them may also not be comparable to similarly titled or analogous metrics reported by other AI developers, and direct comparison of such metrics across companies may be misleading. Investors should consider these metrics in light of the assumptions and processes used in calculating such metrics and the limitations as a result thereof. In addition, our internal systems and tools have a number of limitations, which could result in unexpected changes to our metrics, including the metrics we publicly disclose. Further, certain of our operating metrics are based in part on data reported to us by our third-party partners. If the internal systems and tools we use to track these metrics or the data reported to us by our third-party partners undercount or overcount performance, or contain algorithmic or other technical errors, the data we report may not be accurate. While our operating metrics are based on what we believe to be reasonable estimates for the applicable period of measurement, there are inherent challenges in these measurements. We may also refine or change our methodology for tracking certain operating metrics from time to time, to the extent practicable, including to improve overall accuracy and alignment with management’s view of business and operating performance and as a result of acquisitions. Any of these updates may result in changes in certain business and operating trends and may impact comparability of these metrics across periods. Investors should not place undue reliance on these metrics as an indicator of our future or expected results. Moreover, these metrics may differ from similarly titled metrics presented by other companies and may not be comparable to such other metrics. Please refer to “4: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition, Operating Results, and Cash Flows” and “Section 2: Company Overview, 3: Business” for more information regarding our operating metrics. Our business is subject to an evolving and uncertain regulatory and political environment, which could increase our costs, restrict our operations, or adversely affect demand for our models, platform, and applications. The development, deployment, and use of AI technologies are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations, and governmental scrutiny across multiple jurisdictions. Governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and in other countries in which we operate or distribute our models, platform, and applications have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage and privacy, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For example, the EU AI Act, which came into force in August 2024 and will become fully applicable following a transitional period, imposes a range of obligations on AI systems and general- purpose AI models placed on the market or put into service in the EU, including transparency, risk management, and governance requirements, and provides for significant penalties for non-compliance. In the United States, the regulatory framework for AI remains fragmented and uncertain, with evolving federal policy initiatives, continued debate regarding the scope and durability of executive actions, and a growing number of state-level laws and proposals addressing the development and use of AI. For example, several 192 U.S. states, including New York and California, have passed AI safety laws. More generally, proposed legislation in the United States contemplates more expansive governmental oversight of AI, including potential nationalization, mandatory shutdown or discontinuation requirements for frontier intelligence systems, or other strategic measures to prevent or manage the development of SI. Further, in June 2026, the U.S. federal government issued an executive order establishing a voluntary framework for developers of frontier models to engage with the government prior to the deployment of such AI technologies, directing federal agencies to strengthen cyber defenses, and prioritizing enforcement against criminal misuse of AI; although that framework is voluntary and does not establish a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for the development or deployment of AI models, it reflects increasing federal attention to the national security implications of frontier intelligence and the order may be followed by further executive or legislative action. If executive or legislative action of this nature were enacted to regulate AI technologies, it could constrain how we operate our business. We have also advocated, and expect to continue to advocate, for regulation and oversight of frontier intelligence, including industry-wide standards primarily relevant to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that AI capabilities do not advance faster than the safety, alignment, and security practices needed to support them, and we have proposed working with the U.S. government and other frontier model developers to establish safety standards. Regulatory or other measures of the kind we advocate, if adopted, would apply to us and could increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth. The effect that any such measures would have on the rate at which AI capabilities advance, and on our business, is uncertain and would depend on the specific requirements adopted and on the extent to which safety, alignment, and security practices advance together with model capabilities. There is no assurance that policymakers will adopt the approaches we support, and our advocacy has in the past drawn, and may continue to draw, criticism, heightened scrutiny, or other challenges. Regulatory approaches to AI also vary significantly by geography and may be influenced by local political, economic, social, or environmental considerations. In some jurisdictions, public concern regarding the potential displacement of labor by AI systems, the perceived societal impacts of automation, or the environmental footprint associated with AI development and deployment, has led, or could lead, to restrictive legislation or other governmental actions. In particular, to the extent the rate of job displacement rapidly increases due to the adoption of AI or for related reasons, whether actual or perceived, governments or other regulatory authorities may intervene to slow the rate of adoption of AI, restrict its use, or take other actions that increase the cost of developing, deploying, or commercializing AI systems. Even in the absence of any legal or regulatory requirements, we may from time to time voluntarily elect to take actions intended to ameliorate the impact of such displacement. Any such actions would represent additional costs and expenditures for which we may not receive a corresponding commercial benefit, and there can be no assurance that any such actions would be effective in reducing displacement-related harms or in mitigating the associated reputational, regulatory, or political risks. Increasingly restrictive AI regulation in the United States and other Western jurisdictions could enable competitors operating in less regulated environments to innovate, scale, and deploy AI technologies more rapidly, potentially allowing such competitors to become more advanced and pose greater competitive or strategic threats over time. In particular, increasing strategic competition between the United States and China in AI development may lead to divergent regulatory approaches, with the potential for the United States to impose restrictions on AI companies’ interactions with Chinese entities or markets, and for China to impose reciprocal measures that limit access to or demand for U.S.-origin AI models, platforms, and

 
193 applications. As a result of these and other regulatory developments, our business could be subject to a wide range of regulatory limitations, obligations, or restrictions, including, among other things: • limitations, conditions, or prohibitions on certain AI use cases, applications, or deployment contexts; • requirements to modify, restrict, delay, or withdraw specific models, features, or functionalities in particular markets or for specific customers; for example, in early 2026, the U.S. Department of War suggested it could invoke the Defense Production Act to compel us to remove the limitations we have placed on the use of our models for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance; • heightened transparency, documentation, auditing, governance, or human-oversight obligations; • restrictions on the collection, use, transfer, localization, or retention of data used to train or operate AI systems, based on intellectual property, privacy, or other frameworks; • mandated safety, risk-management, or evaluation frameworks, certifications, or approvals, including requirements for independent, third-party review or approval prior to model development, training, or release; for example, in September 2026, a state attorney general asked a court, in pending litigation alleging harm to minors, to enjoin an AI company from developing new AI models without independent, third-party guardrails and approval; • restrictions on data center development or expansion, including permitting, zoning, or limits on energy or water usage; • heightened energy efficiency, sustainability, or environmental compliance requirements; • limitations on cross-border deployment, access, or commercialization of AI models, including through export controls, national security determinations, or other governmental measures that could restrict our ability to sell our models, platform, and applications in certain markets or to certain customers; for example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, which were subsequently lifted after we updated our safeguards, and other models may be subject to these or similar export restrictions in the future; for more information, please refer to “—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets” below; • AI-specific taxes, fees, reporting obligations, or other financial burdens; or • outright bans or moratoriums on activities material to our business or the businesses of our customers and partners. Because AI regulation is developing rapidly and in a fragmented manner, including as a result of political considerations, public sentiment, and geopolitical dynamics, we will not be able to fully anticipate how existing laws will be interpreted or enforced, how new legal frameworks will evolve, or whether regulatory regimes across jurisdictions will converge or diverge over time. Compliance with new or changing requirements may require substantial investment in research and development, compliance systems, operational processes, or localized offerings, and we may need to adjust or limit our activities in certain jurisdictions to address conflicting or inconsistent legal obligations. In addition, regulatory actions affecting our customers or partners, including restrictions on their ability to develop, deploy, or commercialize AI- 194 enabled models, platforms, or applications, could indirectly reduce demand for our models, platform, and applications. Any failure, or perceived failure, to comply with applicable laws and regulations, or any significant increase in the cost or complexity of compliance, could result in litigation, enforcement actions, penalties, reputational harm, delayed or reduced adoption of our offerings, or other adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Additionally, as AI systems become more sophisticated, emerging debates regarding whether AI systems possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status may lead to regulatory requirements, public pressure, or advocacy efforts that could constrain how we develop, train, deploy, or modify our models, increase our costs, or affect our reputation, regardless of the ultimate resolution of these philosophical and scientific questions. In addition, given our focus on developing frontier intelligence, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. Our sales to government entities and highly regulated organizations are subject to challenges and risks. Our customers include U.S. and non-U.S. government agencies. Revenue from government agency contracts represented, in aggregate, less than 2% of our revenue in each of the periods presented in this document; however, the risks described below, including the governmental actions described in this “Business and Other Risks”, are not limited to revenue generated directly from government agencies and could affect our relationships with commercial customers and partners. Sales to government agencies involve additional risks, including, but not limited to: • changes in government fiscal or procurement policies, or decreases in government funding available for procurement of goods and services generally, or for our federal government contracts specifically; • changes in government programs or applicable requirements; • our ability to agree on commercial terms with government entities, including with respect to the permitted use of our models, platform, and applications; • restrictions in the grant of personnel security clearances to our employees; • our ability to maintain facility clearances required to perform on classified contracts for U.S. government and non-U.S. government agencies, as applicable; • changes in the political environment, including before or after a change to the leadership within the government administration, and any resulting uncertainty or changes in policy or priorities and resultant funding; • changes in the government’s attitude towards us as a company or our technology;

 
195 • appeals, disputes, or litigation relating to government procurement, including but not limited to bid protests by unsuccessful bidders on potential or actual awards of contracts to us or our partners by the government; • the adoption of new laws or regulations or changes to existing laws or regulations; • budgetary constraints, reductions in government spending, operating under continuing resolutions, disruptions from government shutdowns, or similar measures and constraints imposed by any lapses in appropriations for the federal government or certain of its departments and agencies; • influence by, or competition from, third parties with respect to pending, new, or existing contracts with government customers; • changes in legal obligations or political or social attitudes with respect to security or privacy issues; • potential delays or changes in the government appropriations or procurement processes, including as a result of events such as war, incidents of terrorism, natural disasters, and public health concerns; and • increased or unexpected costs or unanticipated delays caused by other factors outside of our control. Any such event or activity, among others, could cause governments and government agencies to delay, pause, or cancel contracts or seek to modify their contracts, or refrain from entering into contracts with us or purchasing our models, platform, and applications in the future, undermine our ability to pursue future contracts, damage our relationships with partners and customers who also sell models, platforms, or applications to governments, or reduce the size or timing of payment with respect to our services to or purchases from existing or new government customers. Any of the foregoing could have an adverse effect on our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations. For example, in February 2026, in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President of the United States stated that he had directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology. At the same time, the Secretary of War directed the Department of War to designate us as a “supply-chain risk to national security” and stated that “effective immediately, no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity” with us. On March 4, 2026, the Department of War sent us two letters—one pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 3252 and the other pursuant to Section 4713 of the FASCSA—asserting that our models, platform, and applications present a supply-chain risk. These actions referenced above are defined herein as “Challenged Actions.” We vigorously challenged these Challenged Actions in Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (N.D. Cal.) and Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (D.C. Cir.). After first obtaining an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The court ruled that the Challenged Actions were retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions, particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. 196 § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment largely in our favor. The defendants filed a notice of appeal of the preliminary injunction. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, however, denied our motion to stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a supply-chain risk pending review on the merits. On September 25, 2026, in a 2-1 split decision, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals denied our petition for review, ruling that the Department of War’s Section 4713 supply-chain risk designation was proper, and that our rights under the First Amendment and Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment were not violated. We filed a petition for rehearing en banc asking the full D.C. Circuit to review the panel’s decision. We cannot predict the ultimate outcome of these lawsuits. While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S. government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Further, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, which we disabled for all customers until those restrictions were lifted, as described in “—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets” below. Similar restrictions could be imposed again in the future. Each of the foregoing may result in significant reputational harm, including adverse media coverage, public scrutiny, and negative perceptions among existing and prospective customers, partners, employees, and investors, regardless of the ultimate outcome of the litigation. Such perceptions may lead customers, including commercial enterprises and international customers, to delay or forgo purchasing our models, platform, and applications, or to impose additional diligence, contractual restrictions, or termination rights in connection with engagements with us. Further, these developments may create uncertainty in the broader market regarding our long-term ability to operate in certain sectors, which could result in increased volatility in demand for our models, platform, and applications, reduced willingness of counterparties to enter into long-term or strategic arrangements with us, and fluctuations in investor sentiment, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. The bidding process for government contracts can be highly competitive, expensive, and time-consuming, often requiring significant upfront time and expense without any assurance that these efforts will generate revenue. Government agencies often undertake a significant evaluation process that results in a lengthy sales cycle. Some contracts with government agencies are structured in phases or include options, where each phase is subject to satisfaction of certain conditions and where the exercise of options is discretionary. As a result, the actual scope of work performed pursuant to any such contracts, in addition to related contract revenue, could be less than total contract value. In addition, product purchases by such organizations are frequently subject to budget constraints, multiple approvals, and unanticipated administrative, processing, and other delays. All of these factors can add further risk to business conducted with these customers and could lead to lower revenue results than originally anticipated. We also must comply with both local and international laws and regulations relating to the formation, administration, and performance of contracts. Contracts with government agencies are subject to extensive, evolving, and sometimes complex regulations which provide public sector customers rights, many of which are not typically found in commercial contracts. For example, government contracts generally include the ability of government agencies to terminate for convenience, which, if exercised, would result in a lower contract value and lower-than-anticipated revenue generated by such arrangement. Any changes to the

 
197 government regulations applicable to government contracts could affect our ability to enter into, or the profitability of, contracts with government entities. Our subsidiary, Anthropic Public Institutions, LLC, is required to maintain a facility security clearance to perform on classified contracts for the U.S. federal government and must comply with National Industrial Security Program requirements. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in Anthropic Public Institutions, LLC’s facility clearance being revoked. To the extent Anthropic Public Institutions, LLC, is not able to maintain its facility security clearance, we may not be able to bid on or win new classified contracts, and existing contracts requiring a facility security clearance could be terminated, either of which could have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Contracts with government agencies are also subject to audits and reviews of contractors’ administrative processes and other contract-related compliance obligations. Breaches of government contracts, failure to comply with applicable regulations, failure to obtain and maintain required facility and/or security clearances, or unfavorable findings from government audits or reviews could result in contract terminations, reputational harm, or other adverse consequences, including ineligibility to sell to government agencies in the future, government refusal to continue buying our subscriptions, or fines or civil or criminal liability, which could adversely affect our results of operations. Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment relationships with us and are our customers, creates complex dynamics that could give rise to conflicts of interest and adversely affect our access to compute. We rely on a limited number of CSPs—Amazon, Google, and Microsoft—and suppliers, such as Broadcom, for compute and critical components of our compute infrastructure. These relationships are governed by contractual arrangements that, while providing us with significant committed compute, also create dependencies and potential vulnerabilities. These CSPs may experience service outages, security incidents, or capacity constraints that affect our operations. The terms of our arrangements, including pricing, compute commitments, and service levels, are subject to negotiation upon renewal, and we may be unable to secure renewals on terms as favorable as our current arrangements. Migrating workloads to alternative providers would be costly, time-consuming, and operationally complex, and may not be feasible within timeframes that would avoid material disruption to our model development roadmap or our ability to serve customers. The engineering investment required to maintain the performance of our unified compute platform across new hardware environments means that any such migration could degrade our compute efficiency, increasing the compute and infrastructure costs required to support a given level of business activity during and following any such migration period. Our relationships with these CSPs are multifaceted and complex. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, through their respective affiliates, have made significant equity investments in our company. At the same time, they may have made, and may in the future make, equity investments in, provide financing to, or otherwise support companies whose models, platforms, or applications compete with ours. These CSPs are also our customers, purchasing our intelligence service for internal use or for their own products and services. Their purchasing decisions may be influenced by their own competing offerings, which could affect their demand for our intelligence service. Additionally, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are among the largest technology companies in the world, each with substantial AI research and development programs, AI-powered models, platforms, and applications that compete with ours, and strategic interests that may not be fully aligned with our own. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft each offer AI services and develop and deploy competing AI models through their respective cloud platforms. We make certain of our models available through these 198 cloud platforms, and our distribution relationships with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft generate revenue for us, but they also create dependencies, give them visibility into our pricing and commercial terms across the platforms they operate, and may influence their incentives regarding pricing, compute allocation, service quality, sales prioritization, and compensation structures. To the extent these CSPs promote, integrate, prioritize, or provide customer access to our models, platform, and applications on terms that are less favorable than those applicable to their own competing offerings or to the offerings of other companies, including with respect to pricing, commercial terms, product placement, integration, or access to compute or sales incentives, our competitive position, customer adoption, and business results could be adversely affected. Our relationships with our strategic partners—whether with Amazon, Google, or Microsoft, which simultaneously serve as our investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors, or with Broadcom, which simultaneously serves as a supplier and lessor—create potential conflicts of interest that are difficult to fully anticipate or mitigate. These CSPs may prioritize their own compute needs or those of their other customers, including competitors in which they have invested, may gain insight into our operations and compute requirements through their roles as providers that could inform their competitive strategies, or may make business decisions regarding their platforms that disadvantage our models, platform, and applications relative to their own offerings or the offerings of other companies they support. Similarly, Broadcom may prioritize the supply of accelerators and infrastructure capacity to other customers, alter the terms of our equipment lease or the operation of our dedicated facilities, or make decisions regarding the availability or pricing of hardware that adversely affect our access to the compute infrastructure it provides. Any deterioration in these relationships, or any decision by Amazon, Google, Microsoft, or Broadcom to reduce their support for our models, platform, and applications or limit our access to compute, could adversely affect our business. In addition, such relationships, including any exclusive or preferential arrangements, investment ties, bundling of services, or cooperative initiatives, have attracted and may in the future attract antitrust or competition law scrutiny from regulators and private plaintiffs in the United States or non-U.S. jurisdictions, and any resulting investigations, enforcement actions, or required modifications to our business arrangements could be costly, distracting, and harmful to our business. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. We are pursuing initiatives to develop our own data center infrastructure, which involves significant capital commitments, operational complexities, and execution risks that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. To help reduce our dependence on CSPs, address constraints on available compute, and secure access to compute at the scale necessary for frontier model development, we are pursuing initiatives to develop our own dedicated on-premise data center infrastructure. These efforts include long-term leases and partnerships with third-party partners to procure the underlying real estate, power, and data center facilities while we lease capacity in those facilities and contract with specialized third-party operators for ongoing facility management. We also procure certain compute and infrastructure equipment directly and operate it in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification. For example, under the 2026 Lease Arrangement, the rent payments over the five-year equipment lease are equal to an aggregate of approximately $125.2 billion excluding interest, with rent payable in quarterly installments and payment obligations typically commencing upon AI infrastructure equipment becoming “ready for service” at the applicable data center facility. The 2026 Lease Arrangement is non-cancelable by the parties to such agreement during the applicable lease period except in the case of a default. In addition, we deposited cash

 
199 into a restricted account in April 2026 for the benefit of Broadcom to secure compute capacity, which amount may be released or applied toward obligations under the lease depending on the satisfaction of specified conditions. Under certain circumstances, we may be required to place additional cash into this restricted account for future amounts due under the 2026 Lease Arrangement. Upon the occurrence of certain uncured events of default, such as certain payment or performance failures pursuant to the terms of the 2026 Lease Arrangement, a substantial portion of our obligations under the 2026 Lease Arrangement would be accelerated and, while we have access to multiple sources of capital and are not dependent on the potential financing capacity provided in the Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA that we entered into in connection with the 2026 Lease Arrangement, we may not be permitted to elect to issue the convertible promissory notes under the Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA to finance such obligations. Furthermore, we may in the future continue to directly procure such data center infrastructure and we may also undertake other efforts to build out our own compute and infrastructure and invest more deeply in the compute supply chain, which could result in significantly higher upfront costs and adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. For more information about such lease arrangements, please refer to “4: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition, Operating Results, and Cash Flows— Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations” and “—If our actual compute requirements differ materially from our projections, we may fail to secure sufficient compute to meet our needs or we may be committed to excess compute that remains underutilized.” We have limited experience in managing such data center infrastructure projects at scale. Successfully executing on these data center infrastructure initiatives requires us to recruit personnel with relevant experience and manage complex multi-year deployment timelines and relationships with developers, contractors, and service providers. As we continue to build out our own compute and infrastructure and further vertically integrate across the compute supply chain, these multi-party structures will become more prevalent and will expose us to a structural timing and liquidity risk in our payment obligations that differs from our historical compute arrangements. Historically, we have generally obtained compute from a limited number of CSPs under arrangements in which our compute and infrastructure expenses are paid as compute becomes available to us. In the future, we expect we will increasingly enter into separate arrangements with a greater number of different counterparties, each responsible for discrete services or inputs across the compute supply chain. Under many of these arrangements, we may be obligated to pay a counterparty once it performs its discrete obligation, even if delays or failures by others prevent us from assembling those discrete services or inputs into usable compute we can deploy to generate revenue. In addition, counterparties may deliver their services or inputs later than scheduled, or may fail to deliver them at all, and any such delay or non-delivery by a single counterparty could postpone or prevent our deployment of the associated compute. As a result, we could incur significant cash outflows without obtaining usable compute on a timely basis, which could adversely affect our liquidity, financial condition, and results of operations. Certain of our data center infrastructure arrangements involve complex multi-party structures in which chips are procured from or through our CSPs, leased to us by third-party financing entities, installed in data center facilities procured by or through other third-party partners, and operated by yet another set of third-party service providers. The complexity of these arrangements increases execution risk, as delays or failures by any participant in the chain could affect the availability or performance of the resulting compute. In addition, to meet the substantial energy demands of large-scale AI workloads, we have entered into, and may in the future enter into, arrangements involving dedicated power generation assets and/or the development, operation, or control of power stations or other energy infrastructure. Such arrangements expose us to new operational, regulatory, and environmental liabilities, and require expertise and 200 capabilities that differ from our core competencies. Successfully executing on these power infrastructure projects requires us to recruit personnel with relevant experience and manage complex multi-year deployment timelines and relationships with developers, contractors, service providers, and regulators, including aligning project completion schedules with the data centers such projects are expected to serve in order to avoid timing delays that constrain our ability to utilize this compute and to generate revenue and recoup costs from such investments. Deployment of our data center and power infrastructure projects involves execution risks, including delays due to permitting issues, change in law, force majeure, lack of network connectivity between facilities, supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, or contractor performance; cost overruns due to equipment pricing changes, design modifications, or unanticipated requirements; and technical risks that facilities may not perform as specified or achieve expected reliability or efficiency levels. Certain of our arrangements are also subject to conditions precedent that must be satisfied before construction can commence, and completion guarantees that may terminate upon a lender foreclosure before construction is complete, leaving us without contractual recourse to compel completion. Certain of these arrangements also depend on the continued performance of credit support provided by a third party that is also a competitor, the loss or impairment of which could jeopardize the underlying arrangements. Such credit support provided to third- party data center developers or hardware providers, from which we derive no direct contractual rights or obligations, may also affect the availability and cost of data center capacity and hardware generally. Additionally, new tariffs or import fees enacted after the effective date of certain arrangements may be passed through to us as additional costs. Any delay in or limitation on the amount of compute delivered to us could adversely affect our business. The capital-intensive and long-term nature of leasing and equipping data center capacity creates financial risk, as large upfront investments and long-term payment commitments must be made months before facilities become fully operational. If our compute requirements or technology needs change, we may find ourselves with leased or dedicated infrastructure that is poorly suited to our actual needs, and technological changes in AI hardware or training methodologies could render such infrastructure less efficient than newer alternatives. Unlike CSP arrangements where compute can be adjusted relatively dynamically, long-term leases, reserved compute, and dedicated infrastructure investments are much less flexible and create long- term financial obligations regardless of whether the capacity continues to meet our needs. For example, certain of our dedicated power and data center infrastructure arrangements have initial terms of 20 years with annual escalators and include take-or-pay compute payment obligations and uncapped fuel cost pass- throughs that apply for the duration of the term regardless of actual utilization. Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP arrangements is generally paid as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute becoming operational. Our existing commitments are substantial, and we expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we continue to expand our compute and infrastructure build- out. Please refer to “4: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition, Operating Results, and Cash Flows—Liquidity and Capital Resources” for more information. As a result, we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future, and our net cash used in these activities may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves. The magnitude and timing of these investments are inherently uncertain and may

 
201 change materially over short periods, including as a result of decisions to accelerate or expand our build- out, and such changes could rapidly and significantly alter our expected results of operations and cash flows for a given period. If our cash flows from operations and available capital are insufficient to fund these investments, we may be required to raise additional capital on unfavorable terms or to reduce, defer, or forgo planned investments, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. If we are unable to successfully execute on our data center infrastructure initiatives, experience significant delays or cost overruns, or find that the infrastructure we lease, deploy, or build does not meet our evolving needs, we may not realize the expected benefits of these investments, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We may not successfully build, expand, and deploy our sales and marketing organization in a timely manner, or we may not successfully hire, retain, train, and motivate our sales personnel. We have grown, and will continue to grow, our direct sales force. Whether we are able to increase our sales to existing customers, identify and engage new customers, and enter new U.S. and non-U.S. markets, each with a focus on broadening use of our models, platform, and applications across departments and entire organizations, will depend, among other things, on our ability to successfully test new market segments and customer types, validate product-market fit through early customer engagement, timely and effectively scale our sales motions, and adapt quickly when market conditions change. We have limited experience building, managing, and scaling a direct sales force. We have dedicated and plan to continue to dedicate significant resources to sales and marketing programs and to expand our sales and marketing capabilities to target potential customers and achieve broader market adoption of our models, platform, and applications, but there is no guarantee that we will be successful in attracting and maintaining additional customers. Moreover, identifying, recruiting, training, and managing sales personnel requires significant time, expense, and attention, including from our senior management and other key personnel, as there is significant competition for sales personnel with the skills and technical knowledge that we require, including the ability to understand and communicate complex and evolving AI use cases, regulatory considerations, customer risk sensitivities, and rapidly changing product capabilities. These challenges are particularly acute for international expansion, which requires qualified personnel with international experience, language skills, cultural competencies in the geographic markets which we target, and an aligned mission-oriented culture. If we are unable to successfully manage the foregoing risks, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. We periodically make adjustments to our sales and marketing organization in response to market opportunities, product introductions or enhancements, acquisitions, and other internal and external considerations. Any future sales and marketing organization changes may result in a temporary reduction of productivity, which could negatively affect our rate of growth. In addition, any significant change to the way we structure and implement the compensation of our sales and marketing organization may be disruptive or may not be effective and may adversely affect our revenue growth. If we are unable to attract, hire, develop, retain, and motivate qualified sales and marketing personnel, if our new sales personnel are unable to achieve sufficient sales productivity levels in a reasonable period of time or at all, if our marketing programs are not effective, or if we are unable to effectively build, expand, and manage our sales organization and operations, our sales and revenue may grow more slowly than expected or decline, and our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. 202 We have a limited history under our current go-to-market strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition, engagement, and retention model may not be successful. We have a limited history selling consumption-based access and subscriptions to our models, platform, and applications under our current business model, and we are continuing to scale our operations and go-to- market strategy. Our future success depends in part on our ability to continue attracting, onboarding, expanding, and retaining customers under this model, including determining whether, when, and how to target, develop, and deepen relationships with individual customers over time. Scaling our operations, including hiring, training, and retaining additional sales, sales engineering, and customer-facing personnel, and evolving our go-to-market strategy may take more time and require more effort than anticipated, and the results of these efforts are difficult to predict. Our business and operating models have not been fully proven, and our limited history with our current approach makes it difficult to evaluate our prospects, plan for future growth, and forecast our results of operations. In addition, our strategy and customer mix expose us to competitive and execution risks as the AI market continues to evolve. We have organized our research priorities, our product roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, and much of the diffusion of Claude to date has been organic—driven by individual users, including software developers and prosumers, who adopt Claude and often serve as internal champions for its broader adoption within their organizations—rather than by a large direct sales organization. This approach has allowed us to scale with a smaller team relative to other large enterprise technology companies, but it assumes that our applications and distribution will be sufficient to deliver the capabilities of our models to customers and that individual adoption will continue to translate into organizational adoption and expansion. Companies with stronger consumer-facing businesses, larger consumer user bases, more established brands, broader distribution, or deeper customer relationships may choose to increase their focus on enterprise customers or enterprise use cases and could leverage their scale, resources, and market presence to compete more effectively with us. In particular, if such competitors capture the individual users from whom our enterprise adoption often originates, whether through their consumer applications, by integrating AI functionality into products those users already use, or otherwise, our pipeline of enterprise opportunities could be reduced in ways that a direct sales organization of our current scale may not be able to offset. Building a substantially larger sales organization, or shifting investment toward consumer and application-layer products to compete for those users, would require significant time and resources beyond our current plans and would involve the tradeoffs described in “— We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected” above. Because we have a limited operating history with our current business model and go-to-market strategy, we have less experience predicting customer adoption, expansion, and retention patterns, and customers may be slower than expected to adopt our models, platform, and applications or expand usage. Any failure to successfully scale our operations or effectively execute on and refine our go-to-market strategy could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Sales to enterprise customers involve complexities and risks that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We derive a large portion of our revenue from sales to enterprise customers. Our ability to attract, retain, and expand relationships with enterprise customers depends in significant part on our ability to meet their generally heightened operational, technical, security, reliability, and compliance requirements. Enterprises typically expect high levels of system uptime, performance consistency, data security, auditability, internal controls, and scalability, as well as robust support and service levels. These requirements may be

 
203 heightened for our agentic offerings, where enterprise customers may require detailed logs of each action taken by an autonomous agent within their environment, including the agent’s reasoning, tool invocations, and interactions with external systems. Any inability on our part to provide such logs at the level of granularity customers require could limit adoption of our agentic offerings by enterprises or result in customer attrition. If we are unable to deliver models, platforms, and applications that satisfy these enterprise-grade requirements, or if we experience outages, performance degradation, security incidents, or other operational failures, our ability to retain and expand with enterprise customers could be adversely affected. In particular, as we deploy our Virtual Collaborators, like Claude Code and Claude Cowork, within enterprise environments, these systems will require broad permissions and deep integrations with customers’ internal tools, data, and workflows in order to operate effectively. The scope of access required for extended autonomous operation within enterprise environments increases the potential consequences of any security incident, unauthorized action, or system error, and customers may be reluctant to grant the level of access necessary for these systems to operate as designed if they are unable to satisfy themselves regarding the security, reliability, and controllability of such systems. Our sales efforts targeted at enterprise customers also involve risks and challenges that may not be present, or that are present to a lesser extent, with sales to individuals or smaller organizations. These customers typically have longer decision-making cycles, require greater security, functionality, and scalability, expect a broader range of services, demand that providers take on a larger share of risks, require higher levels of customer service and support, and expect greater payment flexibility from vendors. We are often required to spend significant time and resources to familiarize potential customers with the value proposition of our models, platform, and applications, and this process can take substantially longer with enterprise customers. Enterprises may also require extensive customization, integration support, and vendor evaluations and demand more features than we currently offer or than we can deliver within their expected timeframes, including enterprise-grade functionality such as audit logs, compliance features, security controls, and monitoring tools, which may require us to make additional investments in product development or services capabilities, before committing to a purchase. As a result of these factors, sales opportunities with enterprises require us to devote greater sales and administrative support and professional services resources to each such enterprise customer, which increases our costs, lengthens our sales cycle, and diverts our sales and customer service resources to a smaller number of enterprise customers. We may spend substantial time, effort, and money in our sales efforts without successfully producing any sales. In addition, many enterprise customers procure and deploy our models, platform, and applications through third-party CSP marketplaces, which can introduce additional complexity into the sales and deployment process, including reliance on the CSPs’ procurement, security, and billing workflows and coordination with multiple counterparties. As a result, our ability to attract, retain, and expand relationships with enterprise customers may also depend in part on factors outside of our direct control, including the policies, priorities, and operational requirements of such CSPs. A number of factors influence the length and variability of our sales cycle. The need to educate potential customers about the uses and benefits of our models, platform, and applications, the discretionary nature of purchasing and budget cycles, competitive evaluation and purchasing approval processes, procurement requirements, legal review of contract terms, and internal budget authorization procedures all contribute to sales cycle variability. The length of our sales cycle, from identification of the opportunity to deal closure, may vary significantly from customer to customer. Sales to enterprises typically take longer to complete than sales to individuals or smaller organizations. A meaningful portion of our revenue is attributable to a relatively small number of such enterprise customer 204 relationships, which increases the variability of our financial results. Our revenue in any given quarter could be substantially affected if these customers decide to significantly reduce their spend. Enterprises may have deep existing relationships with our competitors for models, platforms, and applications we do not offer, or relationships with others in the ecosystem, which may delay our sales process or cause us to not succeed with such enterprises. Enterprise customers are particularly sensitive to our ability to maintain the uptime of our models, platform, and applications, and any degradation in uptime could adversely affect our ability to retain and expand with our enterprise customers. Sustaining the uptime, performance, and scale that enterprise customers expect can place additional demands on our overall compute, and any failure of our capacity management systems to direct sufficient compute to support such demands could adversely affect our ability to serve all workloads. For more information about the foregoing, please refer to “—If we fail to manage our technical operations infrastructure, or experience service outages, interruptions, or delays in the deployment of our models, platform, and applications, our results of operations may be adversely affected” below. Our sales strategy for these enterprise customers also depends on our ability to build and maintain an effective sales organization. If we fail to effectively manage these risks associated with sales to enterprises, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. For additional discussion of our personnel-related risks, please refer to “—We may not successfully build, expand, and deploy our sales and marketing organization in a timely manner, or we may not successfully hire, retain, train, and motivate our sales personnel” above. If our marketing strategies, such as our free trials and free tiers, fail to generate the benefits we expect, or if their costs exceed those benefits, our ability to grow our revenue could be adversely affected. A portion of our users access our models, platform, and applications through free tiers or promotional offerings, and we seek to convert these users into paying customers over time. We may not always be successful in doing so, as free users may be satisfied with the limited functionality available in free tiers, may not have budgets to support paid subscriptions, or may choose to use our free offerings indefinitely without converting to paid plans. The availability of free tiers may cannibalize potential paid subscriptions, as some users who would have otherwise paid for our services may instead rely exclusively on free access. Additionally, providing free access to our models, platform, and applications involves costs, including compute and infrastructure, customer support, and other operational costs. In addition, we offer free access in significant part to build awareness of, familiarity with, and engagement with our products, and as a means of reaching individuals engaged in knowledge work outside of a business or organizational context. However, these benefits are inherently difficult to measure, free usage may not generate the awareness or advocacy we expect, and individual adoption of our products may not translate into organizational adoption or expansion. Please refer to “—We have a limited history under our current go-to-market strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition, engagement, and retention model may not be successful” above. If the costs of supporting free users exceed the value we derive from their eventual conversion or other benefits such as network effects and word-of-mouth referrals, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

 
205 If we fail to maintain high-quality customer support, our ability to retain and expand customers could suffer, which may adversely affect our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our customers rely on our customer support services to resolve issues and realize the full benefits that our models, platform, and applications provide. In order to deliver high-quality customer support and engagement, we must successfully assist our customers in deploying and continuing to use our models, platform, and applications, resolve performance issues, discover and deploy our models, platform, and applications in new use cases, provide hands-on technical implementation, customization, and solution engineering support, provide training and guidance to help customers effectively adopt and scale their use of our models, platform, and applications, address interoperability challenges, and respond to security threats and cyberattacks and performance and reliability problems that may arise from time to time. The importance of our support function will increase as we expand our business and pursue new customers. Many enterprises have complex internal systems and require high levels of focused support to fully realize the benefits of our models, platform, and applications. If we do not help our customers quickly resolve issues and provide effective ongoing support and enablement, or a market perception develops that we do not maintain high-quality customer support and experience, our ability to maintain and expand our subscriptions to existing and new customers could suffer, particularly with respect to our enterprise customers. In addition, our growth model depends significantly on driving deeper adoption and expanded use cases within our existing customer base. If we are unable to effectively provide support and integration efforts that enable customers to identify, deploy, and scale additional high-value use cases, demonstrate measurable return on investment, or integrate our models, platform, and applications into their core workflows, customers may limit usage, fail to renew at expected levels, or reduce their spend, which could materially slow our revenue growth. Further, there can be no assurance that we will be able to hire sufficient support personnel as and when needed, particularly if our sales exceed our internal forecasts. We expect to continue to increase our customer base, and that growth may put additional pressure on our customer support teams, which may require additional personnel to respond to customer demand. We may be unable to respond quickly enough to accommodate short-term increases in customer demand for services. To the extent that we are unsuccessful in hiring, training, and retaining adequate support personnel, our ability to provide high-quality and timely support to our customers will be negatively impacted, and our customers’ satisfaction and their use and subscription of our models, platform, and applications could be adversely affected. In addition, as we continue to grow our operations and reach a larger and increasingly global customer base, we need to be able to provide efficient services that meet our customers’ needs globally at scale, and our customer support teams may face additional challenges, including those associated with delivering support, training, and documentation in languages other than English and providing services across expanded time zones. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
