(Note 4) Represents the income tax effect of the above adjustments, which relates to stock-based compensation expense and, in certain periods, other adjustments. 298 Liquidity and Capital Resources Since inception, we have financed our operations, corporate investments, and capital expenditures primarily through proceeds from the issuance of convertible promissory notes, redeemable convertible preferred stock, cash generated from sales, and SAFEs. To date, we have financed our compute and infrastructure primarily under arrangements with our CSPs, as well as through proceeds from the financing activities described above and cash generated from operations. As of September 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $95.6 billion, $36.3 billion of short-term investments, and $14.8 billion available under the A&R Credit Facility, as described below. Cash and cash equivalents consist of cash held in checking and interest-bearing accounts, money market funds, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less from the date of purchase. We have generated losses from our operations, as reflected in our accumulated deficit of $156.2 billion, which includes $135.1 billion related to changes in the fair value of our convertible notes driven by increases in our enterprise valuation and derivative liabilities since 2023, including $94.3 billion during the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Additionally, we have generated negative cash flows from operating and investing activities in 2023, 2024, and 2025, driven by ongoing expenditures to support business growth including investments to secure access to more compute and infrastructure capacity. We generated positive cash flows from operating activities of $6.6 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. We continue to invest in our own data center infrastructure and enter into compute and infrastructure capacity arrangements to support anticipated demand for our intelligence service. Given the long lead times between contracting for, purchasing, or leasing compute and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure these arrangements well in advance of anticipated demand. To secure certain data center development projects, which require significant capital commitments in advance of deployment, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements with financing sources or partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center capacity that is expected to host such partners’ chips or computing infrastructure. Our ability to expand compute and infrastructure capacity through these arrangements in the future may depend on the continued willingness and ability of a limited number of CSPs, partners, and financing sources to enter into and perform under such arrangements. In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the delivery of the equipment or infrastructure. We anticipate making significant and increased investments for the foreseeable future, including for owned or leased compute and infrastructure in advance of delivery. These investments help ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the frontier of AI. Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP arrangements is generally paid for as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute becoming operational. We expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we expand our build-out, and we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. Our net cash used in these activities may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves. The magnitude and timing of these investments are inherently uncertain and may change materially over short periods, including as a result of decisions to accelerate or expand our build-out, and such changes could rapidly and significantly affect our cash flows for a given period. In addition, these investments are subject to known trends and uncertainties that could adversely affect our results of operations. The compute and chips necessary for frontier model development

 
299 are available from a limited number of suppliers and geographies and are subject to intense competition, supply constraints, and evolving export controls, and we have historically operated in a compute- constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs and chip partners on which we rely provide us capital or credit support, serve as our infrastructure vendors, and develop and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest that affect our access to compute, its cost, the prioritization of our workloads, or the terms on which such capital or credit support is provided. For a discussion of these and other risks, please refer to “3: Business and Other Risks.” We also intend to use a portion of the net proceeds we receive from this offering and the concurrent private placement to satisfy our anticipated tax withholding and remittance obligations of $3.8 billion related to the RSU Settlement. This amount is based upon the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the Initial Preliminary Price Range (or, if subsequently revised, the Revised Preliminary Price Range), and an assumed 50.90% tax withholding rate. Each $1.00 increase or decrease in the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share would increase or decrease, as applicable, the amount we would be required to pay to satisfy our tax withholding and remittance obligations related to the RSU Settlement by $52 million. We believe our existing available cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments, together with cash generated from sales and amounts available under our A&R Credit Facility, will be sufficient to support working capital, operating and finance lease payments, and capital expenditure requirements for at least the next 12 months from the date of this document. However, our future capital requirements will depend on many factors, including our revenue growth, the timing and extent of our investments in compute and infrastructure capacity, including additional or expanded CSP, equipment lease, and data center arrangements, the success and expansion of our sales, marketing, and business development strategies, any potential future investment in complementary businesses, products, technologies, assets, and talent, risks associated with the AI industry, and other factors described under “—Key Factors Affecting Our Performance.” As a result of these and other factors, we may be required to seek additional financing sooner than we currently anticipate. If we determine that additional financing is required, we may not be able to raise it on terms acceptable to us or at all. Any such financing, if completed, may be costly, dilutive, or lead to restrictions on how we operate our business. If we are unable to raise additional capital when required, or if we cannot expand our operations or otherwise capitalize on our business opportunities because we lack sufficient capital, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows would be adversely affected. Over the longer term, we expect to have significant cash requirements as we continue to invest in our business, primarily for compute and infrastructure, including our data center infrastructure build-out, as well as for general operating needs. We expect to fund these long-term cash requirements through a combination of cash flows from operations, proceeds from equity financings, including the net proceeds from this Offering and the concurrent private placement, proceeds from debt financings and potential future indebtedness, and financing arrangements with our partners, including under our note purchase agreements and our equipment lease and data center arrangements. Our ability to meet these requirements over the long term depends on our ability to grow our revenue and generate cash flows from operations and to access additional capital on acceptable terms. If sufficient funds are not available, we may be required to reduce, defer, or forgo planned investments, which could adversely affect our business, competitive position, and results of operations. 300 Revolving Credit Agreement In May 2025, we entered into a Credit Agreement (as amended from time to time prior to the A&R Credit Agreement (as defined below), the “Credit Agreement”) with certain lenders from time to time party thereto and Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., as administrative agent and collateral agent for the lenders, which initially provided for a $2.5 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with a $400 million letter of credit sublimit (the “Initial Credit Facility”). In September 2025, we amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $2.75 billion, and in November 2025, we further amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $3.25 billion. In September 2026, we entered into an Amended and Restated Credit Agreement (the “A&R Credit Agreement”), which amended and restated the Credit Agreement to provide for a $15.0 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with the full amount thereof available for letters of credit (the “A&R Credit Facility”). The A&R Credit Facility will mature on September 4, 2031, subject to earlier springing maturity if more than $500 million in aggregate scheduled cash principal payments on certain of our indebtedness are required within the 91-day period preceding the date on which any such scheduled principal payment is due, and we do not have sufficient liquidity to make all such payments then due and remain in pro forma compliance with our financial covenant, subject to certain other exceptions and conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The proceeds of the A&R Credit Facility may be used for working capital, general corporate purposes, and other lawful purposes. We may request borrowings in U.S. dollars or certain other agreed currencies, subject to the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement. As of September 30, 2026, we had no borrowings drawn under the A&R Credit Facility and $205 million of standby letters of credit outstanding. As of September 30, 2026, we were in compliance with all covenants under the A&R Credit Agreement. We may borrow, repay, and reborrow amounts under the A&R Credit Facility from time to time. We are required to pay commitment fees on the unused portion of the A&R Credit Facility and fees in connection with letters of credit. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date (as defined below), such commitment fees will vary depending on our credit ratings, as set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. Our obligations under the A&R Credit Facility are required to be guaranteed by certain of our material subsidiaries and secured by substantially all of our assets and the assets of such subsidiary guarantors, subject to certain exceptions and exclusions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The A&R Credit Agreement further provides that, on and after the date we have obtained an Investment Grade Rating (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement) from at least two out of three of Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch, at our election, all guarantees and security interests securing the obligations under the A&R Credit Facility will be released, discharged, and terminated, subject to certain conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement (such date, the “Guarantee and Collateral Release Date”). Borrowings under the A&R Credit Facility bear interest at rates based on the Alternate Base Rate (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), Term SOFR Rate (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), or other applicable benchmark rates in the case of foreign currencies, plus an applicable margin. From and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, such applicable margin will vary depending on our credit ratings, as more fully set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. In addition, the A&R Credit Agreement includes customary affirmative and negative covenants, including, but not limited to, restrictions on additional indebtedness, liens, asset sales, investments, mergers, and restricted payments. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, the negative covenants limiting asset sales, investments, restricted payments, and affiliate transactions will cease to apply and the negative covenants restricting additional indebtedness and liens will be modified in certain respects, including to permit additional indebtedness, subject to a cap on certain indebtedness that is secured by assets that do not secure the A&R Credit Facility

 
301 or that is incurred or guaranteed by restricted subsidiaries that are not guarantors under the A&R Credit Facility. The A&R Credit Agreement includes a financial covenant requiring that we maintain liquidity of at least $5.0 billion as of the last day of each fiscal quarter, beginning with the fiscal quarter ending December 31, 2026. The A&R Credit Agreement also includes customary events of default, which, if triggered, could result in the acceleration of amounts due under the A&R Credit Facility and termination of the commitments thereunder. AMD Agreement In July 2026, we entered into a hardware supply framework agreement (the “Hardware Supply Agreement”) with AMD to purchase, lease, or access AMD-based Helios rack-scale systems featuring AMD Instinct™ MI450 series GPUs. Pursuant to the terms of the Hardware Supply Agreement, AMD has provided a commitment to purchase up to $5.0 billion of our Class N common stock (the “AMD Equity Commitment”), which becomes available for us to draw on in increments following the achievement of specified AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones. In connection with the concurrent private placement, we entered into a letter agreement with AMD under which, upon the closing of the concurrent private placement, the $2.5 billion purchase price paid by AMD for shares of our Class N common stock in the concurrent private placement will satisfy a portion of the AMD Equity Commitment by reducing, on a dollar-for-dollar basis, the amount available for us to draw. As a result, following the closing of the concurrent private placement, up to $2.5 billion of the AMD Equity Commitment will remain, which will become available for us to draw only to the extent that the cumulative amount accrued based on AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones exceeds the aggregate purchase price paid by AMD in the concurrent private placement. Based on the deployment schedule contemplated by the Hardware Supply Agreement, we expect the first of the AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones to be achieved in 2027. Following the completion of this offering, any subsequent purchases of our Class N common stock by AMD pursuant to the Hardware Supply Agreement will be made at a price per share equal to the volume-weighted average price of our Class A common stock over the 30 trading days immediately preceding the applicable closing date of such purchase, and we must make any draw request within 12 months following the final delivery and deployment of AMD GPU capacity under the Hardware Supply Agreement. 302 Convertible Notes Overview We have entered into NPAs with each of Google (through Google LLC), Amazon (through Amazon Web Services, Inc.), and Broadcom that provide for the issuance of convertible promissory notes and, in certain cases, shares of our non-voting capital stock. Our NPAs with Google consist of agreements entered into in September 2023 and August 2024, pursuant to which all convertible promissory notes previously issued thereunder have been fully converted into non-voting redeemable convertible preferred stock and under which no additional notes may be issued, and an agreement entered into in March 2026 (“Google 2026 NPA”), which provides for potential future financing capacity, subject to certain conditions described below. Our NPAs with Amazon consist of the Amazon 2023 NPA and the Amazon 2024 NPA, pursuant to which we previously issued convertible promissory notes, approximately $6.2 billion aggregate principal amount of which remains outstanding as described below under “—Convertible Notes—Outstanding Notes,” and under which no additional notes may be issued, and the 2026 Stock Purchase and Convertible Note Facility Agreement, dated as of April 20, 2026, by and between us and Amazon (“Amazon 2026 NPA”), which provides for potential future financing capacity, subject to certain conditions described below. The Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA provides for potential future financing capacity, if needed, subject to certain conditions described below. Market risk represents the risk of loss that may impact our financial position due to adverse changes in financial market prices and rates. Our market risk exposure is primarily the result of fluctuations in interest rates and foreign currency exchange rates. Interest Rate Risk As of September 30, 2026, we had $95.6 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $36.3 billion of short- term investments in a variety of securities, including money market funds, U.S. Treasury and agency securities, corporate debt securities, and commercial paper. In addition, we had $2.6 billion of restricted cash primarily due to amounts held as collateral for our lease and other obligations. Our cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments are held for working capital purposes, and we do not enter into investments for trading or speculative purposes. A hypothetical 100 basis point increase or decrease in interest rates would have resulted in a decrease or increase, respectively, of $310 million in the market value of our cash equivalents and short-term investments as of September 30, 2026. Foreign Currency Exchange Risk We transact business globally in multiple currencies, with the vast majority of our revenue denominated in U.S. dollars and, to a lesser extent, other currencies such as euros and British pounds. Our international revenue, as well as costs and expenses denominated in foreign currencies, and intercompany transactions with our foreign subsidiaries, expose us to the risk of fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates against the U.S. dollar. A hypothetical 10% change in foreign currency exchange rates applicable to our business would not have had a material impact on our consolidated financial statements as of September 30, 2026. We have not entered into derivative or hedging transactions, but we may enter into such arrangements in the future if our exposure to foreign currency becomes more significant.

 
315 Critical Accounting Estimates Our discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based upon our financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with GAAP. GAAP requires us to make certain estimates and judgments that affect the amounts reported in our financial statements. We base our estimates on historical experience, anticipated future trends, and other assumptions we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances. Because these accounting estimates require significant judgment, our actual results may differ materially from our estimates. We believe that of our significant accounting policies, which are described in “Section 6: Financial Information—1: Financial Documents—Consolidated Financial Statements—Note 1: Description of Business and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies”, the following accounting policies involve a greater degree of judgment and complexity. Accordingly, these are the policies we believe are the most critical to aid in fully understanding and evaluating our consolidated financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows. Stock-Based Compensation We measure compensation expense for all stock-based payment awards, including stock options and RSUs, granted to employees, directors, and other service providers, based on the estimated fair value of the awards on the date of grant. The most significant input in determining the fair value of a stock option is the estimated fair value of our common stock. The estimated fair value of our common stock is also used to measure the grant-date fair value of RSUs and RSAs, including those subject to performance-based vesting conditions. Stock Options We estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees, consultants, officers, and directors using the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model on the date of grant. The fair value of stock options that are expected to vest is recognized as compensation expense on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period. Forfeitures are accounted for when they occur. The Black-Scholes-Merton model considers several variables and assumptions in estimating the fair value of stock-based awards. These variables include: • Fair Value of Common Stock. Because our common stock is not yet publicly traded, we must estimate the fair value of our common stock. Our board of directors considers numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the fair value of our common stock as discussed in the section titled “—Common Stock Valuations” below. • Expected Volatility. Since we have no trading history of our common stock, the expected volatility of our underlying common stock is estimated by taking the weighted-average historical volatility of a group of comparable publicly traded companies over a period equal to the expected life of the options. • Expected Term. Expected term represents the period over which we anticipate stock-based awards to be outstanding. We estimate the expected term based on the options’ vesting term and contractual terms, such that the expected life is equal to the average of the stock-based award’s weighted-average vesting period and its contractual term. 316 • Risk-Free Rate. The expected risk-free rate assumption is based on the U.S. Treasury instruments whose term is consistent with the expected term of the stock options. • Expected Dividend Yield. The expected dividend yield is zero, as we have never declared or paid any dividends and have no current plans to do so. As of September 30, 2026, there was approximately $1.8 billion of total unrecognized compensation cost related to unvested stock options, which is expected to be recognized over a weighted-average period of 1.2 years. Restricted Stock Units and Restricted Stock Awards We have granted RSUs to our employees and non-employee service providers under our 2021 Plan. RSUs outstanding as of September 30, 2026 have both service-based and performance-based vesting conditions. The service-based vesting period for these awards is typically four years. Upon satisfaction of the performance-based condition, RSUs for which the service-based vesting condition has also been satisfied will vest immediately, and any remaining unvested RSUs will vest ratably over the remaining service period. The performance-based condition is generally satisfied upon the occurrence of a change in control event or the effective date of the registration statement in the United States relating to this Offering. As of September 30, 2026, no stock-based compensation expense had been recognized for such RSUs because the performance-based condition was not satisfied. In connection with this Offering, we will begin recording stock-based compensation expense based on the grant-date fair value of the RSUs (or, for RSUs modified as part of the RSU Modification, their modification-date fair value) using the accelerated attribution method. As of September 30, 2026, there was approximately $32.3 billion of total unrecognized stock- based compensation expense related to RSUs. Of that amount, $8.2 billion relates to RSUs for which the service-based vesting condition had been satisfied or partially satisfied. Following the completion of this Offering, stock-based compensation expense related to our RSUs will result in increases in our expenses in future periods, in particular in the quarter in which this Offering is completed, as the performance-based vesting condition applicable to a significant portion of our outstanding RSUs will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement in the United States relating to this Offering. Upon the completion of this Offering, we will record cumulative stock-based compensation expense of approximately $14.2 billion related to RSUs outstanding as of September 30, 2026, reflecting modifications of such RSUs subsequent to September 30, 2026 at interpolated modification-date fair values based on the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set forth on the cover page of this prospectus, for which (i) the service-based vesting condition will be fully or partially satisfied as of November 19, 2026 and (ii) the performance-based vesting condition will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement in the United States relating to this Offering. We have granted RSAs to founders, early employees, advisors, and in connection with acquisitions. The RSAs consist of awards with a service-based vesting condition. RSAs are measured at fair value of the underlying common stock on the date of grant. We record compensation cost for these awards using the straight-line method over the requisite service period. Common Stock Valuations Prior to our initial public offering, given the absence of a public trading market of our Class A common stock, and in accordance with the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants Accounting and Valuation Guide, Valuation of Privately-Held-Company Equity Securities Issued as Compensation, our board of

 
317 directors exercised reasonable judgment and considered numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the best estimate of the fair value of our common stock, including: • contemporaneous third-party valuations of our common stock; • the prices paid for common or redeemable convertible preferred stock sold to third-party investors by us and prices paid in secondary transactions, including any tender offers; • the rights, preferences, and privileges of our redeemable convertible preferred stock relative to those of our common stock; • actual and forecasted operating and financial performance; • our stage of development; • the industry outlook; • the lack of marketability of our common stock; • the likelihood of achieving a liquidity event, such as an initial public offering or a sale of our company, given prevailing market conditions; • the history and nature of our business, industry trends, and competitive environment; and • general economic outlook, including economic growth, inflation and unemployment, interest rate environment, and global economic trends. Our board of directors determined the fair value of our common stock by first determining the enterprise value of our business and then allocating the value among the various classes of our securities to derive a per share value of our common stock. The enterprise value of our business was primarily estimated by reference to the closest round of equity financing to the date of the valuation. In allocating the enterprise value of our business among the various classes of stock prior to this Offering, we used a hybrid method based on a contingent claims analysis (“CCA”) and a common stock equivalent (“CSE”) method. The CCA is based on the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model, which models each class of stock as a call option with a unique claim on our assets. The CSE method presumes that all shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock convert into common stock based upon their conversion terms and other differences in the rights and preferences of the shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock are ignored. After the allocation of enterprise value to the various classes of stock, a discount for lack of marketability (“DLOM”) is applied to arrive at a fair value of the common stock. A DLOM is meant to account for the lack of opportunity to sell private company stock that is not traded on public exchanges. In making the final determination of common stock value, consideration is also given to the recent sales and/or expected sales of common stock. Application of these approaches involves the use of estimates, judgment, and assumptions that are complex and subjective, such as those regarding our expected future revenue, expenses, and future cash flows, discount rates, market multiples, the selection of comparable companies, and the probability of possible future events. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions or the relationships 318 between those assumptions impact our valuations as of each valuation date and may have a material impact on the valuation of our common stock. Following this Offering, it will not be necessary to determine the fair value of our common stock, as the shares of our common stock will be traded in the public market. Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs We elected to account for our convertible notes at fair value pursuant to Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) Topic 825, Financial Instruments. The convertible notes are recognized at their estimated fair value on our consolidated balance sheet, and changes in fair value are recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in our consolidated statement of operations. We elected the fair value option to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately accounting for the liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation model. In connection with the 2023 and 2024 note purchase agreements with both Amazon and Google, we recognized derivative liabilities representing obligations to issue future convertible notes pursuant to the terms of those agreements. The derivative liabilities were measured at estimated fair value, with changes in fair value recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations. The estimated fair value of the convertible promissory notes is determined using a hybrid approach comprising a CCA and a CSE method. The analysis estimates the fair value of the convertible promissory notes using a scenario-based analysis that considers the probability-weighted present value of the instruments across the range of possible outcomes available to the note holders, including conversion into redeemable convertible preferred stock or Class N common stock, cash repayment at maturity, and cash settlement at a premium upon a change of control. The scenarios included consider the probability-weighted value of the instruments in the CCA and CSE framework. The application of this methodology involves the use of complex and subjective estimates, judgments, and assumptions, including the probability and timing of each settlement scenario such as a qualified equity financing, initial public offering, direct listing, or change of control; the estimated fair value of our equity securities into which the notes may convert; the applicable conversion prices, which vary by note series and are contingent on factors such as elapsed time since issuance and contractual caps and percentage discounts; and the ownership thresholds and rollover provisions that determine the extent to which principal balances convert into equity versus being reissued as rollover notes. In particular, the ownership cap and rollover mechanism—whereby conversion is capped at specified ownership thresholds and any unconverted principal balance is re-issued as a non-interest bearing rollover note that remains subject to fair value measurement—requires significant judgment in estimating what proportion of each note financing will convert versus roll over, because this determination depends on the size and structure of future equity financings that are inherently uncertain. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions, or the relationships between those assumptions, impact our valuations as of each measurement date and may have a material impact on the amounts recognized in our consolidated statement of operations. The fair value option election described above also applied to the SAFEs that we issued during the year ended December 31, 2023. The SAFEs were measured at estimated fair value using the same scenario- based framework, with the monetary settlement amount fixed at inception and the number of equity shares received upon conversion being variable; consistent with the convertible notes, changes in fair value were

 
319 recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations. All SAFEs were converted into redeemable convertible preferred stock during the years ended December 31, 2023 and 2024, and no SAFEs remained outstanding as of December 31, 2024 or 2025. No SAFEs were outstanding at any point during the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Accordingly, the primary ongoing estimation exposure under the fair value option relates to the convertible notes and rollover notes described above. For additional information regarding our convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs, including descriptions of the individual instruments, their key terms, conversion activity, and balances during the periods presented, please refer to “Section 6: Financial Information—1: Financial Documents— Consolidated Financial Statements—Note 9: Convertible Notes, Revolving Credit Agreement and SAFEs.” Leases We lease facilities and equipment, including compute and infrastructure capacity, under operating and finance leases. We determine whether an arrangement is or contains a lease at inception and evaluate the classification of our leases at lease commencement and, as necessary, upon modification. Accounting for leases requires significant judgment, including determining whether an arrangement is or contains a lease, and significant estimates, including the expected lease term, the fair value of the leased property, and our incremental borrowing rate. Given the size and duration of our lease portfolio, changes in our estimate of the fair value of the underlying leased asset, the expected lease term, or the determination of our incremental borrowing rate could result in a different lease classification or a materially different measurement of our right-of-use assets and lease liabilities. Income Taxes We account for income taxes using the asset and liability method, recognizing deferred tax assets and liabilities for temporary differences between the financial reporting and tax bases of assets and liabilities, as well as for net operating loss and credit carryforwards, measured at enacted tax rates applicable in the years of expected reversals. We establish valuation allowances when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to amounts more-likely-than-not expected to be realized, based on the weighting of positive and negative evidence. Assessing the realizability of our deferred tax assets is an area of significant management judgment. We evaluate our deferred tax assets for recoverability based on historical taxable income, projected future taxable income, reversal patterns of existing temporary differences, and available tax planning strategies. As an AI company operating in a rapidly evolving market with significant ongoing investment in compute and infrastructure, our projections of future taxable income are inherently uncertain. Should our assessment of the recoverability of deferred tax assets change, our income tax provision would be adjusted in that period, which could materially impact our results of operations. We account for uncertain tax positions in accordance with ASC Topic 740, Income Taxes. Tax benefits from uncertain positions are recognized when it is more likely than not that the position will be sustained on examination based on its technical merits, measured at the amount that is more likely than not to be realized upon settlement. These assessments require judgment, particularly with respect to the qualification and documentation of research and development tax credits, where supporting evidence may be subject to differing interpretations. The actual outcome of these matters may differ materially from our current 320 estimates. We recognize interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits within our provision for income taxes. Loss Contingencies We are involved in legal claims, proceedings, and other regulatory and administrative matters that arise in the ordinary course of business, certain of which may include speculative claims for substantial or indeterminate amounts of damages. We routinely assess each significant matter and its potential financial exposure. We record a liability when we believe it is both probable that a loss has been incurred and the amount can be reasonably estimated, and we disclose matters for which a loss is reasonably possible and the loss or range of loss can be estimated. These assessments require significant judgment in determining both the likelihood and estimated amount of potential losses. We base our accruals on the best information available at the time, taking into account the specific facts and circumstances of each matter, the merits of our defenses, and the impact of negotiations, settlements, regulatory proceedings, rulings, and advice of legal counsel. Our estimates are subject to change as additional information becomes available and as matters develop, and we have in prior periods revised our assessments based on updated information. We currently intend to retain all available funds and any future earnings to finance the operation and expansion of our business and do not expect to pay any dividends in the foreseeable future. Any future determination to declare cash dividends will be made at the discretion of our board of directors, subject to applicable laws, and will depend on a number of factors, including our financial condition, results of operations, capital requirements, contractual restrictions, general business conditions, and other factors that our board of directors may deem relevant. In addition, the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement place certain limitations on the amount of cash dividends we can pay, even if no amounts are currently outstanding under the credit facility.

 
339 3. 【Status of Corporate Governance, etc.】 (1) 【Overview of Corporate Governance】 Our Governance Structure and Its Goals Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative super intelligence (Note) exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a PBC gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose. In addition, a financially disinterested LTBT, which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission. (Note) For purposes of this document, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably. Public Benefit Corporation We are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law, a structure that enables our commitment to AI safety and responsibility. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and to operate in a responsible and sustainable manner. As a PBC, we are required to balance (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. This requires our board of directors to weigh multiple factors, including relevant long- and short-term externalities of decisions, alongside the pecuniary interests of our stockholders. To date, we have found that the safety and societal benefit of AI and consideration of the best interests of all key stakeholder groups have generally aligned with our long-term commercial success and stockholders’ long- term monetary interests. However, as a PBC, we may make decisions that we believe appropriately balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, but that negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business or the market price of our Class A common stock. There is limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, and there is therefore uncertainty as to how a court would view our directors’ balancing of these potentially competing interests. For a discussion of these risks, please refer to “Section 3: Business Conditions—3: Business and Other Risks—Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock” and “Section 3: Business Conditions—3: Business and Other Risks—As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” In measuring our public benefit performance, our board of directors will consider the objectives set forth in our five mission pillars: that the technical problems of AI safety are solved, that AI safety is a universal 340 practice backstopped by law, that AI strengthens democracy and global stability, that AI expands prosperity and human flourishing, and that AI’s benefits are shared by everyone. We may also address the additional interests of our customers, partners, employees, and other stakeholder constituencies that we may identify from time to time. Neither our amended and restated certificate of incorporation nor our amended and restated bylaws will require that we measure our public benefit performance against an objective third-party standard, and our board of directors will be responsible for establishing and overseeing the standards by which to measure our public benefit performance against these objectives. We currently expect that our objectives and standards will be qualitative in nature and may evolve over time as our business grows and as our understanding of our public benefit impact develops. As required by Section 366(b) of the DGCL, we will provide our stockholders no less than biennially with a statement assessing our promotion of the Company Purpose and of the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct. The statement will set out our objectives and standards and describe the actions we have taken. We intend to make the statement available to stockholders and the public through our website. We also expect to demonstrate our progress towards these goals by continuing to publish evidence-based research on our website regarding our work and its impact. Long-Term Benefit Trust We created the LTBT, which was designed to ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. The LTBT is organized as a common law “noncharitable purpose trust” under Delaware law and governed by the Long-Term Benefit Trust Amended and Restated Trust Agreement (the “Trust Agreement”). The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of Trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Class T common stock has no economic rights. Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors. While the LTBT has significant influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and remove Class T directors, neither the LTBT nor the Trustees have decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of the company. The LTBT’s role is to select directors who are well equipped to responsibly balance our tripartite goals as a PBC, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance. Certain actions, such as a merger, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all of our assets, will require the approval of our board of directors pursuant to Delaware law, a majority of whom are elected by the LTBT. Election and Removal of Directors As the sole holder of Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock will not vote on the election or removal of directors elected by the holders of our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, who will be elected or removed solely by the holders of Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together. For a discussion of the members of

 
341 our board of directors who are currently Class T directors and those who will be Class T directors upon the completion of this Offering, see the section titled “Management—Board of Directors.” Prior to nominating or removing a director, the nominating party must provide at least 30 days’ notice to our NGC, which notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Following the completion of this Offering, our NGC will be composed of one Class T director and two directors who are not Class T directors and will act by majority vote. With respect to one of the Class T director seats (the “Specified Class T Director”), the LTBT’s ability to nominate that director, to remove that director without cause, or to change the director designated as the Specified Class T Director is subject to the concurrence of our NGC. If our NGC does not concur with such nomination, removal, or change in designation within 15 days of receiving notice, the matter will be submitted to a vote of the holders of our Class E common stock unless the LTBT elects to withdraw the notice. If submitted to a vote of the holders of Class E common stock, approval of the LTBT’s proposal will require a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock). The LTBT may withdraw any notice of nomination, removal, or change in designation at any time before the taking of such a vote. Any Class T director, including the Specified Class T Director, may be removed for cause, which will be determined in accordance with Delaware law, without the concurrence of our NGC or the approval of the holders of our Class E common stock; provided, however, that each of the LTBT and the Founder LLC has agreed to provide 30 calendar days’ notice to the other stockholder and our NGC prior to effecting a removal of any director for cause. Changes to the LTBT and Class T Common Stock The terms of the LTBT and the rights of our Class T common stock may be amended as follows (any of which, the “Trust Amendment Threshold”): • if the Trustees are voting in favor of such amendments, upon approval of 80% of the authorized members of our board of directors and 80% of the Trustees then in office (in each case, rounded up or down to the nearest whole number (any exact 0.5 rounding up)); • if our Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of such amendments: (4) until the third anniversary of the completion of this Offering, upon approval by (i) our Class F common stock acting pursuant to the unanimous approval of the Continuing Founders, (ii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of 40% of our outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by our outstanding Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or (5) at any time, upon approval by (i) our Class F common stock acting by decision of 66 2/3% of the Continuing Founders (rounded up to the nearest whole number), (ii) 75% of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or • if no Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of such amendments, upon approval of 85% of our outstanding shares of Class A common stock. 342 In addition, our Class T common stock may be redeemed by us for no consideration upon approval of persons comprising the above thresholds for amendments of the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock. Trustees of the LTBT The LTBT is governed by five Trustees. The Trustees have the authority to appoint the Trustees by majority vote of the Trustees then in office and to remove the Trustees by majority vote of the total number of authorized Trustees or by the unanimous approval of the other Trustees then in office and the approval of our NGC, provided that the LTBT must provide at least 30 days’ prior written notice to our NGC before effecting any such appointment or removal. The notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Trustees may also be removed by order of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware upon petition by a person designated by the Trust Agreement as having the power to enforce the agreement if a Trustee has engaged in disqualifying conduct and removal would best serve the purpose of the LTBT. Trustees will serve annual terms, and there is no limit to the number of terms a Trustee may serve. Trustees are selected based on their expertise in areas relevant to the LTBT’s purpose, including AI safety, national security, public policy, social enterprise, and related fields. In practice to date, the Trustees and company executives have collaborated closely on sourcing, interviewing, and selecting Trustees. Of the five authorized seats for Trustees, one is currently vacant. Dr. Neil “Buddy” Shah has served as a Trustee and Chair of the LTBT since June 2023. Dr. Shah will also serve as an initial manager of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Dr. Shah has served as Chief Executive Officer of the Clinton Health Access Initiative (“CHAI”), a global health organization focused on improving access to health services in low- and middle-income countries, since June 2022. Prior to joining CHAI, Dr. Shah served as Managing Director of GiveWell, a nonprofit organization focused on directing charitable capital to cost-effective global health and development programs, and, before that, as co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of IDinsight, a global advisory, data analytics, and research organization. He holds an A.B. in Economics from Harvard University, an M.D. with an emphasis in global health policy from Albert Einstein College of Medicine, and an M.P.A. in International Development from Harvard Kennedy School of Government. Dr. Shah was selected to serve as a Trustee because of his expertise in global health, impact measurement, and social enterprise, and his experience evaluating the long-term societal effects of large-scale programs. Richard Fontaine has served as a Trustee since April 2025. Mr. Fontaine has served as Chief Executive Officer of the Center for a New American Security (“CNAS”), a bipartisan national security research institution, since February 2019, having previously served as President of CNAS from 2012 to 2019 and as Senior Fellow from 2009 to 2012. Mr. Fontaine serves concurrently as Executive Director of the Trilateral Commission’s North America group, a position he has held since July 2019. Prior to joining CNAS and the Trilateral Commission, Mr. Fontaine served as foreign policy advisor to Senator John McCain, including as advisor to the McCain 2008 presidential campaign and subsequently as Minority Deputy Staff Director of the Senate Armed Services Committee. He has also served as Associate Director for Near Eastern Affairs at the National Security Council, and he has held positions at the U.S. Department of State and on the staff of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Mr. Fontaine holds a B.A. in International Relations from Tulane University and an M.A. in International Affairs from the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.

 
343 Mr. Fontaine was selected to serve as a Trustee because of his extensive background in foreign policy and national security, and he will address the growing intersection between AI capabilities and geopolitical risks. Dr. Ben S. Bernanke has served as a Trustee since June 2026. Since 2014, Dr. Bernanke has been a Distinguished Fellow in Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution, a public policy research organization. Dr. Bernanke served as Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System from February 2006 to January 2014, having been appointed to that position by Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama. Prior to serving as Federal Reserve Chairman, Dr. Bernanke served as chairman of the President’s Council of Economic Advisers and as a member of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Before his government service, Dr. Bernanke was a professor of economics and public affairs at Princeton University, where he also chaired the Economics Department. Subsequent to his government service, Dr. Bernanke served as chair of the Global Advisory Board of and senior advisor to Pacific Investment Management Company, a global fixed income investment management firm. Dr. Bernanke holds an A.B. in Economics from Harvard University and a Ph.D. in Economics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Dr. Bernanke was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2022. Dr. Bernanke was selected to serve as a Trustee because of his expertise in macroeconomics, financial systems, and institutional governance, and his experience overseeing large, consequential institutions during periods of systemic risk and uncertainty. Dr. Christopher Stubbs has served as a Trustee since October 2026. Dr. Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard University, where he has been a member of the faculty since 2003. At Harvard, he served as Senior Advisor for AI to the Faculty of Arts and Sciences from 2024 to 2026, as Dean of Science in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences from 2018 to 2024, and as Chair of the Department of Physics from 2007 to 2010. Prior to joining Harvard, he held faculty positions at the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University of Washington. As a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, Dr. Stubbs shared in the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe, work for which he and his colleagues received the Gruber Prize in Cosmology and the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He also served as the inaugural project scientist of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Dr. Stubbs is a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists that advises the U.S. government on matters of national security. He holds a B.Sc. in Physics from the University of Virginia and a Ph.D. in Physics from the University of Washington. Dr. Stubbs was selected to serve as a Trustee because of his expertise in experimental physics and the application of AI to science and education, and his experience leading scientific projects across academia, government, and the national laboratories. Certain Relationships and Transactions with the LTBT and its Trustees We provide funding to the LTBT, which holds all of our Class T common stock, to support its operations and the compensation of its Trustees. In the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, we paid $2,716,750, $0, and $906,089 to the LTBT, respectively. During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we paid $8,425,213 to the LTBT. The LTBT is accounted for as a consolidated variable interest entity (“VIE”) on our balance sheet (Please refer to “Section 6: Financial Information—1: Financial Documents— Consolidated Financial Statements—Note 1: Description of Business and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies”). The Trust Agreement limits Trustee compensation to a reasonable cash amount fixed annually by the Trustees. Each Trustee receives annual cash compensation of $400,000 for their service as a Trustee. In 344 addition, Dr. Shah receives annual cash compensation of $25,000 for his service as the Chair of the LTBT. Trustee compensation will not vary with or be conditioned upon the profits or any action or inaction of our company. The policies of the LTBT prohibit a Trustee from directly purchasing or holding any of our securities. In addition, in August 2026, we made a $450,000 charitable donation to CNAS, of which Mr. Fontaine is the Chief Executive Officer. The donation will be used to support CNAS research examining how AI is reshaping global competition, national security, international security, democratic governance, and other issues related to emerging technology and security. Founder Voting Structure We believe that our seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah, as a group, are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission. Our co-founders have been instrumental in building our leadership position and establishing the mission-driven values that define our company. In addition, Dr. Amodei serves as our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors and Ms. Amodei serves as our President and Chairperson of our board of directors. Their long-term strategic vision has been critical to our success and will continue to guide our future. In our highly competitive industry, success requires visionary leadership, strong direction, and the kind of decisiveness necessary to make bold investments, pursue transformative opportunities, and compete effectively against formidable competitors, while also balancing the pecuniary interests of our stockholders with the Company Purpose and the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct. We believe that our success depends in part on establishing a capital structure that enables our co-founders, management, and board of directors to focus on strategic initiatives that create lasting value for our stakeholders, rather than facing pressure to prioritize short-term results or purely pecuniary objectives at the expense of our long-term vision and mission. Immediately prior to the completion of this Offering, we will issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to the Founder LLC, a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members and that will be managed by its members. Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will be voted by the Founder LLC in a manner determined in accordance with the Founder LLC Agreement. Generally, the Founder LLC will vote as determined by a majority of the members of the Founder LLC entitled to vote thereunder. Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members. Upon the incapacity or death of any of our co-founders, a successor member may be admitted to the Founder LLC until the tenth anniversary of the completion of this Offering. We refer to our seven co- founders and any successors in the Founder LLC as “Continuing Founders.” When there have been fewer than three Continuing Founders (not including any successor member who is a “Non-Qualifying Member” as defined in the Founder LLC Agreement) for 90 consecutive calendar days, a 450-day transition period will commence (the “Class F Transition Period”). Upon completion of the Class F Transition Period, all of our Class F common stock and Class E common stock then issued and outstanding will be redeemed by us for no consideration and certain other governance changes will take effect.

 
345 Regardless of the length of time that has elapsed since the completion of this Offering or the circumstances that resulted in the removal of a Continuing Founder, one or more successor members may be admitted to the Founder LLC during the Class F Transition Period as needed to ensure that there are three Continuing Founders serving until completion of the Class F Transition Period. The admission of any successor member during the Class F Transition Period will not cure the event that commenced the Class F Transition Period or extend the Class F Transition Period. For additional information, see the section titled “Description of Capital Stock.” A Continuing Founder will be removed from the Founder LLC upon the earliest to occur of (i) such Continuing Founder’s resignation as a member of the Founder LLC; (ii) such Continuing Founder’s death or incapacity; (iii) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, such original co-founder’s ceasing to hold (together with such original co-founder’s related holders) on any record date for a vote of our stockholders a number of shares of Class A common stock (including shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities) equal to at least 2% of the shares of Class A common stock held by such original co-founder and their related holders as of the completion of this Offering; (iv) such Continuing Founder’s removal for “cause” (as defined in the Founder LLC Agreement), which includes specified competitive activities described in the Founder LLC Agreement; (v) with respect to any successor member admitted to the Founder LLC prior to the commencement of the Class F Transition Period, other than a successor member who is a member during the Class F Transition Period, the tenth anniversary of the completion of this Offering; or (vi) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, the commencement of a leave of absence approved by a Supermajority of the other Continuing Founders, which may not be approved during the Class F Transition Period or if the grant of the leave of absence would itself cause the Class F Transition Period to commence. Each Continuing Founder will be entitled to one vote when determining how our Class F common stock will be voted. If a majority of the Continuing Founders cannot agree on how our Class F common stock will be voted, then our Class F common stock will generally be voted proportionately with the votes of our Class A common stock cast on the matter (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock). With respect to certain matters, our Class F common stock will be voted “for” the proposal only if a greater threshold of Continuing Founders agree, and if the greater threshold is not met, our Class F common stock will be voted “against” the proposal. Please refer to “Section 1: Overview of the Legal System in the Home Country—1: Overview of Corporate Structure and Related Matters—(2) Corporate Arrangements under the Articles of Incorporation and Other Governing Documents of the Filing Company—(a) Summary of Information Regarding Shares—Description of Capital Stock—Class F Common Stock Voting Mechanics.” The Founder LLC Agreement will not govern the voting of any shares of our Class A common stock held by the co-founders or their related holders. Each co-founder (or their related holders) will be able to vote shares of our Class A common stock held by them in their discretion, regardless of the manner in which the Founder LLC will vote our Class F common stock. The voting power of our Class F common stock will not be impacted by future issuances of our capital stock that may cause economic or voting dilution to stockholders, such as issuances for capital raising purposes, acquisitions, or employee compensation. This structure will allow the Founder LLC to determine the outcome of matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally, including the election of those directors not elected by the LTBT, certain amendments to our organizational documents, and the approval by our stockholders of any merger, consolidation, sale of substantially all our assets, or other major corporate transaction requiring stockholder approval. 346 Our Co-Founders Our seven co-founders co-founded Anthropic in January 2021. Philanthropy We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. We intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier intelligence is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed, which we refer to as our public benefit initiatives. These initiatives include the Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the future Public Benefit Issuances. In addition, our co-founders have each pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes. For additional information regarding these pledges, including related risks, see the section titled “Section 3: Business Conditions—3: Business and Other Risks—Risks Related to Ownership of our Class A Common Stock.” Separate from the co-founders’ pledges, we also maintain a donation matching program through which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards toward charitable giving, which we match with shares of our Class N common stock. Further, certain donor-advised funds may from time to time receive donations of shares directly from us or from one or more of our stockholders, and we are party to certain irrevocable proxy agreements with such donor-advised funds, as described under “Section 3: Business Conditions—5: Material Contracts—Irrevocable Proxy Agreements.” Class E Common Stock Our Class E common stock will not have any right to vote except on certain specified matters (or as otherwise required by law): the nomination or proposed removal of the Specified Class T Director or a change in the director designated as the Specified Class T Director (in circumstances where our NGC does not concur with the LTBT’s proposed action) and certain proposals to amend the terms of the LTBT and the rights of our Class T common stock or to redeem our Class T common stock. When voting upon a proposal to nominate or remove the Specified Class T Director or a change in the director designated as the Specified Class T Director (in circumstances where our NGC does not concur with the LTBT’s proposed action), the requisite approval of our Class E common stock will require a majority of votes cast by our Class E common stock and quorum will require the presence, in person or by proxy, of a majority of outstanding shares of Class E common stock. When voting on a proposal to amend the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock or to redeem our Class T common stock, in addition to the requisite approval of our Class A common stock as described more fully in the section titled “—Long-Term Benefit Trust—Changes to the LTBT and Class T Common Stock,” the requisite approval of our Class E common stock will require: • until the third anniversary of the completion of this Offering, if our Class F common stock is acting pursuant to the unanimous approval of the Continuing Founders, a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of 40% of our outstanding Class E common stock); or 348 • at any time when our Class F common stock remains outstanding, 75% of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock). Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this Offering, will authorize Class E common stock, which will be issued to our employees as follows: (i) one share of Class E common stock for each six months of employment completed with us and (ii) one share of Class E common stock for each share of Class A common stock that such employee has pledged to donate through our donation matching program, or any similar program we may establish in the future. The timing for issuing Class E common stock will be determined after the completion of this Offering. Our co-founders will not receive any shares of Class E common stock, and to the extent that a holder of Class E common stock later serves as a successor to any co-founder’s interest in the Founder LLC, that holder will not be able to vote any Class E common stock they hold during the period of such service. Following an employee’s separation from employment with us other than for cause, one-half of such employee’s then-outstanding shares of Class E common stock will be automatically redeemed by us annually, and all of such employee’s shares will be automatically redeemed upon such employee’s death, incapacity, termination for cause, or commencement of service with a direct competitor. All shares of Class E common stock will also be automatically redeemed at such time as no Class F common stock remains outstanding. Any redemption of Class E common stock will be made for no consideration. Board Governance Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors. Immediately prior to the completion of this Offering, we will enter into the Stockholders’ Agreement with the LTBT and the Founder LLC, under which they will agree to vote their shares and take other actions to give effect to the board composition, director nomination, and director removal provisions described in our governing documents. Collectively, the LTBT and the Founder LLC will have the ability to elect all members of our board of directors. Regardless of the class or classes of stock by which a director is elected, there is no limit to the number of terms a director may serve. While the LTBT has significant influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, neither the LTBT nor the Trustees have decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of the company. The LTBT’s role is to select directors who are well equipped to make decisions in furtherance of the responsible balancing of the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance. The Trustees aim to choose directors who have the necessary business skills, experience, and expertise to oversee the management of our business effectively and in a manner that responsibly balances (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. The Founder LLC will also have significant influence over our business and affairs through its ability to vote our Class F common stock, which is entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally. The Founder LLC will be able to elect and remove the directors who are not Class T directors and determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally (including the approval of any merger, sale of our company, or other significant corporate transaction requiring stockholder approval) for the foreseeable future.

 
349 We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As such, we are permitted to opt out of compliance with certain Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Accordingly, if we elect not to comply with certain requirements, you will not have the same protections afforded to stockholders of companies that are subject to all of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Although we qualify as a “controlled company,” we do not expect to rely on this exemption except with respect to our NGC, which will not consist entirely of independent directors. Our board of directors currently consists of a majority of independent directors and our audit and compensation committees currently consist entirely of independent directors. We believe that Ms. Amodei is qualified to serve on our board of directors because of the perspective and experience she brings through her deep expertise in the AI industry and as our President and as a co- founder. Krishna Rao. Mr. Rao has served as our Chief Financial Officer since April 2024. Prior to joining Anthropic, Mr. Rao served as Chief Financial Officer at Fanatics Commerce, an online sports merchandise and retail platform, from May 2023 to April 2024. Before that, he served as the Chief Financial Officer of Cedar, a healthcare technology company, from July 2021 to May 2023. From October 2015 to July 2021, Mr. Rao held several key positions at Airbnb, a global vacation rental and hospitality platform, including Global Head of Corporate & Business Development and Director of Financial Planning & Analysis. Prior to Airbnb, Mr. Rao was a Principal in the Private Equity Group at Blackstone, a global investment firm, from September 2011 to September 2015. Mr. Rao began his career as a strategy consultant at Bain, a global management consulting firm, from September 2005 to July 2008. Mr. Rao holds a J.D. from Yale Law School and an A.B. in Economics from Harvard College. Non-Employee Directors Reed Hastings. Mr. Hastings has served as a member of our board of directors since May 2025. Prior to Netflix, Mr. Hastings founded Pure Software, a software development tools company, in 1991 and served as its Chief Executive Officer until its acquisition by Rational Software in 1997. We believe that Mr. Hastings is qualified to serve as a member of our board of directors because of his extensive board experience at major technology companies, his demonstrated commitment to responsible innovation and its societal impact, his deep understanding of technology’s transformative potential, and his philanthropic focus on education and AI’s impact on humanity. Christopher Liddell. Mr. Liddell has served as a member of our board of directors since February 2026.
