Legal Matters The Company is involved from time to time in claims, proceedings, and litigation, including the following: In August 2024, various authors filed suit against the Company alleging infringement of copyrighted books in the case of Bartz et al v. Anthropic in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (“Bartz”). The complaint alleged, among other things, copyright infringement related to the use of literary works used in the training of the Company’s large language models. The complaint sought certification as a class action, unspecified amounts of damages, injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees, costs, and interest. The Company reached a settlement in the amount of $1.5 billion and the interest earned thereon, which was approved by the district court in July 2026. The Company paid $300 million during the year ended December 31, 2025 and recorded liabilities of $1.2 billion in accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities on the consolidated balance sheets as of June 30, 2026. In October 2023, Concord Music Group et al. filed a complaint against the Company in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee (“Concord I”). The complaint alleges, among other things, that in the process of building and operating the Company models, the Company unlawfully copied and disseminated copyrighted lyrics controlled by the publishers. It also asserts a claim for unlawful removal of copyright management information. The complaint seeks unspecified amounts of damages, injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees, costs, and interest. The case was later transferred to the Northern District of California. Fact discovery in the case closed in November 2025. In March 2026, the publishers filed for a partial summary judgment. The Company responded to that motion and filed its own motion for summary judgment in April 2026. A summary judgment hearing is scheduled in October 2026. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in this matter. The Company is also subject to three copyright actions in Canada. In May and July 2025, two putative class actions were filed on behalf of purported classes of Canadian authors - one in British Columbia ("MacKinnon") on behalf of all Canadian authors, and one in Québec ("Grescoe") on behalf of all Québec authors - each alleging violations of Canada's Copyright Act based on the Company's copying and use of copyrighted books to train its large language models. Grescoe has been stayed pending a final judgment in MacKinnon. In July 2026, La Presse Inc., a Québec news publisher, filed a copyright infringement action against the Company in the Québec Superior Court alleging that the Company reproduced its journalistic works in the data used to train the Company's models. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in these matters.

 
497 In June 2025, Reddit, Inc. filed suit against the Company in California state court alleging various claims, including breach of contract and trespass to chattels, stemming from allegations about the Company’s use of Reddit data in building and operating its models. In July 2025, the Company filed a notice of removal of the case to federal court. The case was remanded to state court in March 2026. The Company filed a demurrer to the complaint in June 2026, a hearing on the demurrer was held in August 2026, and no order has yet been issued. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in this matter. Between January and August 2026, four complaints were filed against the Company in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California by various music publishers and their affiliated entities, including Concord Music Group, Universal Music Publishing Group, ABKCO Music, BMG Rights Management (US) LLC, Round Hill Music LP, Sony Music Publishing (US) LLC, and Warner Chappell Music, Inc. (collectively, the “Music Publisher Matters”). The complaints allege, among other things, that the Company unlawfully copied the plaintiffs’ copyrighted song lyrics and musical compositions, and assert claims for direct and indirect copyright infringement based on both the acquisition and use of copyrighted materials to train the Company's large language models and the outputs of those models, as well as claims for removal of copyright management information. Certain of the complaints also assert claims for unauthorized downloading and distribution of copyrighted works, circumvention of technological protection measures, and violations of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, and certain of the complaints also name two Company executives as defendants. The complaints seek unspecified amounts of damages, injunctive relief, attorneys' fees, costs, and interest. These matters are in preliminary stages: the Company's motion to dismiss is pending in one matter, a second matter is temporarily stayed with a responsive pleading due in October 2026, and responsive pleadings have not yet been filed in the two matters commenced in August 2026. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in these matters. The Company is subject to several putative class action complaints alleging that it markets and sells subscription plans for Claude through false, misleading, and deceptive advertising practices. These matters are generally in early stages. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously. Various authors have opted out of the class action and settlement reached in Bartz and filed individual suits against the Company, generally alleging claims of direct copyright infringement, contributory copyright infringement, and removal of copyright management information related to the use of literary works used in the training of the Company’s large language models. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing in these remaining opt-out actions and intends to defend itself vigorously in all matters. These proceedings remain in various stages. The Company has received notices, demands, and other communications from several authors and individual rights-holders, publishers (including, but not limited to, books, news, and music publishers), platforms and website operators, and trade associations, in the United States and other jurisdictions (collectively, “Rights-Holders”) alleging unauthorized acquisition or use of content, removal of copyright management information, violation of terms of service, and violation of copyrights. Some Rights-Holders have also sought to have their content removed from the Company’s training corpus or sought more information on how their content was used in the development of the Company’s models. Other Rights-Holders have argued that the mere crawling of their sites has harmed them. The Company expects to continue to receive similar notices from Rights- Holders, which may ultimately result in litigation against the Company. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in these matters. In addition, from time to time, the Company is subject to claims, litigation, and other proceedings, including potential regulatory proceedings, involving patent and other intellectual property matters, taxes, labor and employment, competition, privacy and data protection, consumer protection, commercial disputes, and services offered by the Company, and other matters. The outcomes of the Company’s legal proceedings and other contingencies are inherently unpredictable, subject to significant uncertainties, and could be material to its operating results and cash flows for a particular period. The Company evaluates, on a regular basis, developments in its legal proceedings and other contingencies that could affect the amount of liability, including amounts in excess of any previous accruals and reasonably possible losses disclosed, and makes adjustments and changes to its accruals and disclosures as appropriate. For the matters the Company discloses that do not include an estimate of the amount of loss or range of losses, such an estimate is not possible or is immaterial, and the Company may be unable to estimate the possible loss or range of losses that could potentially result from the application of non-monetary remedies. Until the final resolution of such matters, if any of the Company’s estimates and assumptions change or prove to have been incorrect, the Company may experience losses in excess of the amounts recorded, which could have a material effect on its business, consolidated financial position, results of operations, or cash flows. 12. (2) Litigation Please refer to “Section 6: Financial Information—1: Financial Documents—Consolidated Financial Statements— Note 13: Commitments and Contingencies.” 4. 【Major Differences in Accounting Principles and Practices between the United States of America and Japan】 The accompanying consolidated financial statements have been prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, and accordingly, differ from those prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in Japan. Major differences are summarized below. (1) Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets In the United States of America, under the acquisition method of accounting for business combinations, the cost of an acquisition, including the fair value of liabilities assumed, in excess of the fair value of net assets acquired on the acquisition date is recorded as goodwill. In accordance with ASC 350, “Intangibles – Goodwill and Other”, goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets are not amortized, and are evaluated for impairment at least annually or if a triggering event occurs. ASC 350 also requires that reporting units be identified for the purpose of assessing potential future impairments of goodwill. In Japan, “Accounting Standard for Business Combinations” is applied, and under this standard goodwill is amortized on a straight-line basis or other reasonable basis over its useful life, which is not more than 20 years. However, when the amount of goodwill is not significant, it may be charged to income for the year goodwill is generated. Goodwill is also an asset governed by “Accounting Standard for Impairment of Fixed Assets,” and is required to be tested for impairment under the standard, even when it is amortized. (2) Consolidation of Variable Interest Entities In the United States of America, ASC 810, “Consolidation”, provides for the criteria for consideration in determining whether a variable interest entity should be consolidated by a business entity, and further considerations for a reporting entity to be consolidated by their primary beneficiaries. In Japan, generally, subsidiaries should be included in consolidated financial statements when (a) a majority of the other company’s voting rights are owned or (b) a significant amount of voting rights is owned along with certain

 
501 evidence of control over decision making of the board even if a majority of the other company’s voting rights are not owned. In addition, Practical Issues Task Force (“PITF”) No. 20 “Practical Solution on Application of Control Criteria and Influence Criteria to Investment Associations” is applied to the consolidation of investment associations. The PITF requires companies to consolidate investment associations if certain criteria in relation to control of or influence over the investment associations are met. However, there is no explicit provision regarding the consolidation of VIEs. (3) Financial Instruments with Characteristics of both Liabilities and Equity In the United States of America, ASC 480, “Distinguishing Liabilities from Equity” establishes standards for how an issuer classifies and measures certain financial instruments with characteristics of both liabilities and equity. It requires that an issuer classify a financial instrument that is within its scope as a liability (or an asset in some circumstances) because that financial instrument embodies an obligation of the issuer. In Japan, no comprehensive accounting standard has been established for financial instruments with characteristics of both liabilities and equity. (4) Accounting for Uncertainty in Income Taxes In the United States of America, ASC 740, “Income Taxes” clarifies the accounting and reporting for uncertainties in income tax law. This Interpretation prescribes a comprehensive model for the financial statement recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of uncertain tax positions taken or expected to be taken in income tax returns. In Japan, no accounting standard has been established for uncertainty in tax position. (5) Fair Value Option In the United States of America, under ASC 825, “Financial Instruments”, an entity may decide whether to elect the fair value option for each eligible item on its election date. Alternatively, an entity may elect the fair value option according to a preexisting policy for specified types of eligible items. In Japan, there is no fair value option for financial assets and financial liabilities. (6) Leases In the United States of America, ASC 842, “Leases” (the lease standard) requires the recognition of lease assets and lease liabilities on the balance sheet for all lease obligations and disclosing key information about leasing arrangements. The new lease standard requires the recognition of lease assets and lease liabilities by lessees for arrangements that are classified as operating leases. In Japan, the “Accounting Standards for Lease” is applied. However, only finance leases are recognized on the balance sheet and operating leases are accounted for off-balance sheet. In addition, in Japan, ASBJ Statement No. 34, “Accounting Standard for Leases,” was issued on September 13, 2024. Under this standard, lessee lease transactions are not classified as finance leases or operating leases; instead, right-of-use assets and lease liabilities are recognized for all lease transactions of lessees. This standard is effective for fiscal years beginning on or after April 1, 2027, with earlier application permitted. 502 (7) Stock Compensation In the United States of America, ASC 718, “Compensation – Stock Compensation” requires that share-based payment awards, including stock options and restricted stock units, be measured based on the grant-date fair value of the award, with compensation cost recognized over the requisite service period. Excess tax benefits and tax deficiencies arising upon settlement of awards are recognized as a reduction of, or an increase to, the provision for income taxes in the period in which they occur and are classified as cash flows from operating activities. In addition, cash paid by an employer in connection with shares withheld for tax-withholding purposes is classified as a cash outflow from financing activities. In Japan, ASBJ Statement No. 8, “Accounting Standard for Share-based Payment” is applied. Under this standard, unlisted companies are permitted to measure stock options based on their intrinsic value at the grant date instead of fair value. In addition, Japanese GAAP does not contain explicit guidance corresponding to the accounting treatment of excess tax benefits and tax deficiencies related to share-based compensation, or the classification of the related cash flows, as described above under U.S. GAAP.

 
503 Section 7 【Trends in Foreign Exchange Rates】 Since the exchange rate between the currency used in the presentation of the Company’s financial statements (U.S. dollars) and the Japanese yen was published in two or more daily newspapers in Japan that report on current affairs during the reference fiscal year, this disclosure is omitted. 504 Section 8 【Overview of Shareholder Services, Etc. of the Filing Company in Japan】 1. 【Overview of Share Administration in Japan】 (1) Locations for Share Transfer and Transfer Agents In Japan, there is no designated location for handling transfers of Class A Common Stock, nor is there a transfer agent. Acquirers of Class A Common Stock (hereinafter referred to as “Beneficial Shareholders”) are required to enter into Foreign Securities Trading Account Terms and Conditions (hereinafter referred to as the “Terms and Conditions”) with the financial instruments business operator that served as the point of contact for the acquisition (hereinafter referred to as the “Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator”). Pursuant to these Terms and Conditions, a foreign securities trading account (hereinafter referred to as the “Trading Account”) is opened in the shareholder’s name. All matters concerning the execution of trades, settlement of trade proceeds, custody of securities, and other transactions related to the shares shall be processed through this Trading Account. In this case, all matters regarding the execution of trades, settlement of trade proceeds, and other payments related to share transactions shall be processed in accordance with the respective provisions of the relevant agreement. (2) Benefits for Beneficial Shareholders Not applicable (3) Restrictions on Transfer of Shares There are no transfer restrictions on Class A Common Stock. (4) Other Matters Concerning Share Administration (i) Custody of Share Certificates Class A common stock held through a Trading Account is registered in the name of a nominee of a local clearing organization through a custodian in the United States acting as an agent for the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator (hereinafter referred to as the “Local Custodian”) and is kept by the Local Custodian. (ii) Record Date for Dividends, etc. The beneficial owner entitled to receive dividends, etc., from the Company is the person who beneficially owns Class A Common Stock as of the record date set by the Company’s Board of Directors for the payment of dividends, etc. (iii) End of Fiscal Year December 31 of each year (iv) Public Notice to Beneficial Owners In Japan, no public notices regarding Class A Common Stock are issued. (v) Fees for Shareholder Services Beneficial shareholders shall pay a management fee for maintaining a Trading Account as a fee and expense for the procedures and actions specified in the Terms and Conditions, in accordance with the provisions of the Contact

 
505 Financial Instruments Business Operator. Furthermore, beneficial shareholders may also be required to pay other expenses specified in the Terms and Conditions. 2. 【Methods for Exercising Shareholder Rights in Japan】 (1) Procedures for the Exercise of Voting Rights by Beneficial Shareholders The exercise of voting rights is carried out by the nominee of the local clearing organization through the Local Custodian, based on instructions provided by the beneficial shareholders through the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator. However, if a beneficial shareholder does not provide instructions, the nominee of the local clearing organization will not exercise voting rights for the Class A common stock held for the benefit of such beneficial shareholder. (2) Procedures for Claiming Dividends (i) Procedures for the Payment of Cash Dividends In accordance with the Terms and Conditions, cash dividends shall be received in a lump sum by the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator from the nominee of the local clearing organization via the Local Custodian and delivered to the beneficial shareholders through their Trading Accounts. (ii) Procedures for the Delivery of Stock Dividends, etc. Class A common stocks allocated through stock splits are registered in the name of the nominee of the local clearing organization via the Local Custodian, and the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator processes such Class A common stocks through Trading Accounts. However, fractional shares of less than one unit will be sold by the Company’s agent or the Local Custodian acting on behalf of the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator. The net proceeds thereof will be received in a lump sum by the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator from the nominee of the local clearing organization or from the Local Custodian via the Local Custodian and paid to the beneficial shareholders through their Trading Accounts. Class A common stocks allocated as stock dividends will be registered in the name of the nominee of the local clearing organization via the Local Custodian, and the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator will process or sell such Class A common stocks through Trading Accounts in accordance with its prescribed procedures and pay the net proceeds to the beneficial shareholders through their Trading Accounts. (3) Procedures for the Transfer of Shares Settlement between a beneficial shareholder and a Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator when the beneficial shareholder places a sell order for its holdings shall be made in Japanese yen or in a foreign currency within the scope handled by the Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator. The Contact Financial Instruments Business Operator shall settle Class A common stocks for over-the-counter transactions in Japan through customer deposits. In the event that the number of Class A common stocks held by a Local Custodian changes as a result of a transaction of Class A common stocks, the transfer procedures for the relevant Class A common stocks shall be carried out at the local clearing organization in which the Local Custodian participates. (4) Tax Treatment in Japan with Respect to Dividends, etc. An outline of the tax treatment in Japan concerning (i) income tax and local inhabitants tax on (x) dividends on the shares of the Company (hereinafter in this item referred to as the “Shares”) which will be received, through a payment handling agent in Japan, by a beneficial shareholder of the Company who is a Japanese resident individual and who acquired and is holding the Shares through his/her custody account opened in Japan (hereinafter in this item referred to as an “Individual Shareholder”) and (y) capital gains and losses to be 506 derived from the sale of such Shares by an Individual Shareholder, as well as (ii) inheritance tax implication in Japan when inheritance is commenced with respect to the Shares held by an Individual Shareholder, is as set forth below; provided, however, that the following descriptions with respect to income tax and local inhabitants tax, which are made on the assumptions that: (a) the Shares are listed, and (b) Individual Shareholders shall receive dividends on the Shares through payment handling agents in Japan, shall not be deemed to refer to any cases that may fail to satisfy either of the assumptions described above. The following descriptions shall be based on the Japanese tax laws and regulations, which are in force as of the date hereof, and refer solely to matters regarding tax treatment in general, which are subject to change due to amendments to any applicable laws and regulations. Furthermore, due to an application of the exemption provisions, the below-described matters may be handled differently in actual cases than as described below. Please be advised that each investor shall consult his/her own tax advisor with respect to any details of tax treatment and any concrete details of tax treatment applicable to each investor. (i) Tax on Dividends The balance of the dividends which will be received, through a payment handling agent in Japan, by an Individual Shareholder paid in the United States, less any United States withholding tax (if any) imposed thereon when such dividends are paid in the United States, will be subject to Japanese tax by way of withholding (with respect to local inhabitants tax, by way of special collection), at the normal tax rate of 20% (15% income tax and 5% local inhabitants tax), and in addition, up to December 31, 2047, the Special Reconstruction Income Tax (up to December 31, 2026, at the tax rate of 2.1% of the amount of the income tax, and from January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2047, at the tax rate of 1.1% of the amount of the income tax), and, from January 1, 2027, the Defense Special Income Tax (at the tax rate of 1% of the amount of the income tax); therefore, 20.315% in total (such withholding tax shall be hereinafter referred to as the “Payment Handling Agent Withholding Tax”). If the dividends on the Shares received by an Individual Shareholder are subject to the Payment Handling Agent Withholding Tax, the amount of such dividends may not be included in the taxable income to be reported in the final tax return, and therefore, with respect to the dividends on the Shares received by such Individual Shareholder, the Payment Handling Agent Withholding Tax may be made as the final taxation in Japan without including such dividends on the Shares in the taxable income which is subject to an aggregate taxation at the progressive rates in Japan (the combined marginal tax rate is 55% in the aggregate of income tax and local inhabitants tax plus, up to December 31, 2047, the Special Reconstruction Income Tax (up to December 31, 2026, at the tax rate of 2.1% of the amount of the income tax, and from January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2047, at the tax rate of 1.1% of the amount of the income tax), and, from January 1, 2027, the Defense Special Income Tax (at the tax rate of 1% of the amount of the income tax); therefore, the combined marginal tax rate shall be 55.945%). The Individual Shareholders will be able to select the separate self-assessment taxation with respect to dividend income on listed shares, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Separate Self-Assessment Taxation on Dividends”) for each taxable year, with respect to dividend income from listed shares, etc., including dividends on the Shares, in accordance with the provisions of the applicable laws and regulations. When the method of Separate Self- Assessment Taxation on Dividends is selected, the dividend income of listed shares, etc. that is subject to Separate Self-Assessment Taxation on Dividends shall not be included in the dividend income covered by the aggregate taxation procedures described above, and profit and loss aggregation in respect of such dividend income and capital loss derived from listed shares, etc. shall be permitted, in accordance with the requirements and limitations provided under the applicable laws and regulations. Furthermore, if the method of Separate Self-Assessment Taxation on Dividends is selected with respect to dividend income on listed shares, etc., including dividends on the Shares, (i) interests on specified government or company bonds, (ii) profits or losses from redemption of specified government or company bonds, and (iii) profits or losses from transfer of specified government or company bonds, shall be included, in principle, in the amounts subject to

 
507 the profit and loss aggregation. On the other hand, when an Individual Shareholder is subject to taxation under the aggregate taxation procedures described above, with respect to the dividends on the Shares, profit and loss aggregation in respect of such dividends and capital loss shall not be permitted. The tax rates to be applied in the event that the relevant Individual Shareholder selects the Separate Self-Assessment Taxation on Dividends with regard to the dividend income on listed shares, etc., including dividends on the Shares shall be the normal 20% (15% income tax and 5% local inhabitants tax), and in addition, up to December 31, 2047, the Special Reconstruction Income Tax (up to December 31, 2026, at the tax rate of 2.1% of the amount of the income tax, and from January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2047, at the tax rate of 1.1% of the amount of the income tax), and, from January 1, 2027, the Defense Special Income Tax (at the tax rate of 1% of the amount of the income tax), therefore the aggregate tax rate shall be 20.315%. It should be noted that, for individual local inhabitants tax for FY2024 (income for 2023) and thereafter, no taxation method different from that for income tax may be selected with respect to dividend income, etc. on listed shares, etc. In the event of final tax return for the total amount of the dividends on the Shares received by an Individual Shareholder which is subject to (a) an aggregate taxation at the progressive rates for income tax and (b) the Separate Self-Assessment Taxation on Dividends, the United States withholding tax imposed on the above- mentioned dividends on the Shares (if any) shall be subject to a foreign tax credit in accordance with the requirements and limitations provided under the applicable laws and regulations, and the amount of income tax withheld by way of the Payment Handling Agent Withholding Tax at the time of the delivery of the above-mentioned dividends on the Shares shall be deducted by the amount of income tax to be filed and paid pursuant to the requirements and limitations provided under the applicable laws and regulations. (ii) Capital Gains and Losses The tax treatment of capital gains and losses derived from a sale of the Shares by an Individual Shareholder is, in principle, the same as that of capital gains and losses derived from a purchase and sale of the listed shares, etc. of a domestic corporation. but is a Japanese national (limited to the cases in which such individual, a decedent or legator or a donor used to have a domicile in Japan at any time during the 10-year period preceding the 513 Report Of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm To the Stockholders and the Board of Directors of Anthropic, PBC Opinion on the Financial Statements We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheet of Anthropic, PBC (the Company) as of December 31, 2025, the related consolidated statement of operations, comprehensive loss, redeemable convertible preferred stock and stockholders’ deficit and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”). In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of the Company at December 31, 2025, and the results of its operations and its cash flows for the year then ended, in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. Basis for Opinion These financial statements are the responsibility of the Company’s management. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s financial statements based on our audit. We are a public accounting firm registered with the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States) (PCAOB) and are required to be independent with respect to the Company in accordance with the U.S. federal securities laws and the applicable rules and regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the PCAOB. We conducted our audit in accordance with the standards of the PCAOB. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement, whether due to error or fraud. The Company is not required to have, nor were we engaged to perform, an audit of its internal control over financial reporting. As part of our audit, we are required to obtain an understanding of internal control over financial reporting but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. Accordingly, we express no such opinion. Our audit included performing procedures to assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to error or fraud, and performing procedures that respond to those risks. Such procedures included examining, on a test basis, evidence regarding the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. Our audit also included evaluating the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall presentation of the financial statements. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion. Critical Audit Matters The critical audit matters communicated below are matters arising from the current period audit of the financial statements that were communicated or required to be communicated to the audit committee and that: (1) relate to accounts or disclosures that are material to the financial statements and (2) involved our especially challenging, subjective or complex judgments. The communication of critical audit matters does not alter in any way our opinion on the consolidated financial statements, taken as a whole, and we are not, by communicating the critical audit matters below, providing separate opinions on the critical audit matters or on the accounts or disclosures to which they relate. 514 Loss Contingencies Description of the Matter As further described in Note 13 to the consolidated financial statements, the Company is involved in various legal claims, proceedings and other regulatory and administrative proceedings, certain of which may include claims for substantial or indeterminate amounts of damages. The Company’s assessment of loss contingency matters requires significant judgment in determining both the likelihood and estimated amount of potential losses. Auditing the Company’s accounting for and disclosure of certain loss contingencies was especially challenging due to the significant judgment required to evaluate management’s assessments of the probability of loss and its estimate of the potential amounts or range of such losses. How We Addressed the Matter in Our Audit We performed audit procedures that included, among others, obtaining an understanding of the identification and evaluation of loss contingencies, including the Company’s assessment of the likelihood that a loss will be incurred and its ability to reasonably estimate the loss or range of possible losses. We read the Company’s board minutes, requested and received legal counsel confirmation letters, met with legal counsel to discuss the nature of certain matters and obtained representations from management on these matters. We also evaluated the appropriateness of the related disclosures included in the consolidated financial statements. Fair Value of Convertible Notes Description of the Matter The Company accounts for its convertible promissory notes at fair value. As discussed in Note 4 to the consolidated financial statements, the estimated fair value of convertible promissory notes as of December 31, 2025, was $41.7 billion and the recognized loss for the change in the fair value of the convertible promissory notes for the year ended December 31, 2025, was $34.5 billion. The Company estimated the fair value of the convertible promissory notes using a hybrid approach comprising a contingent claims analysis method and a common stock equivalent method which involved the use of complex and subjective estimates, judgments and assumptions. Auditing the Company’s estimated fair value of convertible notes was especially challenging due to the significant judgment required to assess management’s selection of the valuation methodology, determination of the relative weight applied to the contingent claims analysis and the common stock equivalent methods, which involved key judgments and assumptions, including the Company’s stage of development, likelihood of an initial public offering (IPO), need for and terms of financings, and secondary and other market transactions. The estimated fair value of the convertible notes is particularly sensitive to changes in the relative weight applied to the two valuation methods. How We Addressed the Matter in Our Audit We performed audit procedures that included, among others, evaluating the Company’s selection of the valuation methodology, evaluating the key judgments and assumptions noted above used by the Company’s valuation specialist, and evaluating the completeness and accuracy of the underlying data supporting the key judgments and assumptions. We involved our valuation specialists to assist with our evaluation of the methodology used by the Company and the key judgments and assumptions. Specifically, we focused on the Company’s determination of the relative weight applied to the contingent claims analysis and common stock equivalent methods and the key judgments and assumptions that affected the weighting. For example, we evaluated the stage of the Company’s development, inspected the Company’s written plans and internal presentations relating to an IPO process, and evaluated secondary and other market transactions during the period and their impact on the relative weight applied to the two valuation methods by the Company. /s/ Ernst & Young LLP We have served as the Company’s auditor since 2025. San Jose, California June 1, 2026, except for the effects of the stock split described in Note 1, which is as of September 30, 2026

 
515 Report Of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm Board of Directors and Stockholders Anthropic, PBC Opinion on the financial statements We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheet of Anthropic, PBC (a Delaware public benefit corporation) and subsidiaries (the “Company”) as of December 31, 2024, the related consolidated statements of operations, comprehensive loss, redeemable convertible preferred stock and stockholders’ deficit, and cash flows for each of the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023, and the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”). In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of the Company as of December 31, 2024, and the results of its operations and its cash flows for the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023, in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. Basis for opinion These consolidated financial statements are the responsibility of the Company’s management. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s consolidated financial statements based on our audits. We are a public accounting firm registered with the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States) (“PCAOB”) and are required to be independent with respect to the Company in accordance with the U.S. federal securities laws and the applicable rules and regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the PCAOB. We conducted our audits in accordance with the standards of the PCAOB. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement, whether due to error or fraud. The Company is not required to have, nor were we engaged to perform, an audit of its internal control over financial reporting. As part of our audits we are required to obtain an understanding of internal control over financial reporting but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. Accordingly, we express no such opinion. Our audits included performing procedures to assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to error or fraud, and performing procedures that respond to those risks. Such procedures included examining, on a test basis, evidence regarding the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. Our audits also included evaluating the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall presentation of the financial statements. We believe that our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion. /s/ GRANT THORNTON LLP We have served as the Company’s auditor from 2023 to 2025. San Francisco, California June 1, 2026 (except for the effects of the stock split described in Note 1, as to which the date is September 30, 2026)
